Unlike in other studies, the diagnosis of bone and bone marrow metastases was based on posttreatment scans during therapy, which has to be regarded as more sensitive than somatostatin receptor scintigraphy, and this may be one possible explanation for this high figure. Although in none of our patients was an absorbed dose of 2 Gy to the bone marrow reached, 22% had to stop therapy due to bone marrow-related events.

# Author manuscript
## Abstract
Targeted radionuclide therapies using  131 I-metaiodobenzylguanidine ( 131 I-MIBG) and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy ( 177 Lu or  90 Y) represent several of the therapeutic options in the management of metastatic or inoperable pheochromocytoma and/or paraganglioma (PPGL). Recently, high-specific-activity-131 I-MIBG therapy was approved by the FDA and both  177 Lu-DOTATATE and  131 I-MIBG therapy were recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines for the treatment of metastatic PPGL. However, a clinical dilemma often arises in the selection of targeted radionuclide therapy, especially when a patient can be treated with either type of therapy based on eligibility by MIBG and somatostatostatin receptor imaging. In order to address this problem, we assembled a group of international experts including oncologists, endocrinologists, and nuclear medicine physicians, with substantial experience in treating neuroendocrine tumors with targeted radionuclide therapies in order to develop consensus and provide expert recommendations and perspectives on how to select between these two therapeutic options for metastatic PPGL. This manuscript aims to summarize the survival outcomes of the available targeted radionuclide therapies, discuss personalized treatment strategies based on functional imaging scans, address practical issues including regulatory approvals, and compare toxicities and risk factors across treatments. Further, it discusses the emerging targeted radionuclide therapies.

The clinical decision making in the selection of patients for appropriate TRT should be personalized. Due to lack of controlled studies, we recommend a pragmatic approach based on expert consensus and opinion that is primarily based on the imaging results of MIBG and SSTRI scans. # Author manuscript
## HSA-131 I-MIBG therapy
In a single-arm phase II trial, 68 PPGL patients were treated with up to two cycles of HSA-131 I-MIBG. The primary endpoint, reduction in baseline antihypertensive medication lasting ≥6 months, was reached in 25% of patients ( 2). Furthermore, an objective partial response (PR, 23%) or stable disease (SD, 69%) within 12 months was seen in 92% patients by RECIST 1.0; and 68% showed complete response (CR) or PR in serum chromogranin levels. The median overall survival (OS) was 36.7 months from the first treatment ( 2). Moreover, the PR rate increased from 6% at 3 months to 23% at 12 months among patients receiving at least one therapeutic dose, indicating that HSA-131 I-MIBG effects can evolve over many months ( 2).

## Lu-DOTATATE for PPGL
When a patient with metastatic/inoperable PPGL presents to the clinic for the evaluation of TRT, first and foremost step is to consider whether systemic therapy is indicated based on several factors: the disease course (progression vs stable disease), catecholamine/ metanephrine secretion and related symptoms (e.g. controlled vs uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, cardiovascular events, psychiatric symptoms), tumor location, and risk for complications (e.g. neurologic toxicity from vertebral metastases). Consideration of these factors is necessary because some patients with PPGL have indolent disease and are often safely followed with active surveillance and medical management of catecholamine excess (14 -16 ). If the patient is potentially eligible for systemic therapy, particularly TRT, the second step is to evaluate MIBG and SSTRI scans to determine the degree and extent of uptake. It is of prime importance to ensure that the tumors can be targeted by TRT at a whole-body level by comparison of uptake in target lesions to total tumor burden noted on CT/magnetic resonance imaging and/or  18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT (Figure 1).

In such a scenario, where the imaging results of  123 I-MIBG and SSTRI scans allow TRT with either agent, the next step is to carefully consider the toxicity profile of each and patient’s characteristics (age, marrow reserve, renal function, prior chemotherapy with alkylating agents or radiotherapies, and location and size of tumors). There is no major preference between HSA-131 I-MIBG and  177 Lu-DOTATATE in patients with impaired renal functional and/or underlying risk factors for nephropathy (diabetes, essential hypertension, older age, prior nephrotoxic therapies or procedures), although parameters for renal function need to be monitored prior and during follow-up after the administration of both TRTs, and neither of the reagents have been adequately studied in patients with severe renal impairment (30mL/min) (Table 1). The impact of liver tumor burden on the choice between HSA-131 I-MIBG and  177 Lu-DOTATATE is equivocal: the median survival was similar for HSA-131 I-MIBG with or without lung/liver metastases, and baseline liver tumor burden did not have an impact on PFS in phase 3 NETTER-1 trial of
> 177

In cases of heterogeneous disease with mismatched MIBG/SSTR avid lesions, the disease coverage may potentially be achieved by combining these therapeutic agents in sequential order, with the first therapy agent being the radiopharmaceutical demonstrating the highest focal uptake in the highest number of lesions (surrogate of total tumor burden) ( 11 ) or in a combined regimen (“cocktail”) as demonstrated in a very small prospective cohort (n=10) of patients ( 18 ). If there is multifocal non-avid disease, these patients are often better served with other systemic treatment options, most commonly cytotoxic chemotherapy. Also, conventional  131 I-MIBG TRT should be considered in cases where HSA-131 I-MIBG cannot be administered due to logistical reasons. In some jurisdictions, the cost of HSA-131 I-MIBG is prohibitive in the absence of reimbursement and mandates consideration of conventional  131 I-MIBG.

# Author manuscript
## Lu-DOTATATE for PPGL
In cases of heterogeneous disease with mismatched MIBG/SSTR avid lesions, the disease coverage may potentially be achieved by combining these therapeutic agents in sequential order, with the first therapy agent being the radiopharmaceutical demonstrating the highest focal uptake in the highest number of lesions (surrogate of total tumor burden) ( 11 ) or in a combined regimen (“cocktail”) as demonstrated in a very small prospective cohort (n=10) of patients ( 18 ). However, both the approaches have not yet been rigorously tested and should be explored in future. Further, if any progressive lesions lack uptake by both of the above imaging scans, then they can be targeted by additional external beam radiation ( 11 ). If there is multifocal non-avid disease, these patients are often better served with other systemic treatment options, most commonly cytotoxic chemotherapy. Also, conventional  131 I-MIBG TRT should be considered in cases where HSA-131 I-MIBG cannot be administered due to logistical reasons. In some jurisdictions, the cost of HSA-131 I-MIBG is prohibitive in the absence of reimbursement and mandates consideration of conventional  131 I-MIBG.

### Data analysis
Systematic and random differences in the estimated AD per cycle between methods B to I and the protocol method P were investigated using Bland-Altman analysis [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#ref-CR29 "Bland JM, Altman DG. The 1-way classification. In: Variance components. Results were summarized quantitatively in terms of the Limits of Agreement (LOAs) that were defined as the average difference ± 2SD. Method A was not included in the Bland-Altman analysis as the AD/cycle used was in this case determined using the reference method (P).

## Methods
### Data analysis
The effect of the different treatment planning strategies on the final cumulative AD was also analysed. For each patient, the left-right mean renal AD was calculated for each cycle and then summed over the actually given number of cycles. For method A, the ADs for the first 4 cycles given were summed. The cumulative AD for each alternative method was set in relation to the AD for the protocol-specified dosimetry method. In order to be able to conclude which methods would have given an equivalent cumulative AD, an analysis of the uncertainty in the AD/cycle for the protocol method was done (see Additional file[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#MOESM1)), giving an estimated fractional uncertainty of 10% (1SD). The uncertainty in the cumulative AD from multiple cycles was calculated using the law of propagation of uncertainty [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#ref-CR31 "Evaluation of measurement data—guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement. JCGM 100:2008. GUM 1995 with minor corrections. JCGM member organizations (BIPM, IEC, IFCC, ILAC, ISO, IUPAC, IUPAP and OIML). 2008.")]. As information on the covariance in the AD estimates between cycles was not available, it was not considered in the uncertainty propagation. The confidence interval (CI) of the protocol-specified dosimetry was estimated as the cumulative absorbed dose ± 2SD.

## Results
### Per-cycle analysis
The results of the Bland-Altman analysis of the per-cycle AD of the alternative dosimetry methods B–I vs the protocol-specified dosimetry method are shown in Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Fig3). None of the methods studied resulted in marked systematic differences in the mean AD/cycle. The planar-based methods (B, C and I) resulted in the largest random differences with LOAs of − 3 ± 51%, 6 ± 43% and 8 ± 45%, respectively. Performing dosimetry in the first cycle and none thereafter also yielded wide LOAs of − 3 ± 36% with method D (hybrid dosimetry method) and − 2 ± 39% when applying Eq. [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Equ5) (method H). Using method F, i.e. one SPECT/cycle at 24 h, and a constant value of the effective half-time (51.6 h), the LOAs were − 2 ± 25%, while when using SPECT/CT hybrid dosimetry in the first treatment cycle and one SPECT/cycle in subsequent cycles (method E), LOAs were 1 ± 17%. The method whose results were most consistent with those achieved using the protocol-specified dosimetry method was method G (one SPECT/cycle at 96 h and application of Eq. [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Equ5)) resulting in LOAs of 1 ± 11%.
**Fig. 3**

## Results
### Cumulative absorbed dose analysis
Results of the comparisons of the total cumulative AD with methods A–I vs the AD achieved with the protocol-specified dosimetry method (± 2SD) are shown in Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Tab3). Giving 4 cycles to all patients (method A) yielded ADs that were consistent with dosimetry-based treatment in 4/22 (18%) patients, i.e. there were four patients who received 4 cycles when treated according to protocol. Planar dosimetry first cycle only (method B) and in all cycles (C and I) were consistent with method P in 3/14 (21%), 6/14 (43%) and 4/14 (29%) patients, respectively. SPECT-based dosimetry first cycle only (methods D and H) yielded consistency in 11/22 (50%) and 7/22 (32%) patients, respectively. The methods including SPECT in each cycle (E, F and G) were consistent with the reference ADs in 20 (91%), 19 (86%) and 22 (100%) of the 22 patients, respectively.
**Table 3 The cumulative AD over all cycles that would have been reached using alternative treatment strategy A (4 cycles to all) or estimated using alternative dosimetric methods (B–I) given the same no. of cycles as per protocol. “nd” indicates that the AD was not determined by that method**

## Discussion
The overall aim in this study was to elucidate whether it is possible to use a less demanding treatment strategy or dosimetry method in individualized 177 Lu-dotatate therapy, as compared to that used in the ongoing clinical trial (Iluminet), while maintaining a similar degree of accuracy in renal AD estimates.
For the clinical trial protocol, a hybrid dosimetry method has been used. This choice was a compromise between the axial coverage offered by the whole-body planar images, and the superior accuracy of SPECT/CT. Moreover, at the time of the writing of the clinical trial protocol, performing serial SPECTs in each cycle, including the subsequent processing and analysis of 3D images, was deemed too time-consuming to be feasible.
For the evaluation of the AD per cycle for the alternative treatment strategies (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Fig3)), we conclude that the dosimetry methods in which SPECT/CT are included are superior to the purely planar-based methods and that including one SPECT/CT in each cycle improves the dosimetric accuracy considerably. Results based on the cumulative AD (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Tab2)) are consistent with results from the per-cycle analysis. Dosimetry method G, including one SPECT/CT in each cycle at 96 h, yields results that are equivalent with the protocol dosimetry method P but with much lower demands on resources. Methods E and F, which also use SPECT in every cycle, give similar but slightly less consistent results.

The overall aim in this study was to elucidate whether it is possible to use a less demanding treatment strategy or dosimetry method in individualized 177 Lu-dotatate therapy, as compared to that used in the ongoing clinical trial (Iluminet), while maintaining a similar degree of accuracy in renal AD estimates.
For the clinical trial protocol, a hybrid dosimetry method has been used. This choice was a compromise between the axial coverage offered by the whole-body planar images, and the superior accuracy of SPECT/CT. Moreover, at the time of the writing of the clinical trial protocol, performing serial SPECTs in each cycle, including the subsequent processing and analysis of 3D images, was deemed too time-consuming to be feasible.
For the evaluation of the AD per cycle for the alternative treatment strategies (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Fig3)), we conclude that the dosimetry methods in which SPECT/CT are included are superior to the purely planar-based methods and that including one SPECT/CT in each cycle improves the dosimetric accuracy considerably. Results based on the cumulative AD (Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#Tab2)) are consistent with results from the per-cycle analysis. Dosimetry method G, including one SPECT/CT in each cycle at 96 h, yields results that are equivalent with the protocol dosimetry method P but with much lower demands on resources. Methods E and F, which also use SPECT in every cycle, give similar but slightly less consistent results.

## Discussion
For an imaging time near 50 h (_t_ ref ≈ _T_ 1/2), the systematic component of the error is equally low as for 96 h, while the SD is higher, thus yielding a slightly higher RMSD. The RMSD is also more sensitive to the exact acquisition time at 50 h than at 96 h. Thus, acquisition at approximately 4 days appears to be a valid choice for this approximation. This is also confirmed by the uncertainty analysis based on SPECT/CT on day 4 (Additional file[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#MOESM1)), where method G yields ADs that are equivalent to the protocol results. One drawback with our evaluation of method G is that the effective half-time estimated for the individual patient is included in the calculation of the absorbed-dose rate at 96 h since our SPECT/CTs were not acquired at 96 h. However, we still find it motivated to perform an independent evaluation of this new method, and the included implementation is deemed to be the fairest.

## Discussion
The conversion from activity to absorbed-dose rate is, according to the clinical protocol, performed using Monte Carlo-based radiation-transport calculation in a voxelized geometry. Since the range of the electrons emitted from 177 Lu is shorter than the spatial resolution of the SPECT images, the radiation-transport calculation could possibly have been simplified to a multiplication by the assumption that the electron kinetic energy is absorbed locally in the voxel [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-018-0210-2#ref-CR24 "Ljungberg M, Sjogreen-Gleisner K. The accuracy of absorbed dose estimates in tumours determined by quantitative SPECT: a Monte Carlo study. Acta Oncol. 2011;50:981–9.   
                  https://doi.org/10.3109/0284186X.2011.584559
.")]. However, it was considered important not to neglect the photon contribution, since parts of the kidneys are located near organs with high uptake such as the spleen, and since in addition to gamma radiation, there are also low-energy X-rays emitted in the 177 Lu decay that contribute to the self-absorbed dose. The Monte Carlo method was considered the best choice based on accuracy and availability. ## Discussion
The methods which best fit these criteria are E and G, both of which incorporate SPECT-based dosimetry in every cycle but are less resource-intense than the reference method P. The strategy that deviates the most is unequivocally method A, i.e. giving 4 cycles to all patients, followed by the planar-based dosimetry methods (B, C and I). This is consistent with what is already known about the drawbacks of planar dosimetry, namely the difficulties in taking into account individual variations in activity concentration, especially in tumours, the liver and intestines, which may then lead to over- or underestimation of the renal AD.
When choosing between methods E and G, one aspect to take into account is that for most PRRT centres, it would be more resource-consuming to perform a SPECT at 96 h since the patients would have to come back to the hospital. Whether or not to still go for method G then becomes a matter of whether or not the small difference seen in the Bland-Altman analyses (2SD of 11 and 17% for methods G and E, respectively) makes a relevant difference in real-life patient management.
From a clinical perspective, on the other hand, some would argue that to give 4 cycles to all patients is already a very effective treatment with a low degree of toxicity, so the need for further optimization is marginal. There are two objections to this: firstly, our obligation to know what we are doing when employing radiation for therapeutic purposes (analogous to the demands in other radiation therapy modalities), and secondly, when these patients progress months or years after their 4 cycles of PRRT, we would like to retreat them since the majority of the cases have not reached the limits for the organs at risk. Without initial dosimetric estimates, we have no grounds on which to plan further treatment.

When the tumour later progresses, the patient can be re-treated to risk organ tolerance limits. ## Abstract

_Objective_. Multicentre studies in molecular radiotherapy face challenges in ensuring the comparability of dosimetry results. The aim of this study was to develop a validation protocol to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across centres, consisting of a test exercise in combination with an action level. _Approach_. 177 Lu-SPECT/CT imaging of 3D-printed kidney phantoms with non-uniform activity distributions was conducted at five hospitals in Sweden and the UK. In total, 12 quantification systems (QSs) were included, where a QS was defined as the combination of a given camera system, reconstruction method and image-analysis method. The accuracy of image-based estimates of the activity concentration was investigated for three approaches to multicentre dosimetry: one site-specific, and two variants of centralised approaches. For the site-specific approach, the reference value was blinded to the evaluating operators. Prior to the evaluation, the participants agreed on an action level, specified as an obtained deviation larger than ±10% from the reference value. Sites responsible for a QS that yielded larger deviations, and therefore did not comply, were required to present an action plan, i.e., a plan for further method optimisation. _Main results_. For the site-specific approach, deviations larger than 10% were obtained for six out of 12 QS (range −11% to +27%). Action plans were presented for these QS and was implemented by one site (two QS). For the two variants of centralised approaches, where nine QS were included in total, deviations of within 10% were obtained for nine and seven QS, respectively. _Significance_. A quantification test combined with an action level can serve as an initial validation to enable further development and to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites.

Export citation and abstract[BibTeX](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_bib&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)[RIS](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_ris&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)

The interest in molecular radiotherapy (MRT) is currently expanding, and also the interest in integrating patient-specific dosimetry. Achieving equivalence in absorbed-dose estimates across centres is essential to enable interpretation, comparison and pooling of dosimetry data.

During the last decade, several multicentre comparison exercises of quantitative SPECT have been undertaken to investigate the accuracy in quantitative imaging and the possibilities of standardisation. These exercises have mostly been based on stylised phantom geometries, such as spheres or cylinders, and the adoption of a predefined protocol for image acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis (Willowson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib29), Zimmerman _et al_[2017](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib30), Wevrett _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib28), Gregory _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib7), Peters _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib17), [2020](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib16)). Instead of utilising stylised phantoms, the MRTDosimetry project employed a 3D-printed anthropomorphic phantom for comparison across sites (Tran-Gia _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib26)). A recent initiative is the SNMMI dosimetry challenge, led by the SNMMI Dosimetry Task Force, based on two sets of patient SPECT/CT images. An advantage of this approach was the avoidance of stylised geometries and activity distributions characteristic of most phantom studies, although with the drawback of an unknown ground truth (Uribe _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib27), Brosch-Lenz _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib2)). Currently, an accreditation programme is being developed by the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM) Forschungs GmbH (EARL) to harmonise 177 Lu SPECT/CT imaging, inspired by the existing accreditation programme for PET/CT (Kaalep _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib12)). This SPECT accreditation programme is based on the NEMA body PET phantom, in which the smallest sphere is replaced with a larger sphere more suitable with respect to the SPECT spatial resolution (Dickson _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib3)).

In the context of multicentre clinical trials that include dosimetry as a key component, the most common approach has been to follow predefined procedures for imaging, quantification and dosimetry (Taprogge _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib24), [2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib25), Lassmann _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib14)). One recent example is the multicentre observational trial INSPIRE (NCT04133870) on treatment of thyroid cancer with 131 I-NaI, in which a predefined imaging protocol has been adopted and implemented at eight sites, with dosimetry performed both locally and centrally (Taprogge _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib23)). Multicentre clinical studies that include prospective patient dosimetry and dose planning remain rare. The DOSISPHERE-01 multicentre randomised trial for treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma with 90 Y-loaded glass microspheres (NCT02582034) investigated personalised versus non-personalised dose planning based on 99m Tc-MAA SPECT/CT (Garin _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib6)). While dosimetry methods were not detailed in recent studies, an earlier publication described the development of these methods based on phantom measurements (Garin _et al_[2011](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib5)). The two-centre ILUMINET trial (NCT01456078) investigated dosimetry-guided 177 Lu peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177 Lu-PPRT) (Sundlöv _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib21)). A predefined imaging protocol was employed at both sites, and quantification and dosimetry performed with the Lundadose software (Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)), for which the accuracy for 177 Lu kidney dosimetry was also investigated (Gustafsson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib8), Sundlöv _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib22)).

Clinical multicentre studies that implement dosimetry for treatment planning present special challenges. The multicentre clinical trial START-NET (NCT05387603) involving 177 Lu-PRRT for patients with neuroendocrine tumours, where kidney dosimetry data will be utilised for treatment planning, is currently being launched in Sweden. The setup of the dosimetry in such a study necessitates consideration of several requirements: ensuring comparable and metrologically traceable dosimetry results at all clinical sites; adaptation to local conditions regarding available camera equipment, software and expertise; and complying with national regulatory frameworks for radiation protection. These requirements, and particularly the latter, present challenges in the absence of an established code of practice for validation of dosimetry results. For example, in Sweden and the UK, it is the legal entity that holds the license to use ionising radiation for medical purposes that also has responsibility for ensuring that the exposure is justified, and that the procedure is optimised (SFS [2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib20):396, Health and Safety [2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib9):896). This applies to all patients treated at the local hospital, including those participating in clinical studies, and covers responsibility for the methods used for radioprotective purposes, i.e. dosimetry (Almén and Anders [2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib1)). Consequently, whilst the use of a particular dosimetry software or the access to a centralised dosimetry service can be important steps towards achieving consistent dosimetry across sites, the produced dosimetry data can only be utilised to the extent that the site who delivers treatment, i.e. the permit holder, can take full responsibility of the results. Assuming this responsibility means to be able to verify the results in the patient dosimetry record, which presumably entails validation work by the local medical physics team. Thus, irrespective of the chosen solution for providing dosimetry data, the local team needs to invest time in preparatory work and verification.

Considering these requirements, we have hypothesised that a validation protocol, consisting of a blinded quantification test for a representative geometry, combined with an action level, can serve to achieve accurate and equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites, also when using site-specific methods. An essential component in such a strategy is the agreement among participating sites on the action level, the requirement that participants develop and present an action plan in case of non-compliance to this level, and the undertaking of a renewed test after method adjustments.

The aim of this study is to develop a protocol for initial validation of methods for estimation of 177 Lu activity concentration in kidneys. The validation protocol is based on a test exercise using 3D-printed kidney phantoms in combination with an action level. Three approaches to multicentre 177 Lu-SPECT-based activity quantification are investigated: a site-specific approach that involves blinded testing, and two variants of centralised approaches.

Three different approaches for multicentre activity-quantification studies were applied, here termed Site-specific, Combined and Centralised (table [1](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t1)). Five sites were included, four located in Sweden and one in the UK. Together, these sites included nine SPECT/CT cameras, comprising seven GE systems (GE Healthcare, Haifa, Israel) and two Siemens systems (Siemens Healthineers, Forcheim, Germany). The site-specific approach was based on locally preferred methods for image reconstruction, determination of the image calibration factor, and VOI delineation. To avoid possible operator-induced bias in the manual steps, the reference activity concentration in the phantoms were blinded to the operators performing the image-based quantification. For the combined approach, the local reconstruction methods were used, whilst the VOI delineation was performed centrally. For the centralised approach, both image reconstruction and VOI delineation were performed centrally. For practical reasons, the image analysis in the combined and centralised approaches was performed by a single operator to whom the reference activity concentration was not blinded. An overview of the process is presented in figure [1](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708f1).

### 2.1.Quantification systems (QSs) included

Twelve different QSs were studied. A QS was defined as the combination of a particular SPECT/CT camera, a reconstruction method, and an image-analysis method for determination of the activity concentration. These QS represented the same settings and methods as would be used for patient kidney dosimetry. Table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2) specifies the twelve QS, with further details provided in supplementary file 1. Together, the included QS represented a wide range of settings for image acquisition and processing. The number of acquired SPECT projections ranged from 30 to 120. Nine QS used only the photo-peak at 208 keV of 177 Lu whilst three also used the photo-peak at 113 keV. All QS included CT-based attenuation compensation, and ten QS also included scatter compensation and resolution recovery without post filtering. The QS that did not include resolution recovery included low-pass filtering post reconstruction. The number of updates (number of iterations × number of subsets) varied between 40 and 160, and reconstructions were performed either with commercially available software, Xeleris® (GE Healthcare, Haifa, Israel) or Hermia® (Hermes Medical Solutions, Stockholm, Sweden), or with non-commercial software, Phonsai (Rydén _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib18)) or Lundadose (Frey and Tsui [1996](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib4), Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)). Eight of the QS were included based on their participation in the multicentre trial START-NET (NCT05387603), two QS participated as part of method development, and two QS were included as part of an ongoing scientific collaboration. Each site was allowed to include more than one QS.

### 2.2.Phantoms

All activity measurements for phantom preparation were made using activity meters that had been calibrated for 177 Lu, as previously described (Hindorf _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib10)). To prevent 177 Lu from sticking to the phantom walls, EDTA was added to the water solutions before dispensing 177 Lu.

As a preparatory step, the calibration factor for 177 Lu-SPECT was determined from a uniformly filled cylindrical Jaszczak phantom, and a uniformly filled large spherical insert mounted inside the cylindrical phantom with a non-radioactive background. These phantoms were prepared at each site, with volumes and inserted activities of 177 Lu depending on the local availability of equipment and activity. The volume of the cylindrical phantoms ranged between 6.4 l and 7.4 l, and the activity concentration at the start of SPECT acquisition was between 0.02 MBq ml−1 and 0.11 MBq ml−1. The volumes of the spheres were 113–144 ml, and the activity concentration at the start of SPECT acquisitions was between 0.83 MBq ml−1 and 10.10 MBq ml−1.

The quantitative accuracy for 3D-printed kidney phantoms of 177 Lu-SPECT was investigated using pairs of 3D-printed kidney phantoms (left and right). These were designed using a grid-based technique to create an apparently non-uniform activity distribution, mimicking that of a typical 177 Lu-PRRT patient (Jessen _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib11)). Each kidney phantom encompassed an outer container shaped as cortex, an inner grid structure shaped as medulla and a solid renal pelvis on one side (figure [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708f2)). In-house plates and rods were manufactured to enable mounting of the kidney phantoms in a cylindrical Jaszczak phantom for imaging. The inner phantom volumes were 110 ml and 105 ml for the left and right kidney, respectively. The weights of the phantoms in dry and empty conditions were measured directly after printing and were then filled with water to test for watertightness for a minimum of 24 h.

This was not discovered until evaluation of the SPECT images, and a re-filling of the phantoms then became necessary. To avoid a new site visit, the kidney phantoms were this time prepared by a local medical physicist. To maintain the blinded approach and remain a consistent filling procedure, the local medical physicist, whilst in the lab, was instructed by the coordinating site via online communication. The local medical physicists did not record any data and was also not allowed to participate in the analysis of the phantom SPECT images.

#### 2.3.3.Centralised approach

For the centralised approach, SPECT reconstruction was performed centrally for each unique set of SPECT projections of the kidney phantoms. As some QS used the same set of projection data (QS 5 and 6, QS 7 and 8, QS 9 and 10) this yielded nine individual data points. The small-VOI method presented by Kapidzic _et al_ ([2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib13)) was used. Five spherical VOIs, each of 2 ml, positioned centrally in each kidney in the images was used, and the activity concentration calculated as the arithmetic average. The top and bottom slices were avoided, since in patient studies the spatial resolution in these slices is expected to be affected by kidney motion. Lastly, a recovery coefficient (RC) of 1.1 was used. The image analysis was performed by one operator, using the affinity module 4.0.1 (Hermes Medical Solutions, Stockholm, Sweden).

#### 2.3.4.Combined approach

The combined approach was based on local reconstructions and centralised image analysis. This required DICOM images formatted such that they could be imported into Hermia. This import was successful for all QS except QS 3, 4 and 6, and thus nine individual data points resulted. The SPECT images were analysed using the same VOI method as for the centralised approach, but due to inconsistent reconstructions between the QS, no RC was applied.

This level was decided based on reasoning, taking into account the recommended maximal permissible error of the administered activity of ±5 or 10% (Hindorf _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib10)) and previously obtained results on the relative uncertainty for absorbed dose estimates for 177 Lu-DOTATATE of approximately 6% (Gustafsson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib8)).

After all sites had completed reporting, the obtained deviations and the reference values were revealed to all participants. Sites responsible for a QS that did not meet the action level (site-specific approach) were asked to present an action plan, including an investigation and identification of the source of error and a plan for further development and amendment. As the included QS represented different methods there was no pre-defined action plan, but this was regarded as the responsibility of the local medical physicist team.

The site-specific approach resulted in the largest range of deviations (−17% to +29) % and six out of 12 QS did not meet the 10% criterion. If instead considering the left–right kidney average, this criterion was not met for QS 3, 4, 8 and 10 (4/12 QS). The combined approach yielded the lowest range (−9% to +3 %) with activity concentrations that were slightly underestimated for all data points except three, and all QS (9/9) met the 10% criterion. The centralised approach yielded deviations between −11% and +27 %, and all but two (7/9) met the 10% criterion. The largest deviations were generally observed for the right kidney, which was smaller than the left kidney. Of the parameters for image acquisition and reconstruction listed in table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2), no single factor could be identified as associated with the larger deviations. With respect to the image analysis method (table [4](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t4)), QS 3, 4, 11 and 12 included whole-kidney delineation and all yielded underestimated activity concentrations, whilst the QS that included small-VOI methods showed no such trend but a larger dispersion.

### 3.4.Deviations in relation to the action level

The action level was strictly only actionable for the site-specific approach. For QS 3 and 4 deviations higher than 10% were obtained for the left kidney phantom. This site presented and implemented an action plan, in which the RC, applicable for whole kidney delineation, was re-examined based on additional phantom studies and was thus updated from 0.85 to 0.78. However, this site decided to migrate to another quantification software, and a follow-up blinded evaluation has been planned. For QS 8 and 10 deviations higher than 10% were obtained for both the left and right kidney phantoms. The action plan involved further investigation of the strategy used for VOI delineation, including the development of detailed operator guidance. However, as alternatives were available amongst the QS that met the 10% criterion, this site decided not to pursue this development. QS 11 and 12 underestimated the activity concentration slightly more than 10 %. The proposed action plan included the development of a kidney RC that takes irregular shapes and non-uniform activity distributions into account. Follow-up tests have not yet been performed.

In this work, a validation protocol was investigated as a method to reach equivalence in quantitative 177 Lu SPECT across sites. The quantitative accuracy when using site-specific, combined and centralised approaches was investigated. Overall, the three approaches yielded deviations between −17% and +29% across the QS investigated. The random dispersion was found to be more pronounced for the site-specific and centralised approaches, whereas the combined approach yielded more consistent but slightly underestimated results. For the investigated approaches to multicentre 177 Lu activity quantification, the validation test identified QS that produced biased estimates of the activity concentration.

The site-specific approach was developed from the idea that the primary objective is to establish a centre’s ability to accurately estimate activity concentrations, rather than focusing on the specific means and methods employed to achieve these estimates. This contrasts with the more common approach of adopting a pre-defined protocol for SPECT image acquisition, processing, and analysis across all centres. In practice, clinical centres have access to different camera systems and collimators, various software for tomographic reconstruction, including methods for resolution recovery and scatter compensation, activity quantification and dosimetry. Some of these components may be less straightforward to align to a common protocol, yet they can have a substantial impact on the results. There is also ongoing development of both hardware and software, such as SPECT systems based on CZT detectors and ring-configurations, as well as new tomographic reconstructions and image analysis methods, for which the optimal settings and protocols may differ from those conventionally used. Notable examples in this study are represented by QS 1 and QS 2 that both yielded acceptable results with regards to the action level. QS 1 was based on a CZT camera system. Neither of these QS included compensation for scatter or resolution recovery. Both QS employed a method for determining the calibration factor using a sphere geometry, rather than the more commonly used geometry of a cylindrical phantom, due to the unavailability of scatter compensation. Other notable examples are QS 3 and 4 that both employed an unconventionally low number of 30 projection angles. Whilst the validation test revealed deviations for these QS for the left kidney phantom, these were later found to be associated with the applied RC rather than the number of projection angles. It is also noteworthy that nine QS were based on acquisition using only the 208 keV energy window, whereas three also utilised the 113 keV peak, thereby introducing a higher dependency on accurate scatter correction.

Regarding the QS intended for the START-NET trial (QS 1–7 and 9), an essential component was the agreement between the participants, made prior to the experimental work, concerning both the action level and the requirement of formulating and implementing an action plan in the event of non-compliance. In this agreement, the action level was not regarded as a pass-or-fail judgement, but rather a means of identifying errors and initiating further local investigations and adjustments. Two out of the eight QS did not meet the 10% criterion. Although an action plan was formulated and implemented, this site decided to migrate to another quantification software, and the blinded evaluation is planned to be repeated.

A clear limitation to this study was the small data set used, encompassing only two data points per QS. Consequently, depending on the results obtained, the local investigations could include additional phantom experiments, re-examination of the reconstruction settings, or investigation of the operator dependency. To understand and communicate the reliability of the reference method, the quantification of the uncertainty was considered essential. In retrospect, an action level of ±10% may have been optimistically narrow when considering the ±3.3% (_k_ = 2) coverage interval of the reference activity concentration. However, despite this concern the action level was maintained.

Blinding is a commonly adopted strategy for evaluation of operator-dependent methods. In this work, the blinding was included to ensure a strict separation between method evaluation and optimisation, and to mimic a patient situation where the true activity concentration is unknown. The 3D printed phantoms were well suited for this purpose as the grid volume was only accessible for measurement during the phantom construction and the effective volume (![Image 41: ${V_{{\text{grid}}}} + {V_{{\text{fill}}}}$](https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/0031-9155/70/11/115001/revision2/pmbadd708ieqn29.gif)) could not be determined by the local sites by other means than SPECT measurement. On a larger scale, site visits for phantom preparation may be considered overly cumbersome. A possible solution could be to use online communication and to separate data logging from the local site, as was done in this work for the site where the phantom filling had to be repeated. Another solution to ensure blinding could be to require a written agreement from the local site on the involvement of different operators for phantom filling and image analysis. Based on our experience, communication is a key factor for success in a blinded exercise, such that its purpose is clear to all parties involved.

Both the combined and centralised approaches were, for practical reasons, not blinded and were based on image analysis by a single operator using one software. Results for these approaches were more consistent than for the site-specific approach. However, a disadvantage was the potential risk of introducing consistent bias across all systems. This became evident for the combined approach, which yielded results within the action level for all nine QS but gave slightly underestimated results for 15 out of 18 data points. The centralised approach gave results within ±10% for 15 out of 18 data points and yielded a range of deviations between −11% to +27% across all data points. In particular, the centralised method did not perform well for QS 11. The cause of this deviation was identified as the calibration factor determined with method (iv), resulting in a considerably lower value than for the technically identical camera of QS 12. This exemplifies the necessity of conducting a validation test even when adopting a centralised approach and also underscores the importance of basing the calibration factor on multiple SPECT phantom measurements rather than a single one.

None of the acquisition settings and technical parameters specified in table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2) could be identified as being associated with the larger deviations. Thus, no clear effect of the reconstruction method, the energy windows settings, or the scatter correction, etc. could be discerned. On the other hand, the accuracy appeared to be more dependent on the strategy for VOI delineation combined with the RC. In view of the current availability of iterative reconstruction that include CT-based attenuation correction, we believe the most critical aspects for 177 Lu kidney quantification are the combination of reconstruction settings, the calibration factor, the adopted VOI-method and the applied RC.

Whilst the ongoing EARL project on 177 Lu accreditation (Dickson _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib3)) is focused on large phantom calibration factors and recovery curves for spherical inserts with known volumes, this work is based on anthropomorphic phantoms with non-uniform activity distributions, and thus complements the EARL effort. The non-uniform activity distribution intended to mimic 177 Lu-PRRT patient images, and was generated by a grid structure, which simplified phantom filling compared to a phantom with multiple compartments (Jessen _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib11)). However, a limitation with the 3D printed kidney phantoms was the mass density of the printing material, which was slightly higher than water. This produced CT images where the phantom structures were clearly visible, which may have had an impact on VOI delineation. Another advantage with the validation exercise was the dissemination of phantoms. For example, sites responsible for QS 1, 2, 7, and 9, made further use of the phantoms to investigate the operator dependency and reproducibility of their VOI methods.

In perspective of multicentre clinical trials, either of the proposed approaches; site-specific, combined and centralised, have shown advantages and disadvantages and yielded reasonably low deviations across the QS investigated. The combined approach yielded the most consistent results and the lowest deviations. For retrospective analysis of dosimetry data, such as for analysis of dose-response relationships, the combined or centralised approaches may be preferable. For dosimetry-guided treatment protocols where dosimetry data is used for treatment planning, there are regulatory requirements stating that the responsibility for dosimetry lies with the permit holder for delivering treatment. There are also practical steps in dosimetry that rely on local decisions, such as measures taken in case of delays of radiopharmaceutical delivery, missing or incorrect SPECT/CT acquisition time-points, or extravasation. Local engagement in dosimetry is expected to be beneficial in terms of understanding the consequences of the decisions made. For these practical and regulatory reasons, we have found that for the START-NET clinical trial, the site-specific approach is the most viable option.

Irrespective of the purpose of whether a multicentre dosimetry study is prospective or retrospective, a validation test, such as presented in this work, has been found beneficial for identifying deviations in the adopted quantification methods and to motivate further development.

For multicentre studies, a validation protocol, consisting of a blinded test exercise for a representative geometry, combined with an action level, can be used to reach equivalence in 177 Lu SPECT kidney quantification.

Additionally, we express our gratitude to the staff at the nuclear medicine departments for their assistance in setting up the phantom preparation and SPECT/CT measurements. ## Abstract

_Objective_. Multicentre studies in molecular radiotherapy face challenges in ensuring the comparability of dosimetry results. The aim of this study was to develop a validation protocol to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across centres, consisting of a test exercise in combination with an action level. _Approach_. 177 Lu-SPECT/CT imaging of 3D-printed kidney phantoms with non-uniform activity distributions was conducted at five hospitals in Sweden and the UK. In total, 12 quantification systems (QSs) were included, where a QS was defined as the combination of a given camera system, reconstruction method and image-analysis method. The accuracy of image-based estimates of the activity concentration was investigated for three approaches to multicentre dosimetry: one site-specific, and two variants of centralised approaches. For the site-specific approach, the reference value was blinded to the evaluating operators. Prior to the evaluation, the participants agreed on an action level, specified as an obtained deviation larger than ±10% from the reference value. Sites responsible for a QS that yielded larger deviations, and therefore did not comply, were required to present an action plan, i.e., a plan for further method optimisation. _Main results_. For the site-specific approach, deviations larger than 10% were obtained for six out of 12 QS (range −11% to +27%). Action plans were presented for these QS and was implemented by one site (two QS). For the two variants of centralised approaches, where nine QS were included in total, deviations of within 10% were obtained for nine and seven QS, respectively. _Significance_. A quantification test combined with an action level can serve as an initial validation to enable further development and to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites.

Export citation and abstract[BibTeX](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_bib&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)[RIS](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_ris&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)

The interest in molecular radiotherapy (MRT) is currently expanding, and also the interest in integrating patient-specific dosimetry. Achieving equivalence in absorbed-dose estimates across centres is essential to enable interpretation, comparison and pooling of dosimetry data.

During the last decade, several multicentre comparison exercises of quantitative SPECT have been undertaken to investigate the accuracy in quantitative imaging and the possibilities of standardisation. These exercises have mostly been based on stylised phantom geometries, such as spheres or cylinders, and the adoption of a predefined protocol for image acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis (Willowson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib29), Zimmerman _et al_[2017](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib30), Wevrett _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib28), Gregory _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib7), Peters _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib17), [2020](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib16)). Instead of utilising stylised phantoms, the MRTDosimetry project employed a 3D-printed anthropomorphic phantom for comparison across sites (Tran-Gia _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib26)). A recent initiative is the SNMMI dosimetry challenge, led by the SNMMI Dosimetry Task Force, based on two sets of patient SPECT/CT images. An advantage of this approach was the avoidance of stylised geometries and activity distributions characteristic of most phantom studies, although with the drawback of an unknown ground truth (Uribe _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib27), Brosch-Lenz _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib2)). Currently, an accreditation programme is being developed by the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM) Forschungs GmbH (EARL) to harmonise 177 Lu SPECT/CT imaging, inspired by the existing accreditation programme for PET/CT (Kaalep _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib12)). This SPECT accreditation programme is based on the NEMA body PET phantom, in which the smallest sphere is replaced with a larger sphere more suitable with respect to the SPECT spatial resolution (Dickson _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib3)).

In the context of multicentre clinical trials that include dosimetry as a key component, the most common approach has been to follow predefined procedures for imaging, quantification and dosimetry (Taprogge _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib24), [2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib25), Lassmann _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib14)). One recent example is the multicentre observational trial INSPIRE (NCT04133870) on treatment of thyroid cancer with 131 I-NaI, in which a predefined imaging protocol has been adopted and implemented at eight sites, with dosimetry performed both locally and centrally (Taprogge _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib23)). Multicentre clinical studies that include prospective patient dosimetry and dose planning remain rare. The DOSISPHERE-01 multicentre randomised trial for treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma with 90 Y-loaded glass microspheres (NCT02582034) investigated personalised versus non-personalised dose planning based on 99m Tc-MAA SPECT/CT (Garin _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib6)). While dosimetry methods were not detailed in recent studies, an earlier publication described the development of these methods based on phantom measurements (Garin _et al_[2011](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib5)). The two-centre ILUMINET trial (NCT01456078) investigated dosimetry-guided 177 Lu peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177 Lu-PPRT) (Sundlöv _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib21)). A predefined imaging protocol was employed at both sites, and quantification and dosimetry performed with the Lundadose software (Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)), for which the accuracy for 177 Lu kidney dosimetry was also investigated (Gustafsson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib8), Sundlöv _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib22)).

Clinical multicentre studies that implement dosimetry for treatment planning present special challenges. The multicentre clinical trial START-NET (NCT05387603) involving 177 Lu-PRRT for patients with neuroendocrine tumours, where kidney dosimetry data will be utilised for treatment planning, is currently being launched in Sweden. The setup of the dosimetry in such a study necessitates consideration of several requirements: ensuring comparable and metrologically traceable dosimetry results at all clinical sites; adaptation to local conditions regarding available camera equipment, software and expertise; and complying with national regulatory frameworks for radiation protection. These requirements, and particularly the latter, present challenges in the absence of an established code of practice for validation of dosimetry results. For example, in Sweden and the UK, it is the legal entity that holds the license to use ionising radiation for medical purposes that also has responsibility for ensuring that the exposure is justified, and that the procedure is optimised (SFS [2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib20):396, Health and Safety [2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib9):896). This applies to all patients treated at the local hospital, including those participating in clinical studies, and covers responsibility for the methods used for radioprotective purposes, i.e. dosimetry (Almén and Anders [2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib1)). Consequently, whilst the use of a particular dosimetry software or the access to a centralised dosimetry service can be important steps towards achieving consistent dosimetry across sites, the produced dosimetry data can only be utilised to the extent that the site who delivers treatment, i.e. the permit holder, can take full responsibility of the results. Assuming this responsibility means to be able to verify the results in the patient dosimetry record, which presumably entails validation work by the local medical physics team. Thus, irrespective of the chosen solution for providing dosimetry data, the local team needs to invest time in preparatory work and verification.

Considering these requirements, we have hypothesised that a validation protocol, consisting of a blinded quantification test for a representative geometry, combined with an action level, can serve to achieve accurate and equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites, also when using site-specific methods. An essential component in such a strategy is the agreement among participating sites on the action level, the requirement that participants develop and present an action plan in case of non-compliance to this level, and the undertaking of a renewed test after method adjustments.

The aim of this study is to develop a protocol for initial validation of methods for estimation of 177 Lu activity concentration in kidneys. ## Abstract

_Objective_. Multicentre studies in molecular radiotherapy face challenges in ensuring the comparability of dosimetry results. The aim of this study was to develop a validation protocol to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across centres, consisting of a test exercise in combination with an action level. _Approach_. 177 Lu-SPECT/CT imaging of 3D-printed kidney phantoms with non-uniform activity distributions was conducted at five hospitals in Sweden and the UK. In total, 12 quantification systems (QSs) were included, where a QS was defined as the combination of a given camera system, reconstruction method and image-analysis method. The accuracy of image-based estimates of the activity concentration was investigated for three approaches to multicentre dosimetry: one site-specific, and two variants of centralised approaches. For the site-specific approach, the reference value was blinded to the evaluating operators. Prior to the evaluation, the participants agreed on an action level, specified as an obtained deviation larger than ±10% from the reference value. Sites responsible for a QS that yielded larger deviations, and therefore did not comply, were required to present an action plan, i.e., a plan for further method optimisation. _Main results_. For the site-specific approach, deviations larger than 10% were obtained for six out of 12 QS (range −11% to +27%). Action plans were presented for these QS and was implemented by one site (two QS). For the two variants of centralised approaches, where nine QS were included in total, deviations of within 10% were obtained for nine and seven QS, respectively. _Significance_. A quantification test combined with an action level can serve as an initial validation to enable further development and to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites.

Export citation and abstract[BibTeX](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_bib&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)[RIS](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_ris&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)

The interest in molecular radiotherapy (MRT) is currently expanding, and also the interest in integrating patient-specific dosimetry. Achieving equivalence in absorbed-dose estimates across centres is essential to enable interpretation, comparison and pooling of dosimetry data.

During the last decade, several multicentre comparison exercises of quantitative SPECT have been undertaken to investigate the accuracy in quantitative imaging and the possibilities of standardisation. These exercises have mostly been based on stylised phantom geometries, such as spheres or cylinders, and the adoption of a predefined protocol for image acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis (Willowson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib29), Zimmerman _et al_[2017](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib30), Wevrett _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib28), Gregory _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib7), Peters _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib17), [2020](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib16)). Instead of utilising stylised phantoms, the MRTDosimetry project employed a 3D-printed anthropomorphic phantom for comparison across sites (Tran-Gia _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib26)). A recent initiative is the SNMMI dosimetry challenge, led by the SNMMI Dosimetry Task Force, based on two sets of patient SPECT/CT images. An advantage of this approach was the avoidance of stylised geometries and activity distributions characteristic of most phantom studies, although with the drawback of an unknown ground truth (Uribe _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib27), Brosch-Lenz _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib2)). Currently, an accreditation programme is being developed by the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM) Forschungs GmbH (EARL) to harmonise 177 Lu SPECT/CT imaging, inspired by the existing accreditation programme for PET/CT (Kaalep _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib12)). This SPECT accreditation programme is based on the NEMA body PET phantom, in which the smallest sphere is replaced with a larger sphere more suitable with respect to the SPECT spatial resolution (Dickson _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib3)).

In the context of multicentre clinical trials that include dosimetry as a key component, the most common approach has been to follow predefined procedures for imaging, quantification and dosimetry (Taprogge _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib24), [2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib25), Lassmann _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib14)). One recent example is the multicentre observational trial INSPIRE (NCT04133870) on treatment of thyroid cancer with 131 I-NaI, in which a predefined imaging protocol has been adopted and implemented at eight sites, with dosimetry performed both locally and centrally (Taprogge _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib23)). Multicentre clinical studies that include prospective patient dosimetry and dose planning remain rare. The DOSISPHERE-01 multicentre randomised trial for treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma with 90 Y-loaded glass microspheres (NCT02582034) investigated personalised versus non-personalised dose planning based on 99m Tc-MAA SPECT/CT (Garin _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib6)). While dosimetry methods were not detailed in recent studies, an earlier publication described the development of these methods based on phantom measurements (Garin _et al_[2011](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib5)). The two-centre ILUMINET trial (NCT01456078) investigated dosimetry-guided 177 Lu peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177 Lu-PPRT) (Sundlöv _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib21)). A predefined imaging protocol was employed at both sites, and quantification and dosimetry performed with the Lundadose software (Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)), for which the accuracy for 177 Lu kidney dosimetry was also investigated (Gustafsson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib8), Sundlöv _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib22)).

Clinical multicentre studies that implement dosimetry for treatment planning present special challenges. The multicentre clinical trial START-NET (NCT05387603) involving 177 Lu-PRRT for patients with neuroendocrine tumours, where kidney dosimetry data will be utilised for treatment planning, is currently being launched in Sweden. The setup of the dosimetry in such a study necessitates consideration of several requirements: ensuring comparable and metrologically traceable dosimetry results at all clinical sites; adaptation to local conditions regarding available camera equipment, software and expertise; and complying with national regulatory frameworks for radiation protection. These requirements, and particularly the latter, present challenges in the absence of an established code of practice for validation of dosimetry results. For example, in Sweden and the UK, it is the legal entity that holds the license to use ionising radiation for medical purposes that also has responsibility for ensuring that the exposure is justified, and that the procedure is optimised (SFS [2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib20):396, Health and Safety [2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib9):896). This applies to all patients treated at the local hospital, including those participating in clinical studies, and covers responsibility for the methods used for radioprotective purposes, i.e. dosimetry (Almén and Anders [2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib1)). MAIN RESEARCH ACTIVITIES 

I. Astrophysics, Cosmic Rays & Elementary Particle Physics, Obserwational Astronomy 

1. High-energy hadron-hadron interactions. 

2. Elastic and inelastic  and e interactions. Nucleon structure - theory and astronomy experiments. 

3. Rare decays. 

4. Baryon resonances and near threshold meson production. 

5. Neutrino physics. 

6. Astrophysics: optical detection of short bursts, large-scale structure, dark matter. 

7. Cosmic ray physics. 

8. Cosmology. 

9. Theory of lepton and hadron interactions. 

10. Theory of gravitational systems. 

II. Nuclear physics 

1. Relativistic ion collisions. 

2. Nuclear reactions. 

3. Nuclear structure. 

4. Properties of heavy and superheavy nuclei (theory). 

5. Theory of nuclear matter, hypernuclei & nuclear structure and dynamics. 

6. Exotic nuclei. 9

III. Plasma physics and technology 

1. Development of methods and tools for plasma diagnostics. 

2. Physical phenomena in hot plasma and plasma interaction with solid targets. 

3. Thin Nb and Pb film coating by means of arc discharges under ultra-high vacuum conditions. 

4. Nonlinear effects in extended media & Bose-Einstein condensates (theory). 

5. Fusion power reactors - development of diagnostic tools. 

IV. Accelerators, detectors & electronics 

1. R&D of linear accelerators for high-energy electrons. 

2. Optimization of TiN coating processes for accelerating structures. 

3. New detection methods and their application in physics experiments, nuclear medicine and homeland security. 

4. Electronics and detectors for large-scale experiments. 

5. Systems for nuclear radiation spectrometry. 

6. R&D of special silicon detectors for physics experiments and environmental protection. 

7. POLFEL design projects. 

V. Solid state physics, physics & engineering of materials; applications 

1. Materials structure studies by nuclear methods. 

2. Ion/plasma material modyfication; synthesis of new materials. 

3. Diffusion processes in solids. 

4. Study of ion and electron acceleration mechanisms in new RPI facility IBIS II. 

5. Optimization of neutron diffractometers. 

6. Arheometry: material studies of archeological objects using physical methods. 

VI. Reactor physics, nuclear technology in energy generation, modelling & calculations 

1. Development of computational tools for safety analysis and operation of energy and research reactors. 

2. Nuclear power energy generation. 

3. Management of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste. Nucelar transmutation. 

4. New reactors for non-electric applications (HTGR, VHTR, DFR). 

VII. Nuclear technology in health and enviromental protection, management of hazards 

1. Development of new radiopharmaceuticals for diagnostics and radionuclide therapy. 

2. Dosimetry and nano-dosimetry. 

3. Computer modelling of radiation sources, transport of radiation through matter and radiation dose calculations. 

4. X-ray sources for medicine and industry. 

5. New methods for obtaining radioactive isotopes; radioactivity standards. 

6. Methods of assessment and forecasting of environmental threats from nuclear and industrial facilities. 

7. Air monitoring. 10

# Maria Reactor Operations Division 

Head of Division Ireneusz Owsianko, MSc Eng 

There are 59 employees (engineers and technicians) in the Maria Reactor Operations Division . 

The main activity of this unit is the safe operation of the MARIA research reactor. 

In 2018 the reactor operated for 4508 hours at power levels from 18 MW to 25 MW. 

The main activities carried out at the MARIA reactor were focused on: 

 irradiation of target materials in the vertical channels and in the rabbit system, 

 irradiation of uranium targets for 99 Mo production, 

 neutron scattering condensed matter studies with neutron beams from the reactor horizontal channel, 

 neutron radiography studies, 

 neutron modification of minerals, 

 training. 

Irradiations of target materials such as: TeO 2, KCl, Lu 2O3, SmCl 2, S, Co etc. were performed for the Radioisotope Centre POLATOM and irradiations of uranium targets were performed for CURIUM (formerly Mallinckrodt Medical). 

Based on cooperation with the company QUIREM, irradiations of targets containing holmium microspheres for 

radiotherapy treatment were  performed.  The total activity of irradiated targets in 2018 was  1451 TBq. 

The neutron irradiation services utilising the MARIA reactor also include the colouring of topaz minerals. The irradiation of minerals in special channels located outside the reactor core changes their clear natural state to shades of blue, thereby increasing the commercial value of the product. Blue topaz stones are released to the market as non-radioactive materials, conforming to strict international criteria. 

Commercial irradiat ions of uranium targets for  99 Mo production were carried out  at  the MARIA reactor in 2018 

during 16 reactor operation cycles.  Production of the radioisotope  99 Mo by irradiation of high ly -enriched uranium 

(HEU) and low enriched uranium (LEU) targets reach ed the level of 7676 TBq  in 2018 .

# Maria Reactor Operation 

A. Gołąb, J . Jaroszewicz, I. Owsianko 

The multipurpose high flux research reactor MARIA is a water and beryllium moderated reactor of pool type with graphite reflector and  pressurised  channels 

containing concentric tube assemblies of fuel elements 

(Fig. 1, 2). It  was  designed to provide  a high  degree of 

flexibility. 

Fig. 1. Vertical section of the MARIA reactor. 1. control rod drive mechanism, 2. mounting plate, 3. ionisation chamber channel, 4. ionisation chamber drive mechanism,5. fuel and loop channels support plate, 6. plate support console, 7. horizontal beam tube shutter drive mechanism, 8. beam tube shutter, 9. fuel channel, 10. ionisation chamber shield, 11. core support structure, 12. core and reflector support plate, 13. reflector blocks, 14. beam tube compensation joint. 

The fuel channels are situated in a matrix containing beryllium blocks and enclosed by a lateral reflector made of graphite blocks in  aluminium  cans. The 

MARIA reactor is equipped with vertical channels for 

irradiation of target materials, a rabbit system for short 

irradiations and six horizontal neutron beam channels. 

The main characteristics of the MARIA reactor are as follows: 

 nominal power 30 MW(th) 

 thermal neutron flux density 2.5·10 14 n/cm 2s

 moderator H2O, beryllium 

 cooling system channel type 

 fuel assemblies: 

▫ material U3Si 2Al / UO 2

▫ enrichment 19,75% / 19,7% 

▫ cladding aluminium 

▫ shape 5 MC) or 6 (MR) concentric tubes 

▫ active length 1000 mm 

 output thermal neutron flux 

at horizontal channels 35·10 9 n/cm 2s

The MARIA reactor reached its first criticality in December 1974. The reactor was in operation until 1985 when it was shut down for modernisation. The modernisation encompassed refurbishment and upgrading of technological systems. In particular, the efficiency of the ventilation and cooling systems was improved. In 1993 the MARIA reactor was put into operation again. 

Fig. 2. View of the reactor pool and control rod drive mechanism. 

The main areas of reactor applications are as follows: 

 irradiation of target materials in the vertical channels and the rabbit system 

 testing of fuel and structural materials for nuclear power engineering 

 neutron radiography 

 neutron activation analysis 

 neutron transmutation doping 

 research in neutron and condensed matter physics 

 training
