Neutron irradiation services 

MARIA is one of the biggest research reactors in Europe. The neutron irradiation services provided at the MARIA research reactor include a wide range of radioisotope production, neutron activation analyses and biomedical technology. 

Nuclear reactors remain a key component in the production of useful isotopes mainly for nuclear medicine treatments. Available services cover activation of a large variety of target materials for the production of isotopes, which can be processed at the discretion of the customer. Irradiation services are performed in various facilities constructed at the MARIA reactor, depending on the required neutron flux levels, irradiation time, target mass and geometry. The standard vertical in-core isotope channels as well as special ones equipped with a hydraulic transport system are in operation. Currently four channels with a hydraulic transport system (rabbit system) are operational in the reactor core. 

Targets of TeO 2, KCl, LuCl 3, S, Yb 2O3, Sm 2O3 as well as Cu, Ho, In, Cr, NiO, Re, Cr, W, MoO 3 were irradiated for customers (Fig. 7). Most of them were irradiated for the Radioisotope Centre POLATOM of the National Centre for Nuclear Research for radioisotope production. Total annual isotope production in 2018 reached an activity of 1451 TBq. 

The irradiation of uranium targets for 99 Mo production plays a particular role in the utilization of the Maria reactor. The activity of 99 Mo as a fission product of the irradiation of uranium targets was equal to 7 676 TBq. This production supports the global chain of the research reactor producers of 99 Mo. Among those in Europe are: HFR (Netherlands), BR2 (Belgium) and LVR15 (Czech Republic). 

A key medical isotope is 99m Tc, which is a decay product of 99 Mo. One possible source of 99 Mo can be achieved in the course of the 235 U fission reaction. The main objective of 235 U irradiation is to obtain the 99m Tc isotope, which is widely used in the domain of medical diagnostics. The 99m Tc from a source of decaying 99 Mo can be easily transported to hospitals, where it is extracted and used for a variety of nuclear medicine diagnostic procedures. 

The commercial irradiation of uranium plates for 99 Mo production has been carried out at the MARIA reactor since 2010. In 2018 sixteen reactor operation cycles were dedicated to 99 Mo production. The targets were irradiated according to the order on the two or three positions inside the irradiation rigs. This means that one reactor operation cycle includes irradiation of 16 or 24 uranium targets per cycle. Following the shortage of the key medical radioisotope 99 Mo and its daughter 99m Tc related to long-term reliability the MARIA reactor has declared its readiness to irradiate newly designed LEU targets. Upon agreement with Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals (actual CURIUM ) one of the main producers of 99 Mo, a programme of certification of the new LEU targets (Low-Enriched Uranium) was successfully completed in December 2017 and since the beginning of 2018 only LEU targets have been irradiated. # Reactor Research and Technology Division 

Head of Division Janusz Jaroszewicz, MSc Eng 

There are 36 employees in the Research and Reactor Technology Division including researchers (5 employees with a PhD degree), engineers and technicians. The organisation of the Division was established in 2016 and includes 5 Groups: 

 Reactor Analyses & Measurements Group  (DAP) 

 Irradiation Technology Group (DTN) 

 Designers Group (DTK) 

 Technical Group (DTE) 

 Workshop Group((DTW). 

The main activity of the Division is in supporting the MARIA Reactor Operations Division in safety analyses of the reactor and the irradiation facilities as well as providing new program covering research based on utilisation of the MARIA reactor. In 2018 the Division’s activities were strongly related to program mes which were dedicated to utilisation of the MARIA reactor, mainly for irradiation of targets used to produce radioactive sources for nuclear medicine. Research and development activity was focused on application and led to the implementation of innovative irradiation technologies. In recent years the Division has launched a new irradiation technology for different uranium targets used for 99 Mo production. Among these, an irradiation technology using the new LEU uranium targets composed of UO 2 microspheres was implemented. The programme was performed in cooperation with NWMI (USA). Based on cooperation with a Dutch company, QUIREM Medical BV, the Division completed the technology for Ho-PLLA microsphere irradiation in the MARIA reactor. The microspheres containing holmium are used in radioembolisation procedures as an innovative form of radiotherapy for treatment of liver cancer. The 

Division’s activit ies also cover safety analyses, numerical calculations, irradiation technology as well as design and manufacture of the reactor facilities. 

The Division carries out intensive scientific cooperation with domestic scientific institutions and universities as well as collaborations with foreign institutions taking part in international projects and research programmes. These include collaborations with such institutions as: CEA (France), JAEA (Japan), ANL (USA), CCFE / UKAEA (Great Britain) and others. The effect of collaboration with academic institutions was training organised and provided for students (Technical University of Warsaw). 

The main activities carried out in the Division were focused on: 

 safety analyses and numerical calculations supporting operation of the MARIA research reactor; 

 reactor measurements: neutron parameters (activation measurements, SPND), gamma heating / dose rate (calorimeters, ionisation chambers), temperature measurements (thermocouples, etc.); 

 application of numerical codes: Origen (fuel depletion, radionuclide composition, activity), MCNP6 (neutrons, gamma, charged particles transport), Ansys-Fluent (thermos-hydraulic calculations), etc.; 

 operational measurements, e.g. reactivity measurements of control rods, temperature reactivity coefficient measurements; 

 failed fuel detection system (control and data acquisition, processing); 

 experiments and completed monitoring software; 

 design and manufacture of new elements and facilities for reactor operation systems and for irradiation facilities including gamma sterilisation; 

 technology for irradiation ofmaterials for radioisotope production in cooperation with the Radioisotope Centre POLATOM, QUIREM (Netherlands) and CTC (Japan).

The point kinetics reactor model assumes a constant spatial shape of the neutron flux in a critical reactor, even in transients. According to this approach, a local perturbation in the neutron flux affects reactor reactivity which is a global parameter of the entire reactor and which, in turn, alters the global neutron population. Therefore, when a critical reactor is locally perturbed, the perturbation propagates uniformly across the entire reactor, retaining a constant spatial shape of the neutron flux. As a result, the spatial neutron distribution remains fixed and only the total neutron population changes in time [1]. This means that the neutron flux at any point r

of the considered reactor may be expressed as follows: 

𝜑(𝒓, 𝑡) = 𝜓(𝒓) 𝑛(𝑡) ,

where 𝜓(𝒓) is a shape function and 𝑛(𝑡) is the flux intensity. 

Let us assume that as a result of a perturbation, the shape function changes to 

𝜑 ′(𝒓, 𝑡) = 𝜓 ′(𝒓) 𝑛(𝑡) .

Thus, a measure of the departure of the reactor response to the perturbation from the point reactor kinetics model is given by the following relationship: 

𝜀(𝒓) = 𝜓(𝒓) 𝜓′(𝒓) − 1 

The point applicability of the kinetics reactor model is limited to reactors with dimensions that are only a few neutron migration lengths (or diffusion lengths). The predominant construction material and main neutron moderator in the MARIA reactor core is beryllium. In the case of beryllium the migration length (or diffusion length) is more than 20 cm [2], whereas the extent of the MARIA reactor core reaches approx. 70 cm. 

Answering the question of the Polish National Nuclear Regulatory Body concerning the applicability of the point kinetics model to the MARIA reactor, it was decided to perform an appropriate experiment. 

A peculiarity of the MARIA reactor enables on-line measurement of the neutron flux shape function 𝜓(𝒓) 

spatial distribution. The thermal (fission) power of each of the nuclear fuel elements in the MARIA reactor is measured on-line with 1 Hz frequency by means of the SAREMA system, whereas the fission power distribution is directly proportionaly to the thermal neutron flux distributions. Therefore, it was decided to use the fission power distribution to determine the shape function spatial distribution. 

The experiment was carried out in two steps: on 11 th and 12 th May 2018. Each time the compensation of two control rods was made: control rod PK1 (in channel H-VII) and control rod PK6 (in channel G-VIII), cf. fig. 1. All the other rods were withdrawn except the automatic regulation rod (PAR). 

During the compensation, the reactor was operated with the automatic power control system on, maintaining constant reactor power. In the first step PK1 was withdrawn from 630 mm up to 730 mm, whereas PK6 was simultaneously inserted from 580 mm down to 350 mm. This resulted in inserting of the reactivity equal to +0.46 $ and –0.46 $ respectively. In the second step PK1 was inserted from 740 mm down to 605 mm, whereas PK6 was simultaneously withdrawn from 380 mm up to 1100 mm, Which resulted in inserting of the reactivity equal to –0.92 $ and +0.92 $ respectively. 

Fig. 1. The MARIA reactor core configuration. 

The thermal power of each of the nuclear fuel channels were recorded for 10 minutes before the compensation. Subsequently, 15 minutes after compensation (break for thermal parameter equalisation) the power was recorded once again for a period of 10 minutes .ANNUAL REPORT 2018 _____________________________________________________________________________________

Follow-up calculations of the MARIA reactor core neutronics characteristics are a very important part of the safety analysis. An excess of reactivity for specific core configuration has to be obtained before every operation. 

The analysis is carried out using a three-dimensional diffusion model. To automate these calculations and reduce the errors in preparation of a complex input file a special computing system with easy to use Graphical User Interface was developed (Fig. 1). 

The system consists of the server that manages the execution of calculation tasks by a pool of workers, a database and the user interface. 

The GUI allows for intuitive/easy preparation of a new 

core configuration  (drag’n’drop method), and send s it to the calculating module. Calculations can be carried out in parallel, so many different configurations can be analysed. 

The database stores historical information about fuel elements and beryllium block composition, operational data such as excess of reactivity, power changes during cycles, fuel burn-up, core and fuel storage configurations, reactor start and shutdown dates and results of previous calculations. Data are available for every operational cycle since 2012 (from the beginning of the core conversion from high to low enriched fuel) till now. The historical data are used as a basis for the analysis of proposed core configurations. 

An additional advantage of a GUI is the use of colour maps for fuel burn-up and beryllium block poisoning. This allows quick, visual evaluation of the reactor core state.

# Model for Radionuclide Migration 

# Through the MARIA Reactor Safety Barriers 

M. Lipka 

Migration of the radionuclides gathered in partially burned-up fuel element through the safety barriers is an important issue during a hypothetical incident with fuel cladding integrity loss. The MARIA reactor has several layers of safety barriers and filtration systems that significantly minimise the threat to the reactor personnel and the general public. 

Fission products from cracked fuel elements are released to the fuel channels cooling loop and are then deposited in the filtration system of fuel channels cooling loop, migrate to the pressuriser gas space, and leak through seals to the reactor pool 

Radionuclides in the filtration system are not further removed but they undergo radioactive decay. From the reactor pool, radionuclides are released to the air space below the reactor pool covers, additionally they deposit on the hall surface and some of them are desorbed back. Finally, through the ventilation system protected by the Vokes filters set, radionuclides are released from the reactor stack to the atmosphere. A schematic of radionuclide migration routes through the MARIA reactor safety barriers is presented in figure 1 

Fig. 1: Schematic of radionuclide migration routes through the safety barriers. 

In figure 2 the dose rate in the proximity of certain reactor system is presented. Figure 3 shows the yearly dose to the general population from all routes of exposure (cloud immersion, inhalation and ground deposits). A, D, and F refer to the corresponding Pasquill atmosphere stability class. 

Fig. 2: Dose rates to reactor personnel. 

Fig 3: Yearly dose rates to the general population. 

Calculation results show that a reactor worker might receive a maximum dose in the proximity of the pressuriser (31 mSv) after 5 hours of constant exposure. Both of the doses are within legal limits: 100 mSv for reactor personnel during an accident and a general limit of 1 mSv/a for the general population respectively.

# Thermal Conditions of MARIA Reactor in the Case of Pool Water  Disappearence 

G. Madejowski 

One may observe a turn towards a safety functions-based philosophy in the approach of the Polish National Nuclear Regulatory Body to reactor safety. In this aproach, certain safety functions are assigned to the reactor installations. The reactor behaviour under a set of scenarios, assuming that a certain installation loses one of its safety functions, is then analysed. However, neither the physical possibility of the particular kind of event nor the triggering scenario are taken into account. Probably even more controversial is the neglect of the dynamics of the loss, assuming its immediacy. This paper presents the results of an attempt to evaluate the impact of a disappearence of the pool water, as required by the Regulatory Body. 

The reactor pool fulfils two safety functions – it shields against ionising radiation and removes heat from the core, especially from the control rods (but not from the fuel, as this has a separate cooling system). Disappearence of the pool water should trigger an automatic reactor shutdown; however, the fission power would follow the laws of reactor kinetics, forming a delayed tail. The activities of the Radiological Metrology and Biomedical Physics Division are primarily focused on three main areas: 

1. Dosimetry and radiation measurements in mixed radiation fields 

2. Nanodosimetry and medical physics 

3. Radiobiology 

The main research topics of the dosimetry group consist of: 

 development of methods for the determination of operational dosimetric quantities and dose distribution vs. LET in mixed radiation fields, using high-pressure ionisation chambers; 

 design and construction of recombination ionisation chambers and dosimeters; 

 investigation of ionisation and recombination phenomena in gases; 

 metrology of mixed radiation fields including short-pulse and high energy radiation; 

 neutron dosimetry in a wide energy spectrum; 

 verification of installed dosimetry systems for medical applications; 

 absorbed dose distribution assessment for SIRT therapy; 

 passive dosimetry including TLD and EPR. 

In 2018 the repertoire of available research in the field of dosimetry was expanded by the addition of an EPR spectrometer to the instrument base of the division. The primary use of this apparatus is alanine dosimetry which complements the array of dosimetry methods (such as TLD) already available in the division. Furthermore, the ability to gather EPR spectra has led to the commencement a research project aimed at examining other aminoacids and their derivatives as potential dosimeters in biological applications. This project may also branch out into a radiochemical project aimed at determining free radical structures via the use of EPR spectroscopy. 

Another major focus of the division is the “Neutrony H2” project aimed at constructing and maintaining a research-training facility at the MARIA reactor. The bulk of renovation and construction work has already been completed. The goals of research at this facility are: 

 constructing a uranium neutron converter for a dense neutron beam; 

 thermo-hydraulic analyses (CFD) of the neutron converter, aimed at optimizing and enabling safe output of the epithermal neutron beam; 

 development of a Beam Shaping Assembly (BSA) and room shielding; 

 development of dosimetry methods for hadron therapy, with particular emphasis on boron-neutron capture therapy (BNCT) and investigation of radiation fields near radiation therapy facilities. 

One of the major achievements of 2018 was the creation of the Biomedical Research group. The group is focused on the influence of ionising radiation on biological material, mainly cancer cells and nematodes. The group has swiftly organised a laboratory, entered several research collaborations and expanded in members and competence. One of the focuses of this group is preparation of pre-clinical trials for research related to Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT). Thanks to the actions of members of the group at the ICNCT-18 congress, NCBJ has been nominated to host the ICNCT-20 conference in 2022. This is a large (over 400 expected participants), international event in the field of Boron Neutron Capture Therapy hosted biannually in various major scientific institutions. 

Nanodosimetry focuses on the use of the JetCounter, a unique apparatus for measurements of single ionisation events. In 2018 a new approach was suggested which would expand the JetCounters applications to non-charged particles such as neutrons and photons. Initial research and calculations of this new non-coincidence mode are very promising as measurements from the non-coincidence mode have been successfully recalculated into measured coincidental mode spectra. 

Moreover, the Nanodosimetry and Medical Physics group is engaged in the JINR-NICA project in which they are developing a dosimetric system. Secondary research interests in the group are recombination chambers at the micro scale.

# Based on Organic Compounds 

K. Dobrzelewski, Ł . Bartosik, S. Domański 

EPR spectroscopy allows the measurement of microwave radiation absorption in a variable magnetic field to detect free radicals. Free radicals are formed, for example, during irradiation of organic substances with gamma radiation[1]. # of Recombination Dosimeters: Status  at the End of 2018 

M. Kuć, P. Tulik, M. A. Gryziński 

The scope of this study is the current status of the REM-3.4, REM-3.8 and REM-3.9 recombination chambers designed and made at the National Centre for Nuclear Research in 2010-2014 [1-2]. 

The REM-3 series detectors are cylindrical parallel-plate recombination chambers based on the REM-2 detector with an active volume of about 2000 cm 3

ultimately filled with ethane. The REM-3.4, REM-3.8 and REM-3.9 detectors are respectively: integrating (one large volume with only one voltage terminal), differential (alternating two types of voltage electrodes connected to the two terminals), and dual (two electrically separated active volumes with terminals from both sides) recombination chambers. 

The expected result of the work was to determine the current response of REM-3 series detectors exposed to ionizing radiation. Main goals: to become acquainted with the operation, construction and technology of REM-3 detectors; development of the workplace for assembly and work on the detectors; modification, start-up and calibration of REM-3 chambers. Effects: commissioning and calibration of REM-3.4 and REM-3.9 detectors (Tab. 1); a proposal to redesign the REM-3.8 detector; purchase and manufacture of laboratory equipment and instruments for further work on the detectors. 

Status of the detectors after the work: 

 REM-3.4. Assembled, filled with gas, calibrated in gamma and neutron radiation fields using 137 Cs, Pu-Be and 252 Cf isotopic sources, recombination voltage in recommended range, fully functional. 

 REM-3.8. Disassembled, under reconstruction. 

 REM-3.9. Assembled, filled with gas, calibrated with a 137 Cs isotopic gamma source, recombination voltage outside the recommended range. 

The main conclusion from this research is the need to change the approach to the construction issue. A mechanically stiff construction with a repeatable structure should be obtained. The implementation of a unique detector in individual quantities is undesirable due to the possibility of commercialization. The changes made to the REM-2 detectors were justified, but too radical. Despite the better dosimetric properties, mechanical sturdiness tightness and reproducibility were lost. In the new design the current electrode was redesigned, but the pressure connections and valves were also changed. The effect of the changes is the simultaneous appearance of many new challenges, each of which may have an impact on the final effect, i.e. the result of measurements in radiation fields.

# Evaulation of the Radiation Exposure Around the H2 Channel Rooms 

# in the MARIA Reactor using Thermoluminescence Dosimetry Methods 

M. Wiliński 

Thermoluminescence detectors (TLD) based on Lithium 

Fluoride are detectors that enable α, β, γ and neutron 

dose measurements, as well as measurement in mixed fields, while still being able to have a wide measuring range [1-2]. 

The goal of this study was to determine the radiological hazard in rooms adjacent to the H2 channel in the MARIA reactor. 

For this purpose, LiF: Mg, Cu, P detectors were used. 

They are available commercially as MCP-N (N stands for natural 6Li/ 7Li abundance) and MCP-7 material. MCP-7 contains about 99% 7Li (with negligible cross-section for neutron interaction compared to 6Li). The cross-sections for ionization by gamma radiation are similar in both cases [1-2]. 

Based on previously made measurements [3], five points [Fig. 1] were selected, in which the TLDs were placed for five measuring periods within a year, lasting from 2 to 3 months. 

Fig. 1. Measurement points in rooms adjacent to the H2 channel. 

In addition, a calibration was carried out using a Cs 137 

source with doses from 100 μSv to 1 Sv. Within the scope of this calibration the detectors showed a linear response. 

After the measurement the irradiated detectors were read using a TLD reader – TL RA94. The reading was carried out at a temperature ranging from 50 to 270 °C, with a temperature rise of 1 °C/s. Temperature increased linearly the whole time. 

The results were then analyzed with custom prepared software. The data obtained from glow curves allowed us to calculate the absorbed dose (Hp*(10)) for the measurement period at each examined point. Results are shown in [Fig. 2 and 3]. 

Fig. 2. Neutron dose results, measurement periods marked as I-V. 

Fig. 3. Gamma dose results, measurement periods marked as I-V. 

The study further confirmed previous measurements and showed the radiation distribution inside the rooms adjacent to the H2 channel. Therefore, the proposed method of measurement might be used again for further radiation situation monitoring in rooms adjacent to the H2 channel.

# Nanodosimetry with the Jet Counter  – Progress in the Acquisition System 

M. Pietrzak 1, A. Bancer 1, A. Dudziński 1, E. Jaworska 1, M. Mietelska 1, 2

> 1

National Centre for Nuclear Research,  Świerk , Poland 

> 2

Faculty of Physics, University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Poland 

Experimental nanodosimetry is aimed at direct measurement of the ionisations created by a single ionising particle in a nanometric volume equivalent to a short segment of DNA [1]. 

The track structure of the ionizing particle is frequently considered to play an important role in the whole balance of the radiation damage. 

The nanodosimeter —Jet Counter (JC) —is capable of measuring track structure characteristics on the nanometric scale by counting the number of ions created by a single projectile in a nanometric volume. Ions created in such a nano-volume form an ionization cluster and the number of ions in a cluster is called the cluster-size. An estimation of the ionization cluster-size probability distribution, ICSD, is the main results of a nanodosimetric experiment. For details see Ref. [2]. 

One of the most important components of the device is its acquisition system. The first system was based on simple ion counting with the use of a fast multiscaler. However, it soon became clear that for a full characterization many more parameters should be registered. The new acquisition system is capable of simultaneous registration of the drift time of each ion in the cluster, as well as the arrival time, energy and position of the trajectory of the projectile responsible for the given cluster. 

The current acquisition system (see Fig. 1) consists of one fast oscilloscope with a sampling rate of 1 GS/s (to register ions) and a second one with a sampling rate of 10 MS/s (to register projectiles). 

Fig. 1. Diagram presenting the current acquisition system. 

The oscilloscopes are synchronized to register 5 signals simultaneously (1 for ions, and 4 for projectiles). Waveforms are recorded by a custom developed program that also allows for preliminary data analysis during the experiment. The program window with a sample result is presented in Figure 2. 

The new acquisition system of the Jet Counter has been successfully used during nanodosimetric measurements of the carbon ion beam at Heavy Ion Laboratory, University of Warsaw.

Primary liver cancers (PLC) such as hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma are one of the most frequently diagnosed malignancies and show relatively low survival rates. The most common approaches to cancer treatment include surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy. However, external-beam radiotherapy and chemotherapy affect not only the tumour but also its surrounding tissues. Administration of a radio-pharmaceutical in direct proximity of the tumour yields superior therapeutic results and limits the number of side effects. Radiopharmaceuticals used for PLC treatment are yttrium or holmium microspheres. Microspheres are administered directly to the hepatic arteries supplying the tumour. This ensures the spheres will reach cancer cells and limits the irradiation of healthy tissues surrounding the tumour. The administration of radiolabelled microspheres, called radioembolisation (or Selective Internal Radiation Therapy, SIRT), is a procedure nowadays commonly performed in leading nuclear medicine facilities, in Poland uniquely at the Military Institute of Medicine in Warsaw (WIM). 

Since one of the issues that need to be revised and developed in SIRT is the dosimetry during and after the treatment, NCBJ and WIM formed a consortium and began a common project in 2018. The aim of the project is comprehensively to assess the distribution of radiation emitted by 90 Y microspheres used for liver tumour embolisation in a model. The following activities were performed during the first period of the realisation. 

Task 1. Numerical simulation of dose distribution derived from 90 Y isotope in a patient equivalent phantom 

Software for digital phantom modelling as well as for Monte Carlo simulations was chosen. In order to accomplish this task the FLUKA and MCNP codes were selected. It was decided to use both applications due to the mutual validation of the obtained results, as well as reducing the risk of non-implementation of the task due to possible program limitations. A procedure, based on DICOM images from X-ray computed tomography, for obtaining a digital representation of a bucket phantom (a digital voxel model) was developed (Fig. 1.).

# Activities within the EURADOS  –

# European Radiation Dosimetry Group 

M. Maciak, K. Tymińska, E. Michaś, M. Kuć, M. Murawski, S. Domański, J. Ośko, M. A. Gryziński 

The European Radiation Dosimetry group (EURADOS) is a non-profit organisation promoting research and development and European cooperation in the field of the dosimetry of ionising radiation [1]. EURADOS comprises a self-sustainable network of more than 60 European institutions and 300 scientists active in the field of radiation dosimetry and has established Working Groups (WGs) in various dosimetric disciplines such as harmonisation of individual monitoring, environmental dosimetry, computational dosimetry, internal dosimetry, dosimetry for medical applications, retrospective dosimetry, and dosimetry in high energy radiation fields. 

Researchers from NCBJ participate in research activities within EURADOS (http://www.eurados.org/) in the following groups: 

WG6 – Computational dosimetry 

Working Group 6 promotes good practice in the field of computational methods in radiation dosimetry for radiation protection and applications in radiation medicine. It carries out scientific research and development as well as knowledge transfer activities in the area of computational dosimetry. While Monte Carlo simulations are the dominant method, other aspects of computational dosimetry such as spectra unfolding or the proper use of voxelised geometrical models are also considered. 

In 2018 we took part in an intercomparison study on the usage of the ICRP/ICRU voxel reference computational phantoms together with radiation transport codes. The aim of this activity is to give participants the opportunity to check their own calculations against quality-assured master solutions, and to improve their approach, if needed. The tasks to be solved consider a variety of exposure scenarios (occupational, environmental, and medical) and radiation types (photons, electrons, neutrons). 

WG7 – Internal Dosimetry 

The Internal Dosimetry community dealing with occupational exposure is currently focused on: the harmonis ation of methods and tools to obtain the “best estimate” of the intake and do se due to the incorporation of radionuclides into the body (ICRP, IDEAS Guidelines); networking and coordination of research to promote collaboration of internal dosimetry experts, laboratories and services; normalisation for the establishment of Standards for appropriate quality assurance programmes that guarantee reliability of the results of monitoring and dose E(50) and permit accreditation of internal dosimetry laboratories. 

WG9 – Radiation dosimetry in radiotherapy 

The motivation of this Working Group is to assess and develop existing and potential dosemeters and dosimetric techniques in radiotherapy and, in particular, to assess non-target patient doses and the related risks of secondary malignancy, with the emphasis on a thorough evaluation of dosimetry methods for the measurement of doses remote from the target in two parts at the Cyclotron Centre Bronowice volume in phantom experiments. In 2018 comparative measurements were carried out: 

1) Dosimetry of scattered radiation in 30x30x60cm 3

water phantom after irradiation through a mesh collimator (grid proton therapy). 

2) Measurements of doses from scattered radiation in a child phantom, with a beam formed by a 3D printed compensator. 

The main aim of these studies was to determine the influence of the doses from scattered and secondary radiation fields generated by a high-energy proton beam to the total dose including the planned therapeutic dose. The Polish team from NCBJ participated in the second part of the comparisons with the 3D printed compensator. For the measurements REM-2 and GW-2 ionization chambers were used. Results of the measurement session will be published at the end of 2019. 

WG11 – High energy radiation fields 

The motivation of Working Group 11 is to increase knowledge and expertise regarding field characterisation and dose assessment in various activities where high energy radiation fields are found, such as medicine, research, civil aviation, and space. In addition, the WG contributes to the development of international standards and recommendations (e.g. ISO, ICRU, ICRP). # Materials Research Laboratory 

Head of Laboratory Łukasz Kurpaska, PhD 

The Materials Research Laboratory (MRL) is one of the three laboratories included in the Department of Materials Physics (MPD) of the National Centre for Nuclear Research (NCBJ). MRL is engaged in research work covering all aspects of materials engineering. Investigations are carried out on structural materials and their welded joints including investigations performed on irradiated materials. The MRL Hot laboratory is the only facility in Poland able to handle and perform mechanical, structural and chemical investigations on materials irradiated in nuclear reactors. All studies performed in MRL are conducted according to a Quality Assurance Programme. 

The main part of the Hot Laboratory is a set of 12 hot cells with lead shielding to enable handling of radioactive materials with activity levels up to 4 TBq related to 60 Co. Every cell is equipped with different devices providing flexibility for a wide nuclear research programme involving metallurgical, physical and chemical testing of irradiated structural materials. The main equipment installed at MRL includes: 

 Instron 8500 Dynamic Testing System with two 100 kN frames for testing tensile and compressive strength, low cycle fatigue resistance, fracture toughness, bend characteristics and crack growth resistance over the -150  ᵒC to 1000  ᵒC temperature range (a tender for comprehensive moderni sation of this system  was  completed 

at the end of 2018) ,

 Instrumented Wolpert Pendulum Impact Testing Machine PW 30/15 for dynamic tests of Charpy-V type specimens carried out over the -150  ᵒC to 800  ᵒC temperature range, for determination of significant force and 

deflection values, partial energy values and cha racteristic mechanical  fracture  values, 

 DIA-TESTOR 7521 Wolpert Hardness Testing Machine for tests using the Brinell, Vickers and Rockwell procedures,

 ARL 3460 Spectrometer for quantitative analyses of the chemical composition of metals.

The remaining equipment of the hot cell complex allows us to perform:

# Evaluation of the effect of Consolidation Methods on the Mechanical 

# and Structural Properties of ODS RAF Steel 

M. Frelek-Kozak 1, Ł. Kurpaska 1, E. Wyszkowska 1, J. Jagielski 1,2 , I. J óź wik 1,2 , M. Chmielewski 2

> 1

National Centre for Nuclear Research, Świerk, Poland 

> 2

Institute of Electronic Materials Technology, Warsaw, Poland 

In the present work, the effects of the fabrication method on the mechanical and structural properties of 12% Cr, 2%W, 0.25%Ti, 0.25%Y2O3 steels were investigated. Materials obtained by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS), Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) and Hot Extrusion (HE) methods were studied. The microstructure was characterised using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Electron Backscatter Diffraction analysis (EBSD). The mechanical properties of the studied samples were evaluated using the Vickers micro hardness HV0.1, Small Punch Test (SPT) and nanoindentation (NI) methods. The analysis revealed that samples manufactured via the HIP and SPS processes exhibit very similar properties, whereas the SPS method produces material with slightly lower hardness. In addition, significantly lower mechanical properties of the specimens after the HE process were observed. The study described in this article also addresses the problems of the mechanical parameters measured in micro- and nano-scale experiments and aims to identify possible pitfalls related to the use of various manufacturing technologies. 

Fig. 1. SEM (left) and EBSD (right) images of ODS steels manufactured using A) Spark Plasma Sintering, B) Hot Isostatic Pressing and C) Hot Extrusion technique. 

Conclusions 

Three types of 12% Cr ODS steel specimens consolidated with different methods were investigated in terms of microstructure and mechanical properties. All consolidation methods provide the possibility of manufacturing fine-grained materials with homogenously dispersed nanoprecipitates. The difference between the methods lies in the material volume production feasibility. SPS and HIP methods allows microstructures with grains sim- ilar in terms of size and shape (equiaxed) to be obtained. Thus, materials manufactured with these methods exhibit comparable mechanical properties. HE samples display a strong texture according to the extrusion direction. Complex post-processing including hot forging, cold rolling and heat treatment did not eliminate the microstructural anisotropy. Microstructure texture is related to the anisotropy of the mechanical properties, i.e. yield strength, ultimate strength, Young modulus and hardness. 

Mechanical parameters were evaluated with three different methods: nanoindentation, micro-hardness and small punch tests. Good correlation between nano- and micro-scale measurements was observed. The highest similarity was revealed between nanoindentation and micro-hardness tests. The relationship between nanoindentation and SPT was less accurate, although SPT tests are able to reveal differences and tendencies between materials, so that this method may thus be used for additional screening and selection of materials.

The main aim of this work was to synthesise the holmium-doped monoclinic KGd(WO 4)2 (KGW) nanoparticles by the mechano-chemical method. The second aim was to investigate the chemical, physical, optical properties and viability cells study in the direction of application in medical diagnostics. KGW is an excellent host for RE ions giving possibilities to obtain a wide spectrum of light emission [1]. In recent times, KGW have started to play an important role in nanosize scale form. 

In our work, the structure and morphology of KGW:Ho 10 at.% nanopowders were investigated with the use of X-ray Powder Diffraction, Atomic Force Microscopy and Scanning Electron Microscopy. Emission and excitation spectra of KGW nanocrystals were also measured using a fluorometer with a xenon lamp and OPO laser source. The influence of nanoparticles on the viability of J774.1 mouse BALB/c monocyte macrophage cells was tested by WST8 assay. 

We successfully obtained one phase of nanocrystals of KGW:Ho 10 at.% in the size range 80 –200 nm. We also provided the physicochemical characterisation (agglomeration, solubility, stability in body fluids) and viability in in vitro tests (Fig. 2 a-b). The purpose of this study was to show KGW:Ho 10 at.% nanocrystals as potential nanomaterials for biological imaging. Preliminary immunity cell studies demonstrated a high viability of KGW:Ho 10% at. Our optical and chemical study confirmed their strong luminescence and physicochemical stability in typical organic fluids. Hence, these nanoparticles are promising for imaging applications. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of KGW:Ho 10 at.% nanomaterials regarding their usefulness in bioimaging.

# Nuclear Methods in Solid State Physics Division 

Head of Division Jacek J. Milczarek, PhD 

The Division is involved in research into the microscopic structure and dynamics of condensed matter systems. The techniques employed permit studies to be performed from the atomic level to macroscopic phenomena. Methods based on the interaction of radiations with matter comprise X-ray (XRD and synchrotron radiation) and thermal neutrons (neutron scattering and neutron radiography). Six thermal neutron beams from the MARIA research reactor were used in research till 2017. Some specialised techniques such as high pressure systems, rapid quenching and the sol-gel method have also been applied. 

In 2018 the Division was involved in a major refurbishment of the experimental hall of the MARIA nuclear reactor. The aim is the deployment of the thermal neutron diffractometers from the Ber-II reactor of the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin. The instruments to be transferred to MARIA are equipped with two-dimensional detector systems and special systems for settings changes based on air-cushions. Short summary of chosen, realized project in 2018 (ongoing). 

Optimal doping concentration of RE ions implanted in a single ZnO crystal – ConQRE. 

Financial support of:The Polish Ministry of Science from resources intended for education in 2017-2019 for the implementation of an international co-financed project (Grant No 3846/HZDR/17/2018/0). 

Even though the research focusing on ZnO started many decades ago, this material has been experiencing a renewed interest because of a wide potential application spectrum in microelectronics, organic electronics, biosensors and spintronics. Moreover, the high exciton binding energy (60 meV) of this material also suits it to optical and optoelectronic applications such as light-emitting diodes and phosphors. The basic light emission from ZnO is located in the violet-blue spectral range. Doping with Rare Earths (RE) can modify the optical properties of ZnO and tune the optical emission into the visible spectral range. 

However, the simple recipe of increasing the concentration of dopant to increase the luminescence intensity in the case of RE ions doesn't work due to the increasing energy transfer between the densely packed RE centers, causing an increased probability to lose the excitation energy by non-radiative processes. This phenomenon, called the 

concentration quenching effect has been poorly investigated so far in RE doped ZnO and the achieved results are quite inconsistent. 

The investigations performed within the Project are aimed at studies of the concentration quenching effect for ZnO epitaxial layers doped with RE by ion implantation. Ion implantation is an attractive tool for doping materials commonly used in opto- and micro- electronics. However, an important limitation of this technique is the buildup of lattice disorder due to the ballistic nature of the process. Additionally, in the as-implanted stage, most of the dopants are optically inactive and post-implantation annealing is required. The authors are planning to compare the concentration dependence of the luminescence intensity of Yb 3+ and Er 3+ ions incorporated in the ZnO matrix. Interestingly, the concentration quenching effect also influences the electrical properties of the material, therefore, this aspect will also be studied. The crucial task of this Project is understanding the driving forces for the quenching effects. High-speed stainless (HSS) steel is still a popular material in wood-based material mechanics, especially as it applies to drills, despite the introduction of new tool materials like WC-Co composite, polycrystalline diamond and others. The continued use of HSS can be attributed to lower cost, reduction of breakage in older spindles and hand routers, sharper edges allowing for easier hand feeding, and different geometries [1]. 

Tools are often surface-modified to prolong their lifetime. There are three ways to extend the lifetime of tools: modification of the surface region, deposition of an additional layer, and duplex treatment, i.e., modification of the surface region and the deposition of an additional layer [2]. 

Ion implantation is the method whereby the near-surface area is modified. The modified region is not a layer, therefore no problem occurs with adhesion and a change in the dimensions. This process can be conducted at 

temperatures <100°C. 

HSS Leitz drills (Leitz GmbH and Co. KG, Stuttgart, Germany) with a diameter of 10 mm and total length of 68 mm (dowel drills with 10-mm shanks), commonly used in the furniture industry and presented in Fig. 1, were used for the investigations.

The rake faces of high-speed steel drills were implanted with nitrogen ions with a non-mass separated beam in a homemade semi-industrial implanter (beam current density at a level of 0.3 mA/cm 2) and with a MEVVA type implanter with a direct beam (beam current density at a level of 1 mA/cm 2). Nitrogen of 99.9% purity was used as the source of the implanted ions. The implanted doses were in the range from 2e17 cm -2 to 6e17 cm -2 .The implanted nitrogen was delivered as two kinds of ions, i.e., N2++N +. Ions were implanted at 60 kV acceleration voltage. This paper presents studies focused on improving friction and wear properties of acrylonitrile-butadiene rubber (NBR). The main objective of the present study is to investigate the impact of a wide range of ions, irradiated with different energies and fluencies, and find correlations between friction coefficient, nanohardness and mechanical strength of NBR-type elastomers. 

The studies revealed that both hardness and Young Modulus increase with irradiation dose [10-11]. This effect is more visible in the case of NBR rubber without addition of graphene filler and irradiated with an energy of 150 keV. In this case, the hardness increases from 0.01 GPa up to 0.12 GPa after the irradiation campaign (Fig. 1a). A similar situation can be observed for Young Modulus calculations (Fig. 1b).

This suggests that the hard layer on the surface of the soft bulk may lead to spreading of the load over a much higher volume, hence reducing the deformation of the elastomer below the counter-sample and, in consequence, the work readed for displacement of the counter-sample, hence the friction coefficient. Fig. 2. Friction coefficient measured during a pin-on-disc test of NBR elastomers with a) and without b) graphene filler, before and after He ion irradiation campaigns. 

It thus seems that the reduction of the friction coefficient is related to the higher hardness of the surface layer, which leads to a better distribution of the load over the surface of the material. This phenomenon reduces elastic deformation of the underlying bulk material and, finally, the friction forces. The studies performed in this work allowed us to observe, that the Young modulus and hardness of the irradiated layers increase with the irradiation fluence. The effect is likely due to a massive hydrogen release from the surface layer. The results obtained in friction and wear tests confirm the assumption that He irradiation leads to significant reduction of friction and increase of wear resistance of NBR elastomers. # in the Analysis of Silver -Copper Alloys 

A. M. Gójska, E. A. Miśta -Jakubowska 

The X-ray fluorescence (XRF) is one of the most useful analytical techniqe used in materials composition determinations and it is often used in art and cultural heritage research 1. Since the XRF method is non-destructive, it gives among others an opportunity to analyze the composition of Ag-Cu based artifacts 1,2 . Quantitative analysis of samples requires the application of adequate theoretical methods or empirical approaches. In quantitative XRF analysis, the measured fluorescence intensities are converted into element concentrations. There are several methods which are based on the theoretical relationship between the intensities and concentrations of elements, among others 2: the fundamental parameters method,  Ca sting 

approximatio n and  “par -to -ccr” calibration . These three 

quantitative evaluation method s were used  to 

determine the elemental composition analysis of three 

historical  Polish coins  (Fig.  1). 

Fig. 1. ED-XRF spectrum of boratynka 1664, 

15 kopek/1 złoty 1838 and 2 złot e 1933. 

The XRF system was calibrated for the intensity analysis by means of the ESPI Metals reference material with 75%-90% Ag and 25%-10% Cu (Fig. 2). 

In the XRF elemental composition analysis the possibilities and limitations of the XRF system are crucial for the determination of the sample base alloys and to verify whether the obtained results are consistent. One of the key parameters determining the lowest possible amount of the element that can be detected is the minimum detectable limit: MDL = 2.33C i√B/S , where Ci is the concentration of the element, B is the background counting rate, and S is the net peak counting rate. The minimum detectable limits of the system for Cu and Ag obtained using the ESPI Ag-Cu alloys calibration are ~30 ppm for Cu and ~120 ppm for Ag. 

Fig. 2. XRF spectra of ESPI reference material and background spectrum. 

The Ag content of the Ag-Cu coins obtained using the three quantitative evaluation methods is presented in Fig. 3. 

Fig. 3. Silver concentration obtained using FP,  Ca sting 

and  “par -to -ccr”  methods. 

The differences between the concentrations obtained using the XRF-FP software and the par-to-ccr 

calibration method and Casting approximation are ~1% for copper and ~2% for silver. The obtained results showed the system designed at NCBJ gave comparable values for determining the concentrations so it could be a good alternative to other spectroscopic methods.

# DEPARTMENT OF FUNDAMENTAL RESEARCH 

Director of Department Professor Stanisław Mrówczyński 

The activities of the department in 2018are presented in some detail in the sections devoted to its four Divisions: the Nuclear Physics Division (BP1), Theoretical Physics Division (BP2), High Energy Physics Division (BP3) and Astrophysics Division (BP4). Here only the three main achievements of the department in 2018 are highlighted. 

Observation of Higgs boson coupling to fermions of the third generation. The CMS experiment observed for the first time the Higgs boson decay into a pair of τ leptons and the production of a Higgs boson together with a top quark-antiquark pair. The observations, which were made in proton-proton collisions at a LHC, fully agree with the theoretical predictions of the Standard Model. The group of physicists from NCBJ much contributed greatly to the data analysis. 

Polarisation measurement of gammas from a Gamma Ray Burst by the POLAR experiment. 

The polarisation of gammas originating from a Gamma Ray Burst was measured for the first by the space gamma detector operating on the Chinese satellite TiangGong 2. The measurement, which was achieved by observation of double Compton scattering, shows a very small degree of polarisation which is hard to reconcile with current models of Gamma Ray Bursts. Physicists from NCBJ were responsible for a significant part of electronics and software of the detector. 

Proposal of the FASER experiment. A new experiment ForwArd Search ExpeRiment, or FASER, was proposed to be carried out at the Large Hadron Collider. A theorist from NCBJ was among the proponents. The objective of the experiment is to look for new physics beyond the Standard Model that could have broad implications for particle physics and cosmology, including for dark matter and baryogenesis. The FASER detector will be looking for highly-displaced decays of new light particles decaying into energetic pairs of charged particles of the Standard Model. The experiment is now fully approved by the CERN Research Board.

The Asymptotic Normalization Coefficient or ANC [1,2] has been much in vogue over the past decade or so to quantify the nuclear structure information extracted from direct reaction data, although the concept dates back some fifty years to the reduced renormalisation of Ref. [3]. However, for transfer of charged particles, particularly to states close to emission thresholds, the ANC can become inconveniently large, so the concept of the Coulomb modified ANC was introduced [4], defined as: 

where ℓ is the angular momentum of the transferred 

particle (a) relative to the core nucleus (A),  η =

ZaZAe2μaA /k aA  the Sommerfeld parameter, kaA  =

√(2 μaA ε) the wave number,  μaA  the reduced mass,  ε the 

binding energy,  Γ the gamma function and C the 

standard ANC. 

Fig. 1. Coulomb modified ANC as a function of binding energy ( ε) and excitation energy (E ex ) for the <17 O(1/2 +)| 13 C + α> overlap extracted from (a) 

> 13

C( 6Li,d) 17 O and (b) 13 C( 11 B, 7Li) 17 O data. 

Note that the Coulomb modified ANC depends on the binding energy through both the Whittaker function in the definition of the standard ANC and the argument of the gamma function used in the renormalisation procedure. This suggests that for states close to threshold any uncertainty in the binding energy could impact the accuracy with which the Coulomb modified ANC can be extracted from reaction data. One such state in the 6.356 MeV 1/2 + state of 17 O, ~3 keV below the  α emssion threshold with a stated 

uncertainty of ± 8 keV [5]. 

In Ref. [6] we re-analysed two existing data sets probing the < 17 O(1/2 +)| 13 C + α> overlap via the 13 C( 6Li,d) 17 Oand 13 C( 11 B, 7Li) 17 O reactions using the distorted wave Born approximation to test the dependence of the extracted Coulomb modified ANC on the binding energy. Tests were carried out increasing ε in steps of 1 keV up to the limit of the experimental uncertainty; we did not investigate the effect of reducing ε since this would have led to the state becoming unbound and therefore unsuitable for the extraction of an ANC in this fashion. 

Figure 1 shows our results, which demonstrate a linear dependence of the ANC on ε (the lines on the figure are straight line regression fits assuming a linear dependence), with a variation of approximately a factor of 4 over the range of 8 keV. This represents an intrinsic limit on the precision with which the Coulomb modified ANC can be obtained for this state unless or until the uncertainty in the excitation energy is reduced.

A new setup called EAGLE-EYE has been launched at the Heavy Ion Laboratory (HIL) extending the National Centre for Nuclear Research ’s (NCBJ) scientific portfolio by rapidly developing Fast-Timing techniques. The setup has been developed in cooperation with HIL and consists of 16 high efficiency HPGe spectrometers of the EAGLE array coupled with 24 LaBr 3 detectors forming the EYE Fast-Timing detection device. 24 LaBr 3 detectors of the FATIMA collaboration were used for the first in beam measurements with the full EAGLE-EYE configuration. 

The fast timing logic was based on six ORTEC 935 quad CFD blocks connected with anode signals from 24 LaBr 3 detectors. Three output logic signals from each of 24 CFD units were used forming three sets of 24 output signals utilised for 3 different purposes. Two sets were used for fast timing measurements within the 0-50ns limit using ORTEC TAC 566 blocks. One of the two sets was directly connected to a CEFE unit [1] in order to open appropriate gates for signals coming from another set which was delayed by 15ns. The delayed signals were then redirected to three TAC units where the signal with the lowest number was used as a common start. The remaining signals were fed into three stop TAC inputs allowing the time measurement of subsequent gamma quanta within a two-, three- or four-fold LaBr 3 coincidence. The last set of 24 CFD logic output signals was used for time measurements of delayed gamma quanta within the 0-500ns range with the help of two 16 - channel FERA modules. Such a design has enabled simultaneous fast timing and delayed timing measurements in one event. 

The main features of the EAGLE-EYE setup for in-beam experiments are: 

- proper identification of gamma quanta registered by the LaBr 3 crystals by using additional spectra from the HPGe spectrometers, 

- Fast-Timing measurements in two-, three- or four-fold LaBr 3 coincidence events, 

- cleaning of LaBr 3 energy spectra by gating on contaminating gammas in HPGe detector spectra, 

- Selection of prompt and delayed gamma quanta in theLaBr 3 spectra by using Fast-Timing and delayed-timing logic branches. 

Fig. 1. Schematic drawing of the EAGLE-EYE setup with the LaBr 3 arrangement forming a half-sphere geometry. A single triple LaBr 3 detectors cluster is replaceable by a HPGe spectrometer. 

LaBr 3 detectors from FATIMA, RHOSPHERE, the University of Warsaw and NCBJ were successfully used during recent measurements. The above properties allow several experimental techniques to be applied to the study of isomeric decays, fast single-particle nuclear transitions or collective nuclear states.

# Integrable Toda System as a Quantum Approximation 

# to the Anisotropy of Mixmaster 

H. Bergeron 1, E. Czuchry 2, J.P. Gazeau 3, P. Małkiewicz 2

> 1

SMO, Université Paris -Sud, Orsay, France 

> 2

National Centre for Nuclear Research, Warszawa, Poland 

> 3

The Mixmaster model plays an essential role in our understanding of the near-singularity dynamics of the Universe. The classical Hamiltonian for this model involves an elaborate two-dimensional anisotropy potential. Therefore, the quantisations of the model found in the literature often rely on one of the two approximations to the anisotropy potential: the steep-wall or the harmonic approximation. They enable us analytically to determine the respective eigenstates and eigenvalues and apply adiabatic or nonadiabatic approaches to study the quantum dynamics of the model. 

Fig. 1. A sample solution to the motion of a particle in the anisotropy potential. 

In Ref. [1] we developed an alternative proposal for approximating the anisotropic part of the quantum Hamiltonian with the integrable three-particle Toda system. It approximates the three exponential walls while smoothing out the problematic canyons. This result brings additional possibilities to studies of the quantum dynamics of mixmaster. The periodic three-body Toda system has been analysed both on the classical and quantum levels. Thus, we provide an analytically solvable approximation to the anisotropy potential of the Bianchi IX model, which is valid not only in the large volume and low anisotropy excitation level or in the small volume and high anisotropy excitation level limits (given by the harmonic and steep- wall approximation, respectively), but also in the vast and unexplored in-between region. 

Fig. 2. Contour plot of the Toda potential and a sample solution. 

In our previous work we proved the discreteness of the spectrum originated by the exact Bianchi IX anisotropic potential despite its noncompact character. This result validates all implementations of approximations of the potential, which remove the three nonconfining canyons. Moreover, it was shown on the classical level that the canyons (referred to 

there as “channels”) do not contribute to t he chaotic behaviour of the mixmaster. Therefore, our procedure preserves key properties of the model, specifically those regarding energy levels or possible chaotic behaviour.

The nature of dark matter remains one of the greatest puzzles of particle physics and cosmology. A primary candidate for dark matter is a new kind of elementary particles that has not been discovered yet, in particular weakly-interacting massive particles (WIMPs). They 

are theoretically expected to be “heavy” in the sense 

that they correspond to an energy range from several GeV/c 2 to TeV/c 2. However, the lack of an experimental signal has triggered a surge of interest in exploring another possibility: dark matter could be 

made of “lighter” particles with mass in the range 

from a few MeV/c 2 to hundreds of MeV/c 2.Reproducing WIMP scenarios at the MeV/c 2 scale 

requires the presence of an additional “dark sector”, 

also light but very feebly-interacting with the other elementary particles. 

Fig. 1. Bounds on the forbidden regime from E137 and LSND arising from dark Higgs boson decay (orange shaded regions), from visible dark photon searches and 

from χ2 decay (blue shaded region). The thick black 

lines correspond to points featuring the correct relic density of DM. 

We have explored [1,2] a simple, self-consistent model for such a “dark sector” built to resemble closely what is already known from the visible world. It contained a Dirac fermion DM (a  candidate  for dark matter), 

a dark photon and a dark Higgs boson. The visible and 

dark sector s communicate through a tiny mixing 

between the dark photon and the photon. The key 

finding is that such  a dark matter candidate should be 

primarily searched for in accelerator and fixed -target 

experiments,  at  the so -called “high -intensity frontier” of 

particle physics. Indeed, it turned out that more standard 

limits, such as bounds from the cosmic microwave 

background (CMB) observations and direct searches are 

naturally avoided by such a dark matter, mostly be cause 

most of its interactions with the visible sector are 

strongly suppressed at low velocity. 

We have demonstrated that some of the strongest bounds to date on such dark matter were given by nearly decades-old experiments, LSND and E137, as can be visualised in Figure 1. One of the most interesting signatures of the scenarios, and one which is typical of such light dark sectors, is the presence of long-lived particles. Such particles can travel hundreds of metres in matter before decaying into an electron-positron pair. Since the experimental scene searching for such particles is currently extremely active, the sensitivity to such a dark sector will therefore be strongly enhanced in the course of the next decade. Consequently, it is critical to accompany these experimental advances by identifying and promoting the various recasting possibilities they offer.

New physics has traditionally been expected in the high-pT region at high-energy collider experiments. If new particles are light and weakly-coupled, however, this focus may be completely misguided: light particles are typically concentrated within a few mrad of the beam line, allowing sensitive searches with small detectors, and even extremely weakly-coupled particles may be produced in large numbers there. We have proposed a new experiment [1] at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the ForwArd Search ExpeRiment, or FASER, which will be placed downstream of the ATLAS interaction point in the very forward region and operated concurrently there. 

Fig. 1. Layout of the FASER detector to be placed in tunnel TI12 at the Large Hadron Collider. 

The idea has received a great deal of attention in the community and within a short period of time the growing FASER Colaboration has prepared a Letter of Intent [2] and Technical Proposal [3] for the experiment. The FASER experiment has recently been fully approved by the CERN Research Board to be installed during the Long Shutdown 2 of the LHC and to start taking data during LHC Run 3 in 2021. 

The FASER detector will be looking for highly-displaced decays of light new physics particles into energetic pairs of charged particles from the Standard Model (e.g. electron-positron pairs). The decay products will be detected in the tracker part of the detector and will deposit energy in the calorimeter (see Fig. 1) 

Possible discovery of light and long-lived new physics particles in FASER could have broad implications for particle physics and cosmology e.g. for dark matter studies and baryogenesis. In addition, prospects for TeV-scale neutrino cross section measurements in FASER are analysed where there are no other experimental results. 

FASER will be targeting a number of popular new physics models. In particular, in the initial proposal [1] the prospects for finding dark photons were carefully examined (cf. Fig. 2). More models employing light new physics particles have also be studied in the context of FASER including, e.g., dark Higgs bosons [4], heavy neutral leptons [5], axion-like particles [6], as well as many others in the recently released physics case study [7]. 

Fig. 2. FASER sensitivity to dark photons after the first period of data taking (10 fb -1 ) and after the full LHC Run 3 (150 fb -1 ).

# High Energy Physics Division 

Head of Division Prof essor NCBJ Justyna Łagoda, PhD DSc 

The Division participates in various high energy physics experiments, covering the most interesting topics in article physics, including experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, neutrino oscillations, searches for Dark Matter and accelerator experiments with fixed targets. 

Division employees participate in three experiments at the LHC: CMS, ALICE and LHCb. 

The CMS NCBJ group collaborates with Warsaw University and Warsaw University of Technology. The group continues to work on the improvement of one of the muon triggering subsystems and to perform data analysis. The 

main subjects of interest are decays of the Higgs boson into a pair of τ leptons, in which the significance reached currently is 5σ, and the search for heavy stable charged particles predicted by some extensions of the Standard 

Model, for which no signal has been found yet and only limits on the cross section could be obtained. 

The aim of the ALICE NCBJ group is to study the quark-gluon plasma produced in the collisions of heavy ions and small nuclear systems at high energies. Experimental data have been taken for lead-lead, xenon-xenon, proton-lead and proton-proton collisions at the CERN LHC. The NCBJ group is involved in the reconstruction of the neutral 

pion and ηº -meson spectra and the analysis of the prompt and thermal photon production, which allows the properties of the early stage of the interaction and the thermal properties of the plasma to be determined. The goal of the analysis of the charged particle emission carried out by the group is to infer the degree of plasma thermalisation from the imprint left on the secondary charged particles leaving the interaction region. The group also took part in the construction, maintenance and upgrade of the photon spectrometer and software development for the ALICE experiment. 

The LHCb experiment is dedicated to studies of heavy flavour production and the decays of particles containing the 

b and c quarks. The NCBJ group participates in studies on the violation of the CP and CPT symmetries in the decays of K, D, B and B s mesons, analysis of charmed hyperons and the search for exotic hadronic states. The activity of the group also includes detector maintenance and alignment as well as software development and contribution to computing . 

The neutrino group is mainly involved in the T2K long-baseline experiment in Japan, which aims at a precise determination of the neutrino mixing parameters and a search for CP violation in the lepton sector by observing neutrino oscillations in a muon neutrino beam. The group activity is mostly related to analyses performed in the Near Detector, including measurements of the cross section for (anti)neutrino interactions, in particular a search for interactions of the pair of correlated nucleons, pion production by antineutrinos and strangeness production. The group is also involved in the Near Detector upgrade project for phase II of the T2K experiment and in the Hyper-Kamiokande project. 

Some members of the neutrino group participate in astrophysical activities at the Super-Kamiokande and KM3NeT, performing a search for Dark Matter in the former, and simulations of cosmic ray muon and neutrino production by cosmic ray showers in the latter (which is still under construction). 

Among the fixed-target experiments in which the Division is involved, the NA61/SHINE experiment at the CERN SPS accelerator has a connection with neutrino group, as it provided the differential cross sections for hadron production in the collisions of a proton beam with carbon and the T2K replica target, which allowed the neutrino beam systematic error in the T2K experiment to be greatly suppressed. NA61/SHINE also studied the hadron production in proton-proton and π --carbon collisions. 

COMPASS is a CERN SPS experiment devoted to the study of the intrinsic three-dimensional and spin structure of the proton as well as hadron spectroscopy using high energy hadron and polarised muon beams scattering off polarised and unpolarised targets. Recently, the experiment has provided the first results in the intermediate range of the Bjorken scaling variable xBj on the cross section for deeply virtual Compton scattering on unpolarised protons as a function of the squared four-momentum transfer t. When combined with the results from JLab and HERMES at the valence x Bj region, and with results from the ZEUS and H1 experiments at very small xBj, the COMPASS results allows us to study ‘proton tomography’, i.e. the dependence of the transverse-position distribution of quarks and gluons in the proton as a function of their longitudinal momentum. # Search for CP, CPT Symmetry Violation and Exotic Hadrons 

# at LHCb Experiment 

D. Melnychuk 

The LHCb detector at the LHC accelerator in CERN is a single arm spectrometer which has been designed for CP violation measurements and the search for rare decays. However, due to the exceptional detector properties such as precise tracking and displaced vertex resolution and excellent performance of the PID detectors, its experimental programme has been extended to cover a much wider physics programme including the search for possible CPT violation and hadron spectroscopy. Several topics of this physics programme are covered in the analyses of the Warsaw LHCb group. 

In the Standard Model (SM) CP violation originates from the single irreducible complex phase in the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix and all the measurements of CP violation in particle decays are consistent with this explanation. Nevertheless, the degree of CP violation permitted in the SM is inconsistent with the macroscopic matter-antimatter asymmetry observed in the universe, motivating further studies and searches for non-SM sources of CP violation. 

The Warsaw LHCb group performed an analysis of CP 

symmetry breaking in the decays of charged baryons Ξ +c

→ pK - The expected value of CP violation in the charm sector is below 10 -3 , however, the possible contribution of new physics could enhance it up to 10 -2 ,

which makes it a perfect candidate for the search for new physics. The search for CP violation in multi-body decay gives hope for observation of local CP asymmetries around the resonance states. 

Another test of CP violation consistency with the Standard Model prediction is the measurement of the phase ϕs, which is predicted with very high accuracy. The phase ϕs, is tested in the decays B 0s → J/ψϕ ,where the meson J/ ψ decays into two electrons, and the meson ϕ decays into two kaons. The most precise measurement is performed by LHCb in the same reaction with J/ ψ decays into two muons and the current analysis gives additional 12% to the total statistics. 

The group also performed a search for possible CPT symmetry violation with neutral flavour mesons. Violation of CPT is usually studied in the framework of the Standard Model Extension and any deviation from CPT symmetry would be an indication of physics beyond the Standard Model. The search for CPT symmetry violation is performed in the decays of D mesons and semileptionic decays of B mesons. 

Hadron spectroscopy studies performed by the group are concentrated on the search for exotic hadrons i.e. states different from conventional mesons and baryons. Two analyses have been performed, namely confirmation of the exotic states Z+(4050) and Z+(4250) observed by the Belle experiment in the decay of B + → χc1 π+ π -K+ and possible interpretation 

of excited  Ωc as pentaquarks. 

In addition, the Warsaw LHCb group participates in technical and service tasks for the needs of the LHCb experiment such as development of DIRAC, a general-purpose Interware software for distributed computing systems and technical service and development of a T2-level Grid node for data production. # Border and Skewness Functions from a Leading Order Fit to DVCS Data 

H. Moutarde 1, P. Sznajder 2, J. Wagner 2 

> 1

IRFU, CEA, Universite Paris-Saclay, France  

> 2

Hard exclusive leptoproduction on nucleons has played an important role in studies of hadron structure and gained renewed interest as it allows us to access the Generalised Parton Distributions (GPDs). GPDs provide a novel and comprehensive description of nucleon structure in terms of quarks and gluons, and contain a wealth of new information. In particular, GPDs give a description of the nucleon as an extended object, referred to as three-dimensional nucleon tomography, and give access to the orbital angular momentum of the quarks, which in the future may help to solve the so-called nucleon spin crisis. 

In our recent work we propose new parameterisations for the functions appearing in the description of the 3D nucleon structure in the language of GPDs. These parameterisations are constructed in such a way as to fulfill the basic properties of GPDs, like their reduction to Parton Density Functions and Elastic Form Factors. They also rely on the power behaviour of GPDs in the 

x→1 limit and the propounded analyticity property of 

the Mellin moments of GPDs. We evaluate Compton Form Factors (CFFs), which are Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS) sub-amplitudes, at the leading order and leading twist accuracy. We constrain a restricted number of free parameters of the new parameterisations in a global CFF analysis of almost all existing proton DVCS measurements. The fit is performed within the PARTONS framework, this being the modern tool for generic GPD studies. A distinctive feature of this CFF fit is a careful propagation of uncertainties based on the replica method. 

The fit results genuinely permit nucleon tomography and may give some insight into the distribution of forces acting on partons. As a flavour of the results obtained we show Fig. 1, where a spatial distribution of up quarks is shown as a function of the longitudinal momentum carried by those partons.

appearance and less ͞ ν e appearance events are observed than expected for δCP values of 0 and π. These results can be expressed as allowed regions of the oscillation parameter δCP as shown in Fig.1. Summarizing, the ±2σ 

intervals allow for δCP between [-2.97, -0.63] rad for Normal Hierarchy and [-1.80, -0.98] rad for Inverted Hierarchy. This excludes the CP conserving values of 

δCP at the 2  level so far.

Inverted Hierarchy derived with the Fel dman -Cousins 

method using T2K and reactor data. 

In the near future T2K will enter a new phase of the experiment – T2K-II. In this phase of the experiment we are planning to accumulate 20x10 21 POT by the year 2028 and we may reach 3 σ sensitivity to exclude  δCP  = 0 

and  π. However, to obtain th ese results  an  upgrade of all 

the experiment al  parts is planned:  a beam line upgrade, 

near detector upgrade and doping the far detector Super -

Kamiokande with Gadolinium [2,3]. 

The beam line upgrade will reduce the repetition rate from 2.48s to 1.16s, more protons per pulse (up to 3.2x10 14 ) will be produced and the horn current will reach 320kA to improve beam focusing. Consequently the beam power is expected to reach 1.3MW. 

The current systematic uncertainty related to the precision of the event rate prediction in the far detector is of the order of 6%, but to reach 3 σ sensitivity to CPV 

it needs to be reduced. Th is  can be obtained by reducing 

the systematic errors related to the near detector 

measurements down to 4 %. 

For that purpose a new scintillator target detector is proposed, SuperFGD. It will be built from 1x1x1cm 3

cubes of scintillator read out by 3 WSL fibers and MPPCs. It will provide a 2-ton active target oriented horizontally and interleaved with two horizontal TPCs [4]. Together with the current tracker setup of 2 vertical scintillator detectors, FGD, and 3 TPCs it will provide 4π coverage for detection of muons coming out of the 

CC neutrino interactions in the detector. Additionally, 

thanks to its fine s egmentation it will lower the energy 

threshold for detection of pions and protons. This will 

help with some cross -section measurements of neutrino 

interactions, such as  the  search for the interaction on the 

correlated nucleon pairs. The prototypes of the n ew 

horizontal TPCs and SuperFGD have been buil t and 

tested  using the  CERN particle beam during summer 

2018. We participat ed  in the tests and currently the 

students working within our group are involved in the 

analysis of the beam tests data preparing thei r Master ’s 

thes es (Fig. 2).

The last upgrade is related to the Super-Kamiokande far detector for which the plan is to add Gadolinium (0.02% of Gd 2(SO 4)3) to the water tank by 2020. Since Gadolinium can capture thermal neutrons providing delayed gamma signals, it can help to discriminate interactions of  νμ and and ͞  νμ. The  Super -Kamiokande 

tank was drained and opened in summer 2018 in order 

to perform cleaning of the detector, water sealing, tank 

piping and replacement of dead photomultiplier tubes. 

Many people from  the  Polish Neutrino Group including 

employees and PhD stude nts from NCBJ  participated in 

this  work. At this moment the detector is already filled 

with water and taking data.
