![Image 15: network-scale](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/6voDUQ7XmHDJ9zX0u2IrkW/e347d8fff227565dd30e1e9c85f1fe97/network-scale__1_.svg)

##### Enhance clinician productivity from anywhere

Empower remote clinical teams with fast, reliable access to medical systems from any location, without the frustrations of traditional VPNs.

![Image 16: Cloud icon](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/Hrl9MJuJGcsYRLaNNcCpS/3ca96c403b9a0195da1a8502d79ef76c/performance-cloud-speed.svg)

##### Deliver secure virtual visits and digital experiences

Safeguard patient-facing applications with a unified security platform and intelligent global network that prevents breaches while ensuring uninterrupted availability.

![Image 17: Analytics network orange](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/43PVIP7xl52gR53bMu92mz/0c22ea1cf0886785421e6c426afc8748/analytics-network_outline.svg)

##### Increase IT and security efficiency

Onboard new apps, manage user permissions, investigate incidents, and update policies faster and with more visibility from a single control plane and unified policy engine.

### Revolutionizing digital healthcare through security, speed, and scalability

## Stay ahead of evolving cyber threats

![Image 18: Modernize security problem graphic](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/2fYIJFv08uRUvfu0AfpUhN/a4fce1e1256265ed2e24e4b608cbc7a4/BDES-7450_Modernize-Security_problem-graphic.png)

Cloudflare’s SASE security solutions shield healthcare systems from phishing, ransomware and malware, leveraging peerless threat intelligence to preemptively block hundreds of billions of threats daily. Solutions like Cloudflare Network Firewall, Remote Browser Isolation, and Cloud Email Security reduce the risk of breach, eliminate security gaps, and enhance network visibility.

[Learn more](https://www.cloudflare.com/cybersecurity/)

![Image 19: Modernize security problem graphic](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/2fYIJFv08uRUvfu0AfpUhN/a4fce1e1256265ed2e24e4b608cbc7a4/BDES-7450_Modernize-Security_problem-graphic.png)

## Ensure secure access to systems and PHI

![Image 20: Healthcare Secondary - Images B](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/48dAhr7VNnmSWQURQ3M4mR/75d16d86bccb787a0a9e23ec8974b9f3/Healthcare-Secondary-Images-B.png)

Eliminate reliance on VPNs with Cloudflare’s Zero Trust services, enabling fast, secure, and reliable access to essential medical systems and PHI for internal and third-party clinicians. Products like Zero Trust Network Access and Data Loss Prevention enable healthcare organizations to control access to sensitive patient data, onboard users more quickly, and simplify policy enforcement.

[Learn more](https://www.cloudflare.com/data/)

![Image 21: Healthcare Secondary - Images B](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/48dAhr7VNnmSWQURQ3M4mR/75d16d86bccb787a0a9e23ec8974b9f3/Healthcare-Secondary-Images-B.png)

![Image 22](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/6Br5L0EijimBgwzd96rzhX/ed613e6b43dead19173ec854f81fbea2/Network_Performance_Update.png)

Cloudflare’s single composable platform and unified policy engine help you achieve compliance and manage evolving risk. Zero Trust and network services including Access, CASB, Gateway, and Cloudflare Network Firewall work together to let you establish, enforce, and monitor application access while preventing malware and ransomware from getting onto your network.

[Learn more](https://www.cloudflare.com/cybersecurity-risk-management/)

Flo is the #1 most popular female health app worldwide, with 400 million total installs and 75 million monthly active users. With a global user base, Flo Health must comply with numerous regulations such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). At the same time, the company faces the challenge of defending itself from the rapidly evolving threat landscape which is marked by increasingly sophisticated and frequent cyber attacks.

# Enterprise-grade security and performance for healthcare providers

Transform healthcare delivery and empower care teams with secure access to medical systems and protected health information (PHI). Enhance threat protection, deliver seamless patient experiences, and boost compliance, all from a single, secure cloud platform.

[Request a demo](https://www.cloudflare.com/healthcare/#)[Get solution brief](https://www.cloudflare.com/lp/cloudflare-for-healthcare/)

### Trust Cloudflare to keep patient data safe

[Read all stories](https://www.cloudflare.com/case-studies/?industry=Healthcare+%26+Life+Sciences)

[![Image 10: -icon](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/6P4xF3fjeUUba75IjGnbMH/6e9a3de71f6472c8d56d552fd0f3ce14/doctolib-blue-feature-list.png)](https://www.cloudflare.com/case-studies/doctolib/)[Read story](https://www.cloudflare.com/case-studies/doctolib/)

[![Image 12: -icon](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/7poKZeHtfe3lCZjBCd7bAF/172e09e63f9cbab2520349e5332004e3/mindbody-feature-list-logo-.png)](https://www.cloudflare.com/case-studies/mindbody/)[Read story](https://www.cloudflare.com/case-studies/mindbody/)

![Image 14: security-lock-226x301-cfb9db4](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/5YZDquysdwv0IC1kV0hC6n/0b1b2d81887d494047dbee2d347d2abb/security-lock_1_.svg)

##### Protect patient data and strengthen compliance

Defend against ransomware, malware and unauthorized access across cloud, SaaS, and hybrid environments, reducing risk and boosting regulatory compliance.

![Image 15: network-scale](https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/slt3lc6tev37/6voDUQ7XmHDJ9zX0u2IrkW/e347d8fff227565dd30e1e9c85f1fe97/network-scale__1_.svg)

Empower remote clinical teams with fast, reliable access to medical systems from any location, without the frustrations of traditional VPNs.

Safeguard patient-facing applications with a unified security platform and intelligent global network that prevents breaches while ensuring uninterrupted availability.

##### About National Digital Library of India (NDLI)

![Image 4: NDLI logo](https://ndl.iitkgp.ac.in/assets/img/ndli-logo-lg-green.svg)

National Digital Library of India (NDLI) is a virtual repository of learning resources which is not just a repository with search/browse facilities but provides a host of services for the learner community. It is sponsored and mentored by Ministry of Education, Government of India, through its National Mission on Education through Information and Communication Technology (NMEICT). Filtered and federated searching is employed to facilitate focused searching so that learners can find the right resource with least effort and in minimum time. NDLI provides user group-specific services such as Examination Preparatory for School and College students and job aspirants. Services for Researchers and general learners are also provided. NDLI is designed to hold content of any language and provides interface support for 10 most widely used Indian languages. It is built to provide support for all academic levels including researchers and life-long learners, all disciplines, all popular forms of access devices and differently-abled learners. It is designed to enable people to learn and prepare from best practices from all over the world and to facilitate researchers to perform inter-linked exploration from multiple sources. It is developed, operated and maintained from Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur.

Learn more about this project [from here](http://project.ndl.gov.in/).

##### About National Digital Library of India (NDLI)

![Image 4: NDLI logo](https://ndl.iitkgp.ac.in/assets/img/ndli-logo-lg-green.svg)

National Digital Library of India (NDLI) is a virtual repository of learning resources which is not just a repository with search/browse facilities but provides a host of services for the learner community. It is sponsored and mentored by Ministry of Education, Government of India, through its National Mission on Education through Information and Communication Technology (NMEICT). Filtered and federated searching is employed to facilitate focused searching so that learners can find the right resource with least effort and in minimum time. NDLI provides user group-specific services such as Examination Preparatory for School and College students and job aspirants. Services for Researchers and general learners are also provided. NDLI is designed to hold content of any language and provides interface support for 10 most widely used Indian languages. It is built to provide support for all academic levels including researchers and life-long learners, all disciplines, all popular forms of access devices and differently-abled learners. It is designed to enable people to learn and prepare from best practices from all over the world and to facilitate researchers to perform inter-linked exploration from multiple sources. It is developed, operated and maintained from Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur.

Learn more about this project [from here](http://project.ndl.gov.in/).

##### About National Digital Library of India (NDLI)

![Image 11: NDLI logo](https://ndl.iitkgp.ac.in/assets/img/ndli-logo-lg-green.svg)

National Digital Library of India (NDLI) is a virtual repository of learning resources which is not just a repository with search/browse facilities but provides a host of services for the learner community. It is sponsored and mentored by Ministry of Education, Government of India, through its National Mission on Education through Information and Communication Technology (NMEICT). Filtered and federated searching is employed to facilitate focused searching so that learners can find the right resource with least effort and in minimum time. NDLI provides user group-specific services such as Examination Preparatory for School and College students and job aspirants. Services for Researchers and general learners are also provided. NDLI is designed to hold content of any language and provides interface support for 10 most widely used Indian languages. It is built to provide support for all academic levels including researchers and life-long learners, all disciplines, all popular forms of access devices and differently-abled learners. It is designed to enable people to learn and prepare from best practices from all over the world and to facilitate researchers to perform inter-linked exploration from multiple sources. It is developed, operated and maintained from Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur.

Learn more about this project [from here](http://project.ndl.gov.in/).

About

## The Conference

Emerging Trends in Plant Biology: Climate-Resilient Crops to Biomanufacturing (PLACBIO 2027) will bring together students, researchers, scientists, innovators, and industry professionals to explore the limitless frontiers of plant biology and their applications in sustainable agriculture and biomanufacturing. The conference will highlight advances in plant physiology and biotechnology, plant–environment interactions, plant memory and stress priming, plant-based food and nutrition, plant specialized metabolism and volatiles, biomechanics and plant mechanobiology, and cutting-edge tools and technologies for plant research and development. It will also showcase the transformative potential of plant synthetic biology and biomanufacturing in developing climate-resilient crops and next-generation bio-based products.

About

## Institute and Departments

[Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur](https://www.iitkgp.ac.in/about-iitkgp), established in 1951 at Hijli Detention Camp, West Bengal, is India's first among the IIT system and an Institute of National Importance. As it celebrates its 75 years of excellence, marking its Platinum Jubilee, it carries a distinctive legacy of education, research, innovation, and nation-building. The “PLACBIO 2027” conference is being organized jointly by two Departments of IIT Kharagpur- [Agricultural and Food Engineering](https://www.iitkgp.ac.in/department/AG), and [Bioscience and Biotechnology](https://www.iitkgp.ac.in/department/BT).

**Celem konkursu jest wsparcie kariery młodych badaczy, poprzez stworzenie możliwości pełnoetatowego zatrudnienia i prowadzenia badań naukowych w Polsce oraz umożliwienie zdobycia wiedzy i doświadczenia podczas realizacji staży w wysokiej jakości zagranicznych ośrodkach naukowych.**

SONATINA 9 (16/12/2024 – 17/03/2025)

Opis Projektu:

Konkurs skierowany jest do osób, które posiadają stopień doktora uzyskany w roku wystąpienia z wnioskiem lub w okresie 3 lat przed rokiem wystąpienia z wnioskiem (**w okresie od 1 stycznia 2022 r. do 31 grudnia 2024 r.**) lub którym stopień doktora zostanie nadany do 30 czerwca 2025 r.

Dla kierownika projektu badawczego obowiązkowe jest zaplanowanie zatrudnienia w pełnym wymiarze czasu pracy, na podstawie umowy o pracę, w podmiocie planowanym jako miejsce realizacji projektu i innym niż podmiot, w którym kierownik projektu uzyskał stopień doktora. Kierownik projektu zobowiązany jest do zaplanowania i odbycia stażu zagranicznego trwającego od 3 do 6 miesięcy w zagranicznym ośrodku naukowym.

Projekt może zostać zaplanowany na 24 albo 36 miesięcy.

_Kierownikiem projektu może być osoba spełniająca łącznie dwa poniższe warunki:_

*   posiadająca stopień doktora nadany w roku wystąpienia z wnioskiem lub w okresie 3 lat przed rokiem wystąpienia z wnioskiem (w okresie od 1 stycznia 2022 r. do 31 grudnia 2024 r.) lub której stopień naukowy doktora zostanie nadany do 30 czerwca 2025 r.

oraz

*   dla której we wnioskowanym projekcie badawczym zostanie zaplanowane zatrudnienie na zasadach określonych w[regulaminie](https://www.ncn.gov.pl/sites/default/files/pliki/uchwaly-rady/2024/uchwala84_2024-zal1.pdf),**na podstawie umowy o pracę w pełnym wymiarze czasu pracy na cały planowany okres realizacji projektu**. Zatrudnienie musi zostać zaplanowane w podmiocie innym niż podmiot, w którym kierownik projektu uzyskał stopień doktora.

Wniosek należy złożyć wyłącznie w formie elektronicznej przez system OSF:

[https://osf.opi.org.pl](https://osf.opi.org.pl/)

Nabór wniosków w systemie OSF trwa do**17 marca 2025 r. do godziny 16:00 CET.**

**Więcej informacji dostępnych jest pod adresem:**

[https://www.ncn.gov.pl/ogloszenia/konkursy/sonatina9](https://www.ncn.gov.pl/ogloszenia/konkursy/sonatina9)

Finansowanie

Data zakończenia projektu

17-03-2025

Z dumą informujemy, że już od 7 lat Narodowe Centrum Badań Jądrowych (NCBJ) jest częścią elitarnego grona jednostek badawczych, które mogą poszczycić się prestiżowym wyróżnieniem[**„HR Excellence in Research”**](https://www.euraxess.pl/pl/poland/strategia-hr-hrs4r).

Naszym priorytetem jest wdrażanie wartości określonych w**Europejskiej Karcie Naukowca i Kodeksie Postępowania przy Rekrutacji Pracowników Naukowych**. Te kluczowe zasady są fundamentem działań NCBJ, zapewniając naszym naukowcom przejrzyste warunki pracy, stabilność zatrudnienia i szerokie możliwości rozwoju zawodowego.

![Image 1: hr excellence](http://www.ncbj.gov.pl/sites/default/files/2025-01/hr_tekst.png)

![Image 2: lider](http://www.ncbj.gov.pl/sites/default/files/2024-02/hr3.jpg)

## Lider w Strategii dla naukowców

Dzięki „HR Excellence”, NCBJ jest uznawane za jedną z instytucji spełniających wytyczne**HR Strategy for Researchers (HRS4R)**. Komisja Europejska nie tylko wspiera instytucje wdrażające postanowienia Karty i Kodeksu, lecz także promuje je w międzynarodowym środowisku naukowym jako wzory do naśladowania. Organizowane przez nią panele dyskusyjne oraz wydarzenia są miejscem wymiany doświadczeń i wyznaczania kierunków dalszego rozwoju. Dzięki portalowi Euraxess – naukowcy mają możliwość korzystać z wielu narzędzi wspierających rozwój kariery:[https://euraxess.ec.europa.eu/](https://euraxess.ec.europa.eu/)

Jesteśmy dumni z naszego wkładu w budowanie przyjaznego, wspierającego i innowacyjnego środowiska pracy, które przyciąga wybitnych naukowców z całego świata!

## Plany na przyszłość

Aby utrzymać prawo do posługiwania się tym prestiżowym wyróżnieniem, w listopadzie 2024 roku NCBJ przedstawiło Komisji Europejskiej[**Ocenę okresową**oraz**Plan Działań na lata 2025–2027**.](https://www.ncbj.gov.pl/sites/default/files/prasa/Internal%20Review%20and%20New%20Actions%202025-2027_5.pdf)

Dokumenty te potwierdzają nasze zaangażowanie w nieustanne podnoszenie standardów pracy naukowców i specjalistów badawczo-technicznych. Działania te dotyczą procedur rekrutacyjnych, które mają na celu przyciągnięcie najlepszych talentów naukowych, ale również innych działań mających na celu tworzenie najlepszego miejsca pracy.

Warto podkreślić, że wyróżnienie**„HR Excellence in Research”**nie jest przyznawane na stałe. Instytucje posiadające ten tytuł podlegają regularnym ewaluacjom, które weryfikują ich zgodność ze standardami określonymi przez Komisję Europejską.

![Image 1: IIT Kharagpur](https://www.iitkgp.ac.in/assets/images/about_01.jpg)

## Dedicated to the service of the Nation

#### Motto

The motto of IIT Kharagpur is "योगः कर्मसु कौशलम्". This literally translates to "Excellence in action is Yoga", essentially implying that doing your work well is (true) yoga. This can be traced to Sri Krishna's discourse with Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita. The quote, in the larger context of the Gita, urges man to acquire equanimity because a mind of equanimity allows a man to shed distracting thoughts of the effects of his deeds and concentrate on the task before him. Equanimity is the source of perfection in Karmic endeavours that leads to Salvation.

#### Mission

**The Institute aligns all its activities to serve national interest and seeks**

*   To provide broad-based education, helping students hone their professional skills and acquire the best-in-class capabilities in their respective disciplines
*   To imbibe a spirit of entrepreneurship and innovation in its students
*   To draw the best expertise in science, technology, management and law so as to equip students with the skills to visualize, synthesize and execute projects in these fields
*   To undertake sponsored research and provide consultancy services in industrial, educational and socially relevant areas

#### Vision

*   To be a centre of excellence in education and research, producing global leaders in science, technology and management
*   To be a hub of knowledge creation that prioritises the frontier areas of national and global importance
*   To improve the life of every citizen of the country

### History of IIT KGP

The history of the IIT system dates back to 1946 when a committee was set up by Hon'ble Sir Jogendra Singh, Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council, Department of Education, Health and Agriculture to consider the setting up of Higher Technical Institutions for post war industrial development in India. The 22 member committee headed by Sri N.R.Sarkar, in its report, recommended the establishment of four Higher Technical Institutions in the Eastern, Western, Northern and Southern regions, possibly on the lines of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA, with a number of secondary institutions affiliated to it. The report also urged the speedy establishment of all the four institutions with the ones in the East and the West to be started immediately. The committee also felt that such institutes would not only produce undergraduates but they should be engaged in research, producing research workers and technical teachers as well. The standard of the graduates should be at par with those from first class institutions abroad. They felt that the proportion of undergraduates and postgraduate students should be 2:1.

With the above recommendations of the Sarkar committee in view, the first Indian Institute of Technology was born in May 1950 in Hijli, Kharagpur, in the eastern part of India. Initially the IIT started functioning from 5, Esplanade East, Calcutta and very soon shifted to Hijli in Sept. 1950. The present name 'Indian Institute of Technology' was adopted before the formal inauguration of the Institute on August 18, 1951, by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. IIT Kharagpur started its journey in the old Hijli Detention Camp where some of our great freedom fighters toiled and sacrificed their lives for the independence of our country. The history of IIT Kharagpur is thus intimately linked with the history of the Hijli Detention Camp. This is possibly one of the very few Institutions all over the world which started life in a prison house.

![Image 2: IIT Kharagpur](https://www.iitkgp.ac.in/assets/images/old_building.jpg)

#### About the Detention Camp

The district of Midnapore along with rest of Bengal and India took part in a very significant way in the revolutionary struggle against the British Raj from the early 20th century.

The large number of youth who participated in the armed struggle or the non-cooperation movement could not be accommodated in ordinary jails. Then the British Government decided to establish a few detention camps - the first one was located in Buxa Fort which was followed by the setting up of the Hijli Detention Camp in 1930. The Hijli Detention Camp bears a very significant mark in our freedom movement. Two unarmed detainees were shot dead here by the British Police on Sept. 16, 1931. Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose came to Hijli for collecting the bodies of the two great sons of the freedom movement - Santosh Kumar Mitra and Tarakeswar Sengupta. All the national leaders including Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore voiced their strong protests against the British Raj over this incident. The Hijli Detention Camp was closed in 1937 and was reopened again in 1940 to detain the freedom fighters without trial. In 1942 the camp was again closed and the detainees were transferred elswhere.

#### IIT in its Infancy

There were 224 freshers and 42 teachers in August 1951 when the first session started. The class rooms, laboratories and the Administrative office were housed in the historic building of the Hijli Detention Camp. The Institute started its academic programme with only ten Departments. On March, 1952, Pandit Nehru laid the foundation stone of the New Building.

The layout of the present campus and the design of our buildings were carried out by a host of engineers and architects under the guidance of an eminent Swiss architect Dr. Werner M. Moser. A large amount of financial help was available for procuring a number of machine tools from the ministry of industry and supply. The Institute Workshop was supposed to be one of the best in the country. The Institute was fortunate enough to have Sir J.C.Ghosh, an eminent Scientist as its first Director under whose able stewadship the Institute grew in its formative years. The first Board of Governors was constituted with Dr. B.C. Roy, as the chairman and Mr. N.R.Sarkar, Sir Jehangir J. Gandhi, Dr. Tarachand, Mr. K.R.K. Menon, Mr. T. Sivasankar, Dr. S.S. Bhatnagar, Mr. H. Kabir and Dr. J.C. Ghosh as memebers. Some eminent scholars from Europe had joined this Institute in its formative years and the first two of them were Prof. R.A. Kraus and Prof.H. Tischner, who was incidentally the first Head of Electronics and ECE Department.

On Sept. 15, 1956, the Parliament of India passed an act known as the Indian Institute of Technology(Kharagpur) Act declaring this Institute as an Institute of national importance. The Institute was also given the status of an autonomous University. From this modest start in 1950, IIT Kharagpur has been engaged in a steady process of development in the vast tree-laden campus, spreading over 2100 acres has a self contained township of over 15,000 inhabitants.

Constant media coverages from leading houses helped in understanding the impact of NDLI’s participation in the book fair and its outreach to the communities and masses.

Technical deep dives, product updates, and insights from the teams that are helping to build a better Internet.

October 16, 2026## [Continuous accountability for Verified bots](https://blog.cloudflare.com/verified-bots-accountability/)
Identity alone doesn't guarantee a bot will behave responsibly. We are introducing a system to continuously evaluate whether Verified bots honor site preferences, like robots.txt and HTTP 429s, ensuring they remain accountable over time.

![Image 7: Chris Tsoukaladelis](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M510X23G1YWXBVVEV3X5ZCPK.01M510X2WF46AM3BFDZ8R47H1H.jpg&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)

[Chris Tsoukaladelis](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/chris-tsoukaladelis/)

[![Image 8](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M51ZPERWNWYTD7Z36YMY80A8.01M51ZPFH7VV8EHQTMPJG9FHZ4.png&w=2048&h=1152&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 9](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M51ZQ6NCJ2G1DZVHMZRH6SVF.01M51ZQ7A3WZQKT06FDN7XQ84K.png&w=2048&h=1152&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 10](blob:http://localhost/441e613ac1e7bb04c6a19779ca90d9fa)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/verified-bots-accountability/)

October 15, 2026## [A fully programmable secure web gateway](https://blog.cloudflare.com/programmable-gateway-dlp/)
Cloudflare Gateway and Data Loss Prevention have inherited the flexibility and power of Cloudflare Workers through our full-stack integration with the Cloudflare Developer platform.

![Image 11: AJ Gerstenhaber](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M508VRM0SPP4S4MS7CZXEHJA.01M508VT8EKZQHWR6HJHQVTQPV.png&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 12: Abe Carryl](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01KW46JJ6YPQY3M4A69P72QXE8.jpeg&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)

[AJ Gerstenhaber](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/aj/)and[Abe Carryl](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/abe/)

October 15, 2026## [Deploy with Void](https://blog.cloudflare.com/deploy-with-void/)
Introducing Void: an open-source SDK, CLI, and self-hosted platform for building full-stack Vite apps and deploying them to Cloudflare.

![Image 13: Christoph Nakazawa](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M4EX98BAG8QN2EG73TZW7RKE.01M4EX98Y0AM8PEJP2VR66W6PN.webp&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 14: Michael Dong](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M4EX7VKAAKSR7MZBFE5VQ9JZ.01M4EX7W0EXTB3MQ1C9BZZ5C38.webp&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)

[Christoph Nakazawa](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/christoph-nakazawa/)and[Michael Dong](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/michael-dong/)

October 15, 2026## [Cloudflare and OpenAI: Making AI discovery better for everyone](https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-openai-discovery-agentic-web/)
How Cloudflare and OpenAI are working together to help AI find useful content, keep up with changes, and make fewer wasted requests — making the experience better for users and website owners alike.

![Image 15: Matthew Conroy](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01KWW2PW1QZW47KMHA09RY62FC.jpg&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 16: Jack Galilee](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01KZA3MX64PMX25X6GHJWTCKYT.jpg&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 17: Henry Aspegren (OpenAI)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M4ZF9JPY469VR3ZSXJ5TCC72.01M4ZF9K94YMAVD6CKV497K7W2.jpeg&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 18: James Balfour (OpenAI)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M3Y82NHNS7DZN6RAJ3P8ZZ6Q.01M3Y82P64N5C1T5CGXRENCEAR.png&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)

October 14, 2026## [Yandex outage: Data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move](https://blog.cloudflare.com/yandex-outage/)
When strikes hit Yandex data centers, many assumed Russian bot operations went dark. Cloudflare data reveals that while search crawling stopped, malicious bots simply migrated to other networks.

![Image 19: Marina Elmore](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01KW477HVM8X1SKDG8ADKQJ9T3.png&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 20: Lai Yi Ohlsen](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01KW49DGMNXAW2CZQQAX92W97V.png&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)

[Marina Elmore](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/marina-elmore/)and[Lai Yi Ohlsen](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/lai-yi-ohlsen/)

October 14, 2026## [Inside Hyperdrive: How we solved a rare Hyperdrive MySQL caching bug](https://blog.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive-mysql/)
While adding MySQL support to Hyperdrive, we found a subtle protocol bug when caching query results. Here is how we tracked down a 0.001% rate error and made Hyperdrive MySQL generally available.

![Image 21: Pranoy Dutta](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M4VK61ABP982X8ARDP51MPZ3.01M4VK624NKY2ZRQFDJP3JPHW2.jpg&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)

[Pranoy Dutta](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/pranoy-dutta/)

October 13, 2026## [Under the hood, off the hot path: How D1 scales to millions of databases](https://blog.cloudflare.com/d1-control-plane/)
A deep dive into how D1 architected its control plane to scale and manage millions of databases, while keeping data plane query operations at the edge. We share guiding principles on how to build on the Developer Platform effectively.

![Image 22: David Laban](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01M34XD0TS97ET65W53NTJ30DM.01M34XD1GRAZN4A2HXX71EEZ5N.webp&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)![Image 23: Lambros Petrou](https://blog.cloudflare.com/_image?href=https%3A%2F%2Fblog.cloudflare.com%2F_emdash%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2F01KW47WA9G46YD5HZY63QTNT9A.jpg&w=64&h=64&f=webp&fit=cover&position=center)

[David Laban](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/david-laban/)and[Lambros Petrou](https://blog.cloudflare.com/author/lambros-petrou/)

| Core Tip | Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy has been used successfully in patients diagnosed with metastatic gastroenteropancreatic somatostatin receptor positive tumors when cytoreductive options are limited. In this study we found that overall survival was inversely proportional to toxicity to previous treatments and directly proportional to matching lesion findings between octreoscan and computed tomography pre-peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, tumor grade, bone metastasis and primary tumor and metastasis surgery. Also, that pseudo-progression in the middle of the treatment was a common finding that should be taken into consideration by clinicians in daily practice. |

## Abstract

_Objective_. Multicentre studies in molecular radiotherapy face challenges in ensuring the comparability of dosimetry results. The aim of this study was to develop a validation protocol to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across centres, consisting of a test exercise in combination with an action level. _Approach_. 177 Lu-SPECT/CT imaging of 3D-printed kidney phantoms with non-uniform activity distributions was conducted at five hospitals in Sweden and the UK. In total, 12 quantification systems (QSs) were included, where a QS was defined as the combination of a given camera system, reconstruction method and image-analysis method. The accuracy of image-based estimates of the activity concentration was investigated for three approaches to multicentre dosimetry: one site-specific, and two variants of centralised approaches. For the site-specific approach, the reference value was blinded to the evaluating operators. Prior to the evaluation, the participants agreed on an action level, specified as an obtained deviation larger than ±10% from the reference value. Sites responsible for a QS that yielded larger deviations, and therefore did not comply, were required to present an action plan, i.e., a plan for further method optimisation. _Main results_. For the site-specific approach, deviations larger than 10% were obtained for six out of 12 QS (range −11% to +27%). Action plans were presented for these QS and was implemented by one site (two QS). For the two variants of centralised approaches, where nine QS were included in total, deviations of within 10% were obtained for nine and seven QS, respectively. _Significance_. A quantification test combined with an action level can serve as an initial validation to enable further development and to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites.

Export citation and abstract[BibTeX](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_bib&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)[RIS](https://iopscience.iop.org/export?type=article&doi=10.1088/1361-6560/add708&exportFormat=iopexport_ris&exportType=abs&navsubmit=Export+abstract)

The interest in molecular radiotherapy (MRT) is currently expanding, and also the interest in integrating patient-specific dosimetry. Achieving equivalence in absorbed-dose estimates across centres is essential to enable interpretation, comparison and pooling of dosimetry data.

During the last decade, several multicentre comparison exercises of quantitative SPECT have been undertaken to investigate the accuracy in quantitative imaging and the possibilities of standardisation. These exercises have mostly been based on stylised phantom geometries, such as spheres or cylinders, and the adoption of a predefined protocol for image acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis (Willowson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib29), Zimmerman _et al_[2017](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib30), Wevrett _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib28), Gregory _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib7), Peters _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib17), [2020](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib16)). Instead of utilising stylised phantoms, the MRTDosimetry project employed a 3D-printed anthropomorphic phantom for comparison across sites (Tran-Gia _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib26)). A recent initiative is the SNMMI dosimetry challenge, led by the SNMMI Dosimetry Task Force, based on two sets of patient SPECT/CT images. An advantage of this approach was the avoidance of stylised geometries and activity distributions characteristic of most phantom studies, although with the drawback of an unknown ground truth (Uribe _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib27), Brosch-Lenz _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib2)). Currently, an accreditation programme is being developed by the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM) Forschungs GmbH (EARL) to harmonise 177 Lu SPECT/CT imaging, inspired by the existing accreditation programme for PET/CT (Kaalep _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib12)). This SPECT accreditation programme is based on the NEMA body PET phantom, in which the smallest sphere is replaced with a larger sphere more suitable with respect to the SPECT spatial resolution (Dickson _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib3)).

In the context of multicentre clinical trials that include dosimetry as a key component, the most common approach has been to follow predefined procedures for imaging, quantification and dosimetry (Taprogge _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib24), [2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib25), Lassmann _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib14)). One recent example is the multicentre observational trial INSPIRE (NCT04133870) on treatment of thyroid cancer with 131 I-NaI, in which a predefined imaging protocol has been adopted and implemented at eight sites, with dosimetry performed both locally and centrally (Taprogge _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib23)). Multicentre clinical studies that include prospective patient dosimetry and dose planning remain rare. The DOSISPHERE-01 multicentre randomised trial for treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma with 90 Y-loaded glass microspheres (NCT02582034) investigated personalised versus non-personalised dose planning based on 99m Tc-MAA SPECT/CT (Garin _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib6)). While dosimetry methods were not detailed in recent studies, an earlier publication described the development of these methods based on phantom measurements (Garin _et al_[2011](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib5)). The two-centre ILUMINET trial (NCT01456078) investigated dosimetry-guided 177 Lu peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177 Lu-PPRT) (Sundlöv _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib21)). A predefined imaging protocol was employed at both sites, and quantification and dosimetry performed with the Lundadose software (Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)), for which the accuracy for 177 Lu kidney dosimetry was also investigated (Gustafsson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib8), Sundlöv _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib22)).

Clinical multicentre studies that implement dosimetry for treatment planning present special challenges. The multicentre clinical trial START-NET (NCT05387603) involving 177 Lu-PRRT for patients with neuroendocrine tumours, where kidney dosimetry data will be utilised for treatment planning, is currently being launched in Sweden. The setup of the dosimetry in such a study necessitates consideration of several requirements: ensuring comparable and metrologically traceable dosimetry results at all clinical sites; adaptation to local conditions regarding available camera equipment, software and expertise; and complying with national regulatory frameworks for radiation protection. These requirements, and particularly the latter, present challenges in the absence of an established code of practice for validation of dosimetry results. For example, in Sweden and the UK, it is the legal entity that holds the license to use ionising radiation for medical purposes that also has responsibility for ensuring that the exposure is justified, and that the procedure is optimised (SFS [2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib20):396, Health and Safety [2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib9):896). This applies to all patients treated at the local hospital, including those participating in clinical studies, and covers responsibility for the methods used for radioprotective purposes, i.e. dosimetry (Almén and Anders [2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib1)). Consequently, whilst the use of a particular dosimetry software or the access to a centralised dosimetry service can be important steps towards achieving consistent dosimetry across sites, the produced dosimetry data can only be utilised to the extent that the site who delivers treatment, i.e. the permit holder, can take full responsibility of the results. Assuming this responsibility means to be able to verify the results in the patient dosimetry record, which presumably entails validation work by the local medical physics team. Thus, irrespective of the chosen solution for providing dosimetry data, the local team needs to invest time in preparatory work and verification.

Considering these requirements, we have hypothesised that a validation protocol, consisting of a blinded quantification test for a representative geometry, combined with an action level, can serve to achieve accurate and equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites, also when using site-specific methods. An essential component in such a strategy is the agreement among participating sites on the action level, the requirement that participants develop and present an action plan in case of non-compliance to this level, and the undertaking of a renewed test after method adjustments.

The aim of this study is to develop a protocol for initial validation of methods for estimation of 177 Lu activity concentration in kidneys. The validation protocol is based on a test exercise using 3D-printed kidney phantoms in combination with an action level. Three approaches to multicentre 177 Lu-SPECT-based activity quantification are investigated: a site-specific approach that involves blinded testing, and two variants of centralised approaches.

Three different approaches for multicentre activity-quantification studies were applied, here termed Site-specific, Combined and Centralised (table [1](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t1)). Five sites were included, four located in Sweden and one in the UK. Together, these sites included nine SPECT/CT cameras, comprising seven GE systems (GE Healthcare, Haifa, Israel) and two Siemens systems (Siemens Healthineers, Forcheim, Germany). The site-specific approach was based on locally preferred methods for image reconstruction, determination of the image calibration factor, and VOI delineation. To avoid possible operator-induced bias in the manual steps, the reference activity concentration in the phantoms were blinded to the operators performing the image-based quantification. For the combined approach, the local reconstruction methods were used, whilst the VOI delineation was performed centrally. For the centralised approach, both image reconstruction and VOI delineation were performed centrally. For practical reasons, the image analysis in the combined and centralised approaches was performed by a single operator to whom the reference activity concentration was not blinded. An overview of the process is presented in figure [1](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708f1).

### 2.1.Quantification systems (QSs) included

Twelve different QSs were studied. A QS was defined as the combination of a particular SPECT/CT camera, a reconstruction method, and an image-analysis method for determination of the activity concentration. These QS represented the same settings and methods as would be used for patient kidney dosimetry. Table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2) specifies the twelve QS, with further details provided in supplementary file 1. Together, the included QS represented a wide range of settings for image acquisition and processing. The number of acquired SPECT projections ranged from 30 to 120. Nine QS used only the photo-peak at 208 keV of 177 Lu whilst three also used the photo-peak at 113 keV. All QS included CT-based attenuation compensation, and ten QS also included scatter compensation and resolution recovery without post filtering. The QS that did not include resolution recovery included low-pass filtering post reconstruction. The number of updates (number of iterations × number of subsets) varied between 40 and 160, and reconstructions were performed either with commercially available software, Xeleris® (GE Healthcare, Haifa, Israel) or Hermia® (Hermes Medical Solutions, Stockholm, Sweden), or with non-commercial software, Phonsai (Rydén _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib18)) or Lundadose (Frey and Tsui [1996](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib4), Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)). Eight of the QS were included based on their participation in the multicentre trial START-NET (NCT05387603), two QS participated as part of method development, and two QS were included as part of an ongoing scientific collaboration. Each site was allowed to include more than one QS.

Reconstructions were performed with the Hermia software using eight iterations and ten subsets, including CT-based attenuation compensation, Monte Carlo based scatter compensation and resolution recovery, as detailed in Kapidzic _et al_ ([2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib13)). Image analysis was performed using the Affinity module 4.0.1 (Hermes Medical Solution, Stockholm, Sweden).

### 2.2.Phantoms

All activity measurements for phantom preparation were made using activity meters that had been calibrated for 177 Lu, as previously described (Hindorf _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib10)). To prevent 177 Lu from sticking to the phantom walls, EDTA was added to the water solutions before dispensing 177 Lu.

As a preparatory step, the calibration factor for 177 Lu-SPECT was determined from a uniformly filled cylindrical Jaszczak phantom, and a uniformly filled large spherical insert mounted inside the cylindrical phantom with a non-radioactive background. These phantoms were prepared at each site, with volumes and inserted activities of 177 Lu depending on the local availability of equipment and activity. The volume of the cylindrical phantoms ranged between 6.4 l and 7.4 l, and the activity concentration at the start of SPECT acquisition was between 0.02 MBq ml−1 and 0.11 MBq ml−1. The volumes of the spheres were 113–144 ml, and the activity concentration at the start of SPECT acquisitions was between 0.83 MBq ml−1 and 10.10 MBq ml−1.

The quantitative accuracy for 3D-printed kidney phantoms of 177 Lu-SPECT was investigated using pairs of 3D-printed kidney phantoms (left and right). These were designed using a grid-based technique to create an apparently non-uniform activity distribution, mimicking that of a typical 177 Lu-PRRT patient (Jessen _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib11)). Each kidney phantom encompassed an outer container shaped as cortex, an inner grid structure shaped as medulla and a solid renal pelvis on one side (figure [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708f2)). In-house plates and rods were manufactured to enable mounting of the kidney phantoms in a cylindrical Jaszczak phantom for imaging. The inner phantom volumes were 110 ml and 105 ml for the left and right kidney, respectively. The weights of the phantoms in dry and empty conditions were measured directly after printing and were then filled with water to test for watertightness for a minimum of 24 h.

For the site-specific approach (table [1](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t1)) it was considered essential to maintain the reference activity concentration unknown to the local operator who evaluated the SPECT images, to avoid possible operator-induced bias in the manual steps. For this reason, the phantom filling was performed by two external medical physicists who visited each of the participating sites.

For each site, a new set of kidney phantoms were 3D printed and transported to the site by the external medical physicists. At the local site, the external physicists prepared the kidney phantoms i.e., inserted activity, weighed the filled kidney phantoms and mounted them into the Jazsczak phantom. The effective volume ( and , the reference activity and the activity concentration in the kidney phantoms were thus unknown to the local site at subsequent SPECT acquisition and image analysis. For one site, representing QS 7, 8, 9 and 10, a practical issue was encountered, where the carrier molecules of the used 177 Lu residuals precipitated in the solution. This was not discovered until evaluation of the SPECT images, and a re-filling of the phantoms then became necessary. To avoid a new site visit, the kidney phantoms were this time prepared by a local medical physicist. To maintain the blinded approach and remain a consistent filling procedure, the local medical physicist, whilst in the lab, was instructed by the coordinating site via online communication. The local medical physicists did not record any data and was also not allowed to participate in the analysis of the phantom SPECT images.

#### 2.3.2.Site-specific approach

The reconstructed SPECT image of the kidney phantoms was analysed by one operator from each site, who was assigned to estimate the mean activity concentration over the cortex and medulla. The VOI methods used for the different QS are summarised in table [4](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t4), with more details provided in supplementary file 1. Image VOI analysis was performed using commercial or non-commercial software, as specified in table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2). The strategy used for VOI delineation over the kidneys varied between the different QS, where eight QS included the average activity concentration of multiple small spherical VOIs, and four QS applied whole-kidney delineation (supplementary file 1). The responsible medical physicists at each site reported the estimated activity concentrations for the respective kidney (left and right) to the coordinating site. Separate data were reported for each QS included at the site.

#### 2.3.3.Centralised approach

For the centralised approach, SPECT reconstruction was performed centrally for each unique set of SPECT projections of the kidney phantoms. As some QS used the same set of projection data (QS 5 and 6, QS 7 and 8, QS 9 and 10) this yielded nine individual data points. The small-VOI method presented by Kapidzic _et al_ ([2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib13)) was used. Five spherical VOIs, each of 2 ml, positioned centrally in each kidney in the images was used, and the activity concentration calculated as the arithmetic average. The top and bottom slices were avoided, since in patient studies the spatial resolution in these slices is expected to be affected by kidney motion. Lastly, a recovery coefficient (RC) of 1.1 was used. The image analysis was performed by one operator, using the affinity module 4.0.1 (Hermes Medical Solutions, Stockholm, Sweden).

#### 2.3.4.Combined approach

The combined approach was based on local reconstructions and centralised image analysis. This required DICOM images formatted such that they could be imported into Hermia. This import was successful for all QS except QS 3, 4 and 6, and thus nine individual data points resulted. The SPECT images were analysed using the same VOI method as for the centralised approach, but due to inconsistent reconstructions between the QS, no RC was applied.

The site-specific approach resulted in the largest range of deviations (−17% to +29) % and six out of 12 QS did not meet the 10% criterion. If instead considering the left–right kidney average, this criterion was not met for QS 3, 4, 8 and 10 (4/12 QS). The combined approach yielded the lowest range (−9% to +3 %) with activity concentrations that were slightly underestimated for all data points except three, and all QS (9/9) met the 10% criterion. The centralised approach yielded deviations between −11% and +27 %, and all but two (7/9) met the 10% criterion. The largest deviations were generally observed for the right kidney, which was smaller than the left kidney. Of the parameters for image acquisition and reconstruction listed in table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2), no single factor could be identified as associated with the larger deviations. With respect to the image analysis method (table [4](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t4)), QS 3, 4, 11 and 12 included whole-kidney delineation and all yielded underestimated activity concentrations, whilst the QS that included small-VOI methods showed no such trend but a larger dispersion.

### 3.4.Deviations in relation to the action level

The action level was strictly only actionable for the site-specific approach. For QS 3 and 4 deviations higher than 10% were obtained for the left kidney phantom. This site presented and implemented an action plan, in which the RC, applicable for whole kidney delineation, was re-examined based on additional phantom studies and was thus updated from 0.85 to 0.78. However, this site decided to migrate to another quantification software, and a follow-up blinded evaluation has been planned. For QS 8 and 10 deviations higher than 10% were obtained for both the left and right kidney phantoms. The action plan involved further investigation of the strategy used for VOI delineation, including the development of detailed operator guidance. However, as alternatives were available amongst the QS that met the 10% criterion, this site decided not to pursue this development. QS 11 and 12 underestimated the activity concentration slightly more than 10 %. The proposed action plan included the development of a kidney RC that takes irregular shapes and non-uniform activity distributions into account. Follow-up tests have not yet been performed.

In this work, a validation protocol was investigated as a method to reach equivalence in quantitative 177 Lu SPECT across sites. The quantitative accuracy when using site-specific, combined and centralised approaches was investigated. Overall, the three approaches yielded deviations between −17% and +29% across the QS investigated. The random dispersion was found to be more pronounced for the site-specific and centralised approaches, whereas the combined approach yielded more consistent but slightly underestimated results. For the investigated approaches to multicentre 177 Lu activity quantification, the validation test identified QS that produced biased estimates of the activity concentration.

The site-specific approach was developed from the idea that the primary objective is to establish a centre’s ability to accurately estimate activity concentrations, rather than focusing on the specific means and methods employed to achieve these estimates. This contrasts with the more common approach of adopting a pre-defined protocol for SPECT image acquisition, processing, and analysis across all centres. In practice, clinical centres have access to different camera systems and collimators, various software for tomographic reconstruction, including methods for resolution recovery and scatter compensation, activity quantification and dosimetry. Some of these components may be less straightforward to align to a common protocol, yet they can have a substantial impact on the results. There is also ongoing development of both hardware and software, such as SPECT systems based on CZT detectors and ring-configurations, as well as new tomographic reconstructions and image analysis methods, for which the optimal settings and protocols may differ from those conventionally used. Notable examples in this study are represented by QS 1 and QS 2 that both yielded acceptable results with regards to the action level. QS 1 was based on a CZT camera system. Neither of these QS included compensation for scatter or resolution recovery. Both QS employed a method for determining the calibration factor using a sphere geometry, rather than the more commonly used geometry of a cylindrical phantom, due to the unavailability of scatter compensation. Other notable examples are QS 3 and 4 that both employed an unconventionally low number of 30 projection angles. Whilst the validation test revealed deviations for these QS for the left kidney phantom, these were later found to be associated with the applied RC rather than the number of projection angles. It is also noteworthy that nine QS were based on acquisition using only the 208 keV energy window, whereas three also utilised the 113 keV peak, thereby introducing a higher dependency on accurate scatter correction.

Regarding the QS intended for the START-NET trial (QS 1–7 and 9), an essential component was the agreement between the participants, made prior to the experimental work, concerning both the action level and the requirement of formulating and implementing an action plan in the event of non-compliance. In this agreement, the action level was not regarded as a pass-or-fail judgement, but rather a means of identifying errors and initiating further local investigations and adjustments. Two out of the eight QS did not meet the 10% criterion. Although an action plan was formulated and implemented, this site decided to migrate to another quantification software, and the blinded evaluation is planned to be repeated.

A clear limitation to this study was the small data set used, encompassing only two data points per QS. Consequently, depending on the results obtained, the local investigations could include additional phantom experiments, re-examination of the reconstruction settings, or investigation of the operator dependency. To understand and communicate the reliability of the reference method, the quantification of the uncertainty was considered essential. In retrospect, an action level of ±10% may have been optimistically narrow when considering the ±3.3% (_k_ = 2) coverage interval of the reference activity concentration. However, despite this concern the action level was maintained.

Blinding is a commonly adopted strategy for evaluation of operator-dependent methods. In this work, the blinding was included to ensure a strict separation between method evaluation and optimisation, and to mimic a patient situation where the true activity concentration is unknown. The 3D printed phantoms were well suited for this purpose as the grid volume was only accessible for measurement during the phantom construction and the effective volume () could not be determined by the local sites by other means than SPECT measurement. On a larger scale, site visits for phantom preparation may be considered overly cumbersome. A possible solution could be to use online communication and to separate data logging from the local site, as was done in this work for the site where the phantom filling had to be repeated. Another solution to ensure blinding could be to require a written agreement from the local site on the involvement of different operators for phantom filling and image analysis. Based on our experience, communication is a key factor for success in a blinded exercise, such that its purpose is clear to all parties involved.

Both the combined and centralised approaches were, for practical reasons, not blinded and were based on image analysis by a single operator using one software. Results for these approaches were more consistent than for the site-specific approach. However, a disadvantage was the potential risk of introducing consistent bias across all systems. This became evident for the combined approach, which yielded results within the action level for all nine QS but gave slightly underestimated results for 15 out of 18 data points. The centralised approach gave results within ±10% for 15 out of 18 data points and yielded a range of deviations between −11% to +27% across all data points. In particular, the centralised method did not perform well for QS 11. The cause of this deviation was identified as the calibration factor determined with method (iv), resulting in a considerably lower value than for the technically identical camera of QS 12. This exemplifies the necessity of conducting a validation test even when adopting a centralised approach and also underscores the importance of basing the calibration factor on multiple SPECT phantom measurements rather than a single one.

None of the acquisition settings and technical parameters specified in table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2) could be identified as being associated with the larger deviations. Thus, no clear effect of the reconstruction method, the energy windows settings, or the scatter correction, etc. could be discerned. On the other hand, the accuracy appeared to be more dependent on the strategy for VOI delineation combined with the RC. In view of the current availability of iterative reconstruction that include CT-based attenuation correction, we believe the most critical aspects for 177 Lu kidney quantification are the combination of reconstruction settings, the calibration factor, the adopted VOI-method and the applied RC.

Whilst the ongoing EARL project on 177 Lu accreditation (Dickson _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib3)) is focused on large phantom calibration factors and recovery curves for spherical inserts with known volumes, this work is based on anthropomorphic phantoms with non-uniform activity distributions, and thus complements the EARL effort. The non-uniform activity distribution intended to mimic 177 Lu-PRRT patient images, and was generated by a grid structure, which simplified phantom filling compared to a phantom with multiple compartments (Jessen _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib11)). However, a limitation with the 3D printed kidney phantoms was the mass density of the printing material, which was slightly higher than water. This produced CT images where the phantom structures were clearly visible, which may have had an impact on VOI delineation. Another advantage with the validation exercise was the dissemination of phantoms. For example, sites responsible for QS 1, 2, 7, and 9, made further use of the phantoms to investigate the operator dependency and reproducibility of their VOI methods.

In perspective of multicentre clinical trials, either of the proposed approaches; site-specific, combined and centralised, have shown advantages and disadvantages and yielded reasonably low deviations across the QS investigated. The combined approach yielded the most consistent results and the lowest deviations. For retrospective analysis of dosimetry data, such as for analysis of dose-response relationships, the combined or centralised approaches may be preferable. For dosimetry-guided treatment protocols where dosimetry data is used for treatment planning, there are regulatory requirements stating that the responsibility for dosimetry lies with the permit holder for delivering treatment. There are also practical steps in dosimetry that rely on local decisions, such as measures taken in case of delays of radiopharmaceutical delivery, missing or incorrect SPECT/CT acquisition time-points, or extravasation. Local engagement in dosimetry is expected to be beneficial in terms of understanding the consequences of the decisions made. For these practical and regulatory reasons, we have found that for the START-NET clinical trial, the site-specific approach is the most viable option.

Irrespective of the purpose of whether a multicentre dosimetry study is prospective or retrospective, a validation test, such as presented in this work, has been found beneficial for identifying deviations in the adopted quantification methods and to motivate further development.

For multicentre studies, a validation protocol, consisting of a blinded test exercise for a representative geometry, combined with an action level, can be used to reach equivalence in 177 Lu SPECT kidney quantification.

We would like to thank Adrian Moreno, Joachim Nilsson and Ulrika Estenberg for their participation in the evaluation of the kidney phantom measurements and Muris Imsirovic for 3D-printing of the phantoms. Additionally, we express our gratitude to the staff at the nuclear medicine departments for their assistance in setting up the phantom preparation and SPECT/CT measurements. We would like to thank Mrs Berta Kamprad’s Foundation (FBKS-2024-7 -583, FBKS-2024-31–589) Swedish state ALF agreement (47305) and the Swedish Cancer Foundation (211754Pj01H, 243785Pj01H).

## Abstract
_Objective_. Multicentre studies in molecular radiotherapy face challenges in ensuring the comparability of dosimetry results. The aim of this study was to develop a validation protocol to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across centres, consisting of a test exercise in combination with an action level. _Approach_. 177 Lu-SPECT/CT imaging of 3D-printed kidney phantoms with non-uniform activity distributions was conducted at five hospitals in Sweden and the UK. In total, 12 quantification systems (QSs) were included, where a QS was defined as the combination of a given camera system, reconstruction method and image-analysis method. The accuracy of image-based estimates of the activity concentration was investigated for three approaches to multicentre dosimetry: one site-specific, and two variants of centralised approaches. For the site-specific approach, the reference value was blinded to the evaluating operators. Prior to the evaluation, the participants agreed on an action level, specified as an obtained deviation larger than ±10% from the reference value. Sites responsible for a QS that yielded larger deviations, and therefore did not comply, were required to present an action plan, i.e., a plan for further method optimisation. _Main results_. For the site-specific approach, deviations larger than 10% were obtained for six out of 12 QS (range −11% to +27%). Action plans were presented for these QS and was implemented by one site (two QS). For the two variants of centralised approaches, where nine QS were included in total, deviations of within 10% were obtained for nine and seven QS, respectively. _Significance_. A quantification test combined with an action level can serve as an initial validation to enable further development and to achieve equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites.

## Abstract
The interest in molecular radiotherapy (MRT) is currently expanding, and also the interest in integrating patient-specific dosimetry. Achieving equivalence in absorbed-dose estimates across centres is essential to enable interpretation, comparison and pooling of dosimetry data.

## Abstract
During the last decade, several multicentre comparison exercises of quantitative SPECT have been undertaken to investigate the accuracy in quantitative imaging and the possibilities of standardisation. These exercises have mostly been based on stylised phantom geometries, such as spheres or cylinders, and the adoption of a predefined protocol for image acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis (Willowson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib29), Zimmerman _et al_[2017](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib30), Wevrett _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib28), Gregory _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib7), Peters _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib17), [2020](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib16)). Instead of utilising stylised phantoms, the MRTDosimetry project employed a 3D-printed anthropomorphic phantom for comparison across sites (Tran-Gia _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib26)). A recent initiative is the SNMMI dosimetry challenge, led by the SNMMI Dosimetry Task Force, based on two sets of patient SPECT/CT images.

## Abstract
An advantage of this approach was the avoidance of stylised geometries and activity distributions characteristic of most phantom studies, although with the drawback of an unknown ground truth (Uribe _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib27), Brosch-Lenz _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib2)). Currently, an accreditation programme is being developed by the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM) Forschungs GmbH (EARL) to harmonise 177 Lu SPECT/CT imaging, inspired by the existing accreditation programme for PET/CT (Kaalep _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib12)). This SPECT accreditation programme is based on the NEMA body PET phantom, in which the smallest sphere is replaced with a larger sphere more suitable with respect to the SPECT spatial resolution (Dickson _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib3)).

## Abstract
In the context of multicentre clinical trials that include dosimetry as a key component, the most common approach has been to follow predefined procedures for imaging, quantification and dosimetry (Taprogge _et al_[2019](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib24), [2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib25), Lassmann _et al_[2021](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib14)). One recent example is the multicentre observational trial INSPIRE (NCT04133870) on treatment of thyroid cancer with 131 I-NaI, in which a predefined imaging protocol has been adopted and implemented at eight sites, with dosimetry performed both locally and centrally (Taprogge _et al_[2023](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib23)). Multicentre clinical studies that include prospective patient dosimetry and dose planning remain rare. The DOSISPHERE-01 multicentre randomised trial for treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma with 90 Y-loaded glass microspheres (NCT02582034) investigated personalised versus non-personalised dose planning based on 99m Tc-MAA SPECT/CT (Garin _et al_[2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib6)).

## Abstract
While dosimetry methods were not detailed in recent studies, an earlier publication described the development of these methods based on phantom measurements (Garin _et al_[2011](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib5)). The two-centre ILUMINET trial (NCT01456078) investigated dosimetry-guided 177 Lu peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177 Lu-PPRT) (Sundlöv _et al_[2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib21)). A predefined imaging protocol was employed at both sites, and quantification and dosimetry performed with the Lundadose software (Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)), for which the accuracy for 177 Lu kidney dosimetry was also investigated (Gustafsson _et al_[2015](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib8), Sundlöv _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib22)).

## Abstract
Clinical multicentre studies that implement dosimetry for treatment planning present special challenges. The multicentre clinical trial START-NET (NCT05387603) involving 177 Lu-PRRT for patients with neuroendocrine tumours, where kidney dosimetry data will be utilised for treatment planning, is currently being launched in Sweden. The setup of the dosimetry in such a study necessitates consideration of several requirements: ensuring comparable and metrologically traceable dosimetry results at all clinical sites; adaptation to local conditions regarding available camera equipment, software and expertise; and complying with national regulatory frameworks for radiation protection. These requirements, and particularly the latter, present challenges in the absence of an established code of practice for validation of dosimetry results. For example, in Sweden and the UK, it is the legal entity that holds the license to use ionising radiation for medical purposes that also has responsibility for ensuring that the exposure is justified, and that the procedure is optimised (SFS [2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib20):396, Health and Safety [2024](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib9):896). This applies to all patients treated at the local hospital, including those participating in clinical studies, and covers responsibility for the methods used for radioprotective purposes, i.e. dosimetry (Almén and Anders [2022](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib1)). Consequently, whilst the use of a particular dosimetry software or the access to a centralised dosimetry service can be important steps towards achieving consistent dosimetry across sites, the produced dosimetry data can only be utilised to the extent that the site who delivers treatment, i.e. the permit holder, can take full responsibility of the results. Assuming this responsibility means to be able to verify the results in the patient dosimetry record, which presumably entails validation work by the local medical physics team.

## Abstract
Thus, irrespective of the chosen solution for providing dosimetry data, the local team needs to invest time in preparatory work and verification.
Considering these requirements, we have hypothesised that a validation protocol, consisting of a blinded quantification test for a representative geometry, combined with an action level, can serve to achieve accurate and equivalent 177 Lu-SPECT quantification across sites, also when using site-specific methods. An essential component in such a strategy is the agreement among participating sites on the action level, the requirement that participants develop and present an action plan in case of non-compliance to this level, and the undertaking of a renewed test after method adjustments.
The aim of this study is to develop a protocol for initial validation of methods for estimation of 177 Lu activity concentration in kidneys. The validation protocol is based on a test exercise using 3D-printed kidney phantoms in combination with an action level. Three approaches to multicentre 177 Lu-SPECT-based activity quantification are investigated: a site-specific approach that involves blinded testing, and two variants of centralised approaches.

## Abstract
Three different approaches for multicentre activity-quantification studies were applied, here termed Site-specific, Combined and Centralised (table [1](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t1)). Five sites were included, four located in Sweden and one in the UK. Together, these sites included nine SPECT/CT cameras, comprising seven GE systems (GE Healthcare, Haifa, Israel) and two Siemens systems (Siemens Healthineers, Forcheim, Germany). The site-specific approach was based on locally preferred methods for image reconstruction, determination of the image calibration factor, and VOI delineation. To avoid possible operator-induced bias in the manual steps, the reference activity concentration in the phantoms were blinded to the operators performing the image-based quantification. For the combined approach, the local reconstruction methods were used, whilst the VOI delineation was performed centrally. For the centralised approach, both image reconstruction and VOI delineation were performed centrally. For practical reasons, the image analysis in the combined and centralised approaches was performed by a single operator to whom the reference activity concentration was not blinded. An overview of the process is presented in figure [1](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708f1).

## Abstract
### 2.1.Quantification systems (QSs) included
Twelve different QSs were studied. A QS was defined as the combination of a particular SPECT/CT camera, a reconstruction method, and an image-analysis method for determination of the activity concentration. These QS represented the same settings and methods as would be used for patient kidney dosimetry. Table [2](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708t2) specifies the twelve QS, with further details provided in supplementary file 1. Together, the included QS represented a wide range of settings for image acquisition and processing. The number of acquired SPECT projections ranged from 30 to 120. Nine QS used only the photo-peak at 208 keV of 177 Lu whilst three also used the photo-peak at 113 keV. All QS included CT-based attenuation compensation, and ten QS also included scatter compensation and resolution recovery without post filtering. The QS that did not include resolution recovery included low-pass filtering post reconstruction. The number of updates (number of iterations × number of subsets) varied between 40 and 160, and reconstructions were performed either with commercially available software, Xeleris® (GE Healthcare, Haifa, Israel) or Hermia® (Hermes Medical Solutions, Stockholm, Sweden), or with non-commercial software, Phonsai (Rydén _et al_[2018](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib18)) or Lundadose (Frey and Tsui [1996](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib4), Ljungberg and Sjögreen Gleisner [2016](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/add708#pmbadd708bib15)).
