proteins normally expressed in pancreatic islets. An analysis was performed using Search 

Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins (STRING) for protein network association. 

Statistics 

Fishe r’s exact test was used to compare categorical endpoints, and Mann Whitney -U test was 

performed to compare continuous values. Tests were two -sided and used to determine 

whether differences between two values were significant (p < 0.05). A ll the statistical analyses 

were cal culated using the statistical program R (v. 4.3.0.). Gene expression data were analyz ed 

using ANOVA (ebayes) including false discovery rate in the Transcriptome Analysis Console 

Software (Version 4.0.2 Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA).

# Discussion 

Hereditary v s. s poradic i nsulinoma subtypes have distinctive molecular landscape s. Our study of 

12 sporadic insulinomas revealed a marked genetic heterogeneity with few recurrent alterations 

among 33 candidate genes. The gene expression data revealed an accumulation of differentially 

expressed genes in pathways related to metabolism of cholesterol and fatty acids , compared to 

control beta cells .

Candidate genes 

We identified 3 3 candidate genes by exome sequencing of 1 2 insulinomas. Of these, three 

insulinomas did not harbor variants in genes associated with cancer or hyperinsulinism. The lack of 

variants may be due to a too thorough filtration pipeline , despite the additional ma nual analysis of 

six genes known to be associated with tumorigenesis in PNETs. Further, other factors may lead to 

tumorigenesis, such as epigenetics. A trend towards aberrant epigenetic regulation in PNETs with 

and without MEN1 predisposition has been prop osed before (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017, Wang, 

Bender et al. 2017, Iyer and Agarwal 2018, Pipinikas, Berner et al. 2019) . Variants in the genes 

associated with epigenetic regulation, including MEN1 , YY1 , ATRX and DAXX are well -documented 

and frequent in PNE Ts (Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Li, Huang et al. 2016, Chan, Laddha et al. 2018, 

Pipinikas, Berner et al. 2019, Hong, Qiao et al. 2020, Rindi, Mete et al. 2022) . As shown in Figure 3,

we only identified one somatic MEN1 variant with a low VAF and no DAXX alterations in our 

tumors . Th is low occurrence of MEN1 and DAXX alterations in sporadic insulinomas compared to 

other PNET subtypes is in accordance with other reports (Wang, Bender et al. 2017, Zheng, Liu et 

al. 2021) .Paper III 

> 24

In cohorts of sporadic insulinomas , the frequency of the recurrent p. (Thr372Arg ) mutation in YY1 

have been estimated to 0 -33 % (Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Lichtenauer, Di Dalmazi et al. 2015, Parekh, 

Modali et al. 2018) . In our study we only found th is variant in 1/1 2 sporadic insulinomas (8 %), 

which is similar to newer studies of cohorts of sporadic insulinomas , where only 8 % , and 13 % ,

harbo red the recurrent mutation, respectively (Wang, Bender et al. 2017, Parekh, Mod ali et al. 

2018) . Mutations in ATRX occurred in 3/1 2 (25 %) . In others reports, 0-17.6 % of PNETs ha d an 

acquired ATRX variant (Jiao, Shi et al. 2011, Wang, Bender et al. 2017) .

Likely germline variants 

We identified a likely germline variant in BRCA2 with a VAF of 0.61 in Insulinoma O, suggesting a 

germline origin . According to The Human Protein Atlas, BRCA2 is weakly expressed in normal 

pancreatic islets and o nly one other BRCA2 variant has been described before in a non -functioning 

PNET (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) . The likely germline variant in BRCA2 may represent a novel 

predisposin g factor for PNETs, if not a somatic event such as copy -neutral loss of heterozygosity .

Other likely germline variants with a VAF ≥40 was identified in NKX6.1 , ATP2B1 , GPR1 and 

SLC37A4 . Of special note, Insulinoma O harbored both the BRCA2, NKX6.1 and ATP2B1 variants 

with a high VAF. NKX6 -1 encodes the critical beta -cell programming factor in progenitor cells and 

induce proliferation of beta -cells through activation of Nr4a1, Nr4a3, and Aurora kinase 1 (gene: 

AURKA ) (Hobson, Draney et al. 2015) . The missense v ariant in NKX6.1 (p.( Tyr190Cys ), VAF 0.58) in 

Insulinoma O was associated with a decre ase of 2.25 -fold of NKX6.1 mRNA compared to the beta -

cell line EndoC -βH1. In PNETs and islets from mice with beta -cell specific Men1 -ablat ion, mRNA 

expression of pivotal transcription factors related to islet function including Nkx6.1 , NeuroD1 , Isl -1,Paper III 

> 25

and Maf A, was significantly decreased (Li, Su et al. 2015) . However, i n rat -derived insulinoma cell 

line INS 1E, ablation of NKX6.1 did not lead to a difference in glucose -stimulated insulin secretion 

(Pavluch, Engstová et al. 2023) . H eterozygous germline NKX6.1 -variants , p.(Ser317Leu) and 

p.(Pro329Leu) , have been identified in two patients with maturity -onset diabetes of the young 

(MODY) (Mohan, Radha et al. 2018) . Together, this indicates that loss -of -function in NKX6.1 may 

affect beta cell survival rather than decreased insulin secretion .

The last high allele frequency variant in Insulinoma O was found in ATP2B1 . ATP2B1 is weakly 

expressed in pancreatic islets according to The Human Protein Atlas, and little is known about this 

calcium transporter gene in beta -cells , called PMC A1. The missense variant in  ATP2B1 

p.(His1214Arg) is placed in the proximity of a phosphorylation site (Ser1216), and during GSIS the 

phosphorylation is upregulated  (26) . The positive charge of the His -residue remains after 

substitution to Arg, and ma y potentially facilitate the phosphorylation of the adjacent residue. 

However,  ATP2B1  silencing  results in higher intracellular Ca2+  concentration , which  trigger s insulin 

exocytosis. 

Taken together, the BRCA2 , Nkx6.1 and ATP2B1 variants found in the same insulinoma were likely 

of germline origin, although with little expression of BRCA2 and ATP2B1 in normal pancreatic 

tissue according to literature . A combin ation of these variants in germline may have had causative 

predisposing effects on the tumorigenesis. In the same insulinoma, three other somatic candidate 

genes were identified , suggesting a further complex causality in the combination of multi genetic 

germline and somatic genetic events. Paper III 

> 26

Down -regulated candidate genes 

Interestingly, PAX6 was both represented in the analyses of somatic variants (n=1) and in the 

analysis of the most DEGs (-261.35 FC) . The PAX6 missense variant (NP_000271.1:p. (Gly51Val) ) has 

previously been reported as pathogenic in association with a de novo germline va riant resulting in 

the development of irido -corneo -trabecular dysgenesis (accession ID: RCV000059340.4) (Prokudin, 

Simons et al . 2014) . In the pancreas, PAX6 codes for a key transcription factor regulating beta -cell 

development, integrity and maturity. Deficiency of PAX6 has been associated with a diabetes 

phenotype in mice, presenting with hyperglycemia and loss of beta -cell function (Swisa, Avrahami 

et al. 2017) . On the contrary, the significantly decreased gene expression of PAX6 in our study was 

associated with a phenotype of hyper insulin emic hypoglycemia. However, dedifferentiation of 

beta -cells may be the key event in insulinoma development, and our finding is consistent with the 

mouse study of Li et al . (Li, Su et al. 2015) , identifying that PNETs developed in Men 1 ablated mice 

have decreased Pax6 mRNA expression compared with control islets. Mutations in PAX6 have also 

previously been identified in one insulinoma  (Wang, Bender et al. 2017)  and non -functioning PNET 

(Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) .

Other highly down -regulated DEGs identified in our exome sequencing wa s ATP2B1 (-20.71 FC) 

described above , and DPP4 (-25.36 FC). DPP4 codes for Dipeptidyl peptidase -4 ( DPP4 ), which 

impairs insulin signaling by antagonizing GLP1 and catabolizing incretin hormones , and inhibitors 

of DPP4 ha ve been used as a mean against type 2 diabetes (Ca mpbell 2007) . Studies have found 

that DPP4 may exert negative effects on beta -cell survival and insulin secretion (Barchetta, Cimini 

et al. 2022) . The downregulation of DPP4 in insulinoma s may lead to increased in cretin response Paper III 

> 27

and hence hypersecretion of insulin. This further demonstrates the complexity of tumorigenesis 

and pathogenesis of the hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia in sporadic insulinoma .

Up -regulated candidate genes 

Two highly up -regulated genes were identified among our exome sequencing candidate genes, i.e. 

CCND2 (20.28 FC), and FGFR1 (10.17 FC) . CCND2 was one of the only two genes represented with 

mutations in more than one insulinoma in our multicenter cohort. The CCND2 mutatio ns were 

nonsense , and splice site , respectively. CCND2 codes for Cyclin D2 , which is partly responsible for 

the G1 -S transition dur ing cell cycle in complex with C yclin 4 and 6 (Fassl, Geng et al. 2022) .

Consistently with the high expression in insulinoma, Cyclin D2 has been shown to have a proto -

oncogenic potential (Rojas, Cadenas et al. 2007) , and additionally truncated C yclin D2 may have an 

oncogenic role in tumorigenesis in cytoplasm (Denicourt, Legault et al. 2008) .

FGFR1 encodes the fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) , responsible for e.g. survival and 

proliferation. Insulinoma M contained the variant p. (Glu692Lys ); with a VAF of 0.11 , in the tyrosine 

kinase domain . Identical variants have been detected earlier in analogous residues in the growth 

factor receptors FGFR4 (residue p. (Glu681Lys )) (Marks, McLellan et al. 2007) and ERBB2 (residue 

p. (Glu914Lys )) (Stephens, Hunter et al. 2004) in lung adenocarcinoma and glioblastoma, 

respectively. Furthermore, t he variant has been identified in a breast cancer biopsy (Grissom 

2021) . Point mutations in FGFR 1 leading to overexpression has been demonstrated before 

(Ellinghaus, Neureiter et al. 2022) , in line with the overall upregulation of FGFR1 in our microarray 

analysi s. A direct association between FGFR1 activity and the pancreatic transcription factor PDX1 

has been proposed, and the latter plays a crucial role in the establishment, fun ctionality and Paper III 

> 28

maturity of beta -cells. The activation of FGFR1 induces the gene expr ession of PDX1 , which plays a 

crucial role in the establishment, fun ctionality and maturity of beta -cells , including transcriptional 

activat ion of insulin and somatostatin (Yamashita -Sugahara, Matsumoto et al. 2016) . Consistently, 

the gene expression of SST , which encodes somatostatin, was highly increased in Insulinoma M ,

having the FGFR1 -variant .

Candidate genes not differentially expressed 

The f ive genes PWP1, YY1 , GPR1 , BAIAP3 , and SLC30A5 with variants detected by exome 

sequencing were not differentially expressed compared to control . Each of the se genes were 

altered in one insulinoma only and consisted of four missense mutations and one splice site 

mutation. The lack of differential expression may have three explanations: the combined analysis 

of all 12 insulinomas , missense varia nts often do not lead to change in gene expression , and 

variations in cellular subclones as suggested by the relatively low VAF of the variant s. 

Most differentially expressed genes 

We identified the 20 most up - and downregulated genes, when comparing mRNA expression 

between insulinomas and EndoC -βH1. The gene with the highest FC was SRGN (1 ,030 FC) , which 

encodes serglycin . Serglycin play s a role in inflammation and autocrine signaling and is highly 

expressed in various cancers (Korpetinou, Papachristou et al. 2015, Roy, Attarha et al. 2017, Wang, 

Xiong et al. 2020, Tanaka, Dayde et al. 2022) . Furthermore, serglycin is secreted by various cells, 

including tumor cells (Korpetinou, Papachristou et al. 2015, Chu, Huang et al. 2016) and the Paper III 

> 29

protein may be associated with the aggressiveness and survival rate for certain types of cancer 

(Wan g, Xiong et al. 2020) .

We clust ered the 40 most DEGs into two enriched clusters of annotation: Metabolism of 

cholesterol and metabolism of lipids. However, o nly 9 of the 40 genes (22.5%) were associated 

with the two clusters of annotation , and thereby no significant pathway association was achieved 

for 77.5 % of the DEGs . The two assigned clusters were containing overlapping genes, which may 

be related to the high similarity between the functional annotations. Cholesterol is a lipid which 

can be synthesi zed by all cells (Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) , and m etabolism of cholesterol may 

directly affect insulin secretion (Hao, Head et al. 2007, Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) . Hao et al . (Hao, 

Head et al. 2007) showed that depletion of cholesterol in islets increase s the insulin secretion 

independent on glucose and fatty acid concentratio ns . Further, dysregulation of the metabolism of 

cholesterol and fatty acids has been identified in patients with type 2 diabetes, resulting in loss of 

pancreatic islet cells (Cnop 2008, Oh, Bae et al. 2018, Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) . Especially 

chronic elevation of free fatty acids in the plasma may lead to lipotoxicity and negatively affect the 

beta -cell mass. Conversely, acute and transient elevation of free fatty acid metabolism in beta -

cells has the opposite effect and leads to inc reased insulin secretion and mass (Oh, Bae et al. 

2018) . These studies indicate that metabolism of cholesterol and other lipids may have impact on 

beta -cell function. Paper III 

> 30

Expression in islet tissues 

Using the Human Protein Atlas , we identified 15 of the DEGs in association with normal expression 

in pancreatic islet cells, further highlighting the importance of their gene -products in islets. Four of 

the islet -expressed genes ATG16L1 , MICAL1 , TTC39C , and ZNF5 12, were up -regulated .

ATG16L1 is part of a n E3 -like complex, responsible for autophagy and may also be interacting with 

C3 in regulation of cell death (King, Kulak et al. 2019) . In line with this, MICAL1 codes for a 

regulator of apoptosis, cancer cell growth and producer of reactive oxidative species (Deng, Wang 

et al. 2016) . A pathogenic variant in MICAL1 has previously been ident ified in insulinoma (Wang, 

Bender et al. 2017) . The third and fourth up -regulated gene s, TTC39C and ZNF512 , have unknown 

function s and may be a new candidate for additional functional investigation. 

Methodological considerations 

Formalin fixation of patient samples are suboptimal in molecular studies of variations in nucleic 

acids , particularly when using large -scale sequencing , such as whole -exome sequencing in the 

present study . FFPE samples are difficult to process due to the high degradation of nucleic acids. 

The rarity of insulinomas, however, limits or excludes the access to fr esh frozen insulinoma tissue 

in most centers. Further, our study has a methodological limitation in the compar ison of FFPE 

mRNA with the mRNA obtained from a cell line . Of note, a calculated high FC could not only be 

influenced by a high tumor expression, but also due to the use of mRNA -data from the control cell 

line, which lacks extracellular components, including different cell types and paracrine cell 

signaling. Paper III 

> 31

While germline variants were assessed using blood samples from five of the patients, likely 

germline variants were determined using a VAF score ≥0.40 from tumo r tissues. Guidelines and 

recommendations from The American Society of Clinical Oncology, American College of Medical 

Genetics and Genomics, and College of American Path ologists notes that VAF in tumo r tissue is 

expected to be present at approximately 0.5 and 1.0 , for heterozygous and homozygous germline 

alleles, respectively (Li, Datto et al. 2017, Montgomery, Selitsky et al. 2018) , and that the 

alt eration should be present in all of the sequenced cells. However, the interpretation of VAF 

depends on more factors including germline mosaicism, LOH, CNVs in tumor cells, 

insertions/deletions, structural rearrangements , and sequencing artifacts , such as shallow 

sequencing depths (Kraft and Godley 2020) . In a previous report , 96% of variants with a VAF 

between 0.40 and 0.60 could be confirmed as germline variants (Montgomery, Selitsky et al. 

2018) .

# Conclusion 

The sporadic insulinomas each had a distinct mutational profile, demonstrating a heterogeneity in 

the tumorigenesis of this subtype of PNETs. W e identified 33 candidate genes related to insulin 

hypersecretion and tumorigenesis with p athways of epigenetics, insulin biosynthesis an d

exocytosis, DNA repair, insulin signaling, beta -cell survival and metabolism . The candidate gene 

alteration occurred in only one tumor each , except for ATRX (n=3), and CCND2 (n=2). Three 

candidate genes were highly down regulated, PAX6, ATP2B 1, and DPP4 , and two were highly 

upregulated, CCND2 and FGFR1 , highlighting the importance of these genes. Clusters of 

metabolism of cholesterol and lipids were enriched , w hich may be implicated in the tumorigenesis Paper III 

32 

of insulinomas. Our findings may give novel insights in to beta -cell pathophysiology and insulin 

secretion, which may provide the framework for future studies on possible drug targets in 

diabetes and hyperinsulinism. Further experiments are esse ntial for the validation of the 

candidate genes.

differentially expressed genes by fold change (FC) were analysed for pathway enrichment. Page 7 of 9 2

# Genetic alterations in pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms with and without Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1

*   Kirstine Øster Andersen

*   [KI, OUH, Research unit of Paediatrics (Odense)](https://portal.findresearcher.sdu.dk/en/organisations/ki-ouh-forskningsenhed-for-p%C3%A6diatri-odense/)
*   [Department of Clinical Research](https://portal.findresearcher.sdu.dk/en/organisations/klinisk-institut/)

Research output: Thesis › Ph.D. thesis

382 Downloads (Pure)

[](https://plu.mx/plum/a/?doi=10.21996/fmq5-yq27)

*   [Overview](https://doi.org/en/publications/genetic-alterations-in-pancreatic-neuroendocrine-neoplasms-with-a/)
*   [Fingerprint](https://doi.org/en/publications/genetic-alterations-in-pancreatic-neuroendocrine-neoplasms-with-a/fingerprints/)
*   [Research output(1)](https://doi.org/en/publications/genetic-alterations-in-pancreatic-neuroendocrine-neoplasms-with-a/publications/)

## Abstract

**Background** - Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) are rare, solitary tumours which may occur in isolation or in association with hereditary syndromes, such as Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1). MEN1 is caused by inactivation of the MEN1 gene, encoding the tumour suppressor menin. According to Knudson’s two hit hypothesis, inactivation of MEN1 occurs in two steps; a first ‘hit’, often an inactivating germline mutation in one allele, and a second somatic hit commonly achieved by loss of heterozygosity of the second allele. In addition to MEN1 gene, the chromatin remodelling encoding genes DAXX and ATRX are frequently altered in PNENs. The majority of PNENs are non-functioning, however PNENs may be functioning, producing hormonal hypersecretion syndrome. The main type of functioning PNENs are insulinomas, which synthesize excessive amounts of insulin and may cause events of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. In sporadic insulinomas a recurrent variant in the YY1 gene is often identified. 

**Aims**- The aims of the thesis were to 1) review the previously reported exome and genome data of G1 and G2 pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms to determine the most frequently altered genes, 2) explore the inactivation events of MEN1 gene in PNENs from patients with MEN1 germline variants and 3) investigate the genetic and transcriptomic landscape of collected PNENs.

**Materials and methods** - The first study (Paper I) consisted of a review of published articles using whole exome, whole genome, or targeted gene panel (>400 genes) sequencing of G1/G2 PNENs. Somatic variant data were collated to summarize abundant aberrant genes, cooccurring variants, and variant hotspots in PNENs divided into hereditary tumours with predisposing germline variants and sporadic tumours. Further, non-functioning and functioning PNENs were distinguished into two groups for pathway evaluation. In Paper II, MEN1 variants and potential driver genes were detected using exome and targeted sequencing in PNENs from patients with MEN1 syndrome from our own cohort. Menin expression was determined by immunohistochemistry (IHC). In paper III, sporadic insulinomas from our cohort were analysed using exome sequencing, gene expression microarray and IHC. Gene expression in insulinomas were compared to the human beta-cell line EndoC-βH1 and the 40 most differentially expressed genes by fold change (FC) were analysed for pathway enrichment.

**Results**- In Paper I, 14 datasets from published studies on 225 PNENs were included in the analysis, consisting of sporadic PNENs accounted 72.0% (162/225), hereditary PNENs 13.3% (30/225), and PNENs with unknown germline status 14.7% (33/225). The most frequent somatically altered genes in all PNENs were MEN1 (n=95; 42%), DAXX (n= 37; 16%) and ATRX (n=27; 12%), including mutations and CNVs. New mutational hotspots were identified in the histone-binding domain and ATPase domain of DAXX and ATRX, respectively. While functioning PNENs shared few variated genes, such as YY1, non-functioning PNENs had recurrent genetic alterations in genes associated with Phosphoinositide 3-kinase, Wnt, NOTCH, and Receptor Tyrosine Kinase-Ras signaling onco-pathways.

We collected 19 well-differentiated G1/G2 PNENs, where seven PNENs (37 %) were obtained from patients with MEN1 syndrome and 12 (63 %) were sporadic PNENs (median age 14 (8- 22) vs 27.5 (9-75), p-value=0.03). In Paper II, all MEN1-associated PNENs had absent nuclear menin expression, and consistently, somatic CNV loss of MEN1 was determined for 4/5 sequenced PNENs from MEN1 patients. Potential drivers in DNA repair, chromatin remodelling and mTOR pathways were identified.

Lastly, in Paper III, we identified 33 candidate genes in 12 sporadic insulinomas. Only ATRX (n=3) and CCND2 (n=2) were altered in more than one insulinoma. Through gene expression analysis of the 33 genes, we found two highly upregulated genes i.e. CCND2 (20.28 FC), and FGFR1 (10.17 FC), and three highly down regulated genes i.e. PAX6 (-261.35 FC), DPP4 (-25.36 FC), and ATP2B1 (-20.71 FC). Nine of the 40 most differentially expressed genes (22.5%) were associated with metabolism of cholesterol and lipids.

**Conclusion**- PNENs represent a genetically heterogeneous group of tumours with few recurrent DNA alterations. Somatic variations in the MEN1 gene occur frequently in PNENs from patients with and without MEN1 syndrome. Total MEN1 inactivation was detected in 4/5 PNENs from MEN1 patients, consistent with Knudson’s two hit hypothesis. Further molecular studies are required to better understand the impact of the candidate genes discovered in our molecular analyses. The candidate genes may be of interest in future drug discoveries.

## Abstract

**Background** - Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) are rare, solitary tumours which may occur in isolation or in association with hereditary syndromes, such as Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1). MEN1 is caused by inactivation of the MEN1 gene, encoding the tumour suppressor menin. According to Knudson’s two hit hypothesis, inactivation of MEN1 occurs in two steps; a first ‘hit’, often an inactivating germline mutation in one allele, and a second somatic hit commonly achieved by loss of heterozygosity of the second allele. In addition to MEN1 gene, the chromatin remodelling encoding genes DAXX and ATRX are frequently altered in PNENs. The majority of PNENs are non-functioning, however PNENs may be functioning, producing hormonal hypersecretion syndrome. The main type of functioning PNENs are insulinomas, which synthesize excessive amounts of insulin and may cause events of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. In sporadic insulinomas a recurrent variant in the YY1 gene is often identified. 

**Aims**- The aims of the thesis were to 1) review the previously reported exome and genome data of G1 and G2 pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms to determine the most frequently altered genes, 2) explore the inactivation events of MEN1 gene in PNENs from patients with MEN1 germline variants and 3) investigate the genetic and transcriptomic landscape of collected PNENs.

**Materials and methods** - The first study (Paper I) consisted of a review of published articles using whole exome, whole genome, or targeted gene panel (>400 genes) sequencing of G1/G2 PNENs. Somatic variant data were collated to summarize abundant aberrant genes, cooccurring variants, and variant hotspots in PNENs divided into hereditary tumours with predisposing germline variants and sporadic tumours. Further, non-functioning and functioning PNENs were distinguished into two groups for pathway evaluation. In Paper II, MEN1 variants and potential driver genes were detected using exome and targeted sequencing in PNENs from patients with MEN1 syndrome from our own cohort. Menin expression was determined by immunohistochemistry (IHC). In paper III, sporadic insulinomas from our cohort were analysed using exome sequencing, gene expression microarray and IHC. Gene expression in insulinomas were compared to the human beta-cell line EndoC-βH1 and the 40 most differentially expressed genes by fold change (FC) were analysed for pathway enrichment.

**Results**- In Paper I, 14 datasets from published studies on 225 PNENs were included in the analysis, consisting of sporadic PNENs accounted 72.0% (162/225), hereditary PNENs 13.3% (30/225), and PNENs with unknown germline status 14.7% (33/225). The most frequent somatically altered genes in all PNENs were MEN1 (n=95; 42%), DAXX (n= 37; 16%) and ATRX (n=27; 12%), including mutations and CNVs. New mutational hotspots were identified in the histone-binding domain and ATPase domain of DAXX and ATRX, respectively. While functioning PNENs shared few variated genes, such as YY1, non-functioning PNENs had recurrent genetic alterations in genes associated with Phosphoinositide 3-kinase, Wnt, NOTCH, and Receptor Tyrosine Kinase-Ras signaling onco-pathways.

We collected 19 well-differentiated G1/G2 PNENs, where seven PNENs (37 %) were obtained from patients with MEN1 syndrome and 12 (63 %) were sporadic PNENs (median age 14 (8- 22) vs 27.5 (9-75), p-value=0.03). In Paper II, all MEN1-associated PNENs had absent nuclear menin expression, and consistently, somatic CNV loss of MEN1 was determined for 4/5 sequenced PNENs from MEN1 patients. Potential drivers in DNA repair, chromatin remodelling and mTOR pathways were identified.

Lastly, in Paper III, we identified 33 candidate genes in 12 sporadic insulinomas. Only ATRX (n=3) and CCND2 (n=2) were altered in more than one insulinoma. Through gene expression analysis of the 33 genes, we found two highly upregulated genes i.e. CCND2 (20.28 FC), and FGFR1 (10.17 FC), and three highly down regulated genes i.e. PAX6 (-261.35 FC), DPP4 (-25.36 FC), and ATP2B1 (-20.71 FC). Nine of the 40 most differentially expressed genes (22.5%) were associated with metabolism of cholesterol and lipids.

**Conclusion**- PNENs represent a genetically heterogeneous group of tumours with few recurrent DNA alterations. Somatic variations in the MEN1 gene occur frequently in PNENs from patients with and without MEN1 syndrome. Total MEN1 inactivation was detected in 4/5 PNENs from MEN1 patients, consistent with Knudson’s two hit hypothesis. Further molecular studies are required to better understand the impact of the candidate genes discovered in our molecular analyses. The candidate genes may be of interest in future drug discoveries.

# Genetic alterations in pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms with and without Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1

*   Kirstine Øster Andersen

*   [KI, OUH, Research unit of Paediatrics (Odense)](https://portal.findresearcher.sdu.dk/en/organisations/ki-ouh-forskningsenhed-for-p%C3%A6diatri-odense/)

382 Downloads (Pure)

[](https://plu.mx/plum/a/?doi=10.21996/fmq5-yq27)

*   [Overview](https://doi.org/en/publications/genetic-alterations-in-pancreatic-neuroendocrine-neoplasms-with-a/)
*   [Fingerprint](https://doi.org/en/publications/genetic-alterations-in-pancreatic-neuroendocrine-neoplasms-with-a/fingerprints/)
*   [Research output(1)](https://doi.org/en/publications/genetic-alterations-in-pancreatic-neuroendocrine-neoplasms-with-a/publications/)

## Abstract

**Background** - Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) are rare, solitary tumours which may occur in isolation or in association with hereditary syndromes, such as Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1). MEN1 is caused by inactivation of the MEN1 gene, encoding the tumour suppressor menin. According to Knudson’s two hit hypothesis, inactivation of MEN1 occurs in two steps; a first ‘hit’, often an inactivating germline mutation in one allele, and a second somatic hit commonly achieved by loss of heterozygosity of the second allele. In addition to MEN1 gene, the chromatin remodelling encoding genes DAXX and ATRX are frequently altered in PNENs. The majority of PNENs are non-functioning, however PNENs may be functioning, producing hormonal hypersecretion syndrome. The main type of functioning PNENs are insulinomas, which synthesize excessive amounts of insulin and may cause events of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. In sporadic insulinomas a recurrent variant in the YY1 gene is often identified. 

**Aims**- The aims of the thesis were to 1) review the previously reported exome and genome data of G1 and G2 pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms to determine the most frequently altered genes, 2) explore the inactivation events of MEN1 gene in PNENs from patients with MEN1 germline variants and 3) investigate the genetic and transcriptomic landscape of collected PNENs.

**Materials and methods** - The first study (Paper I) consisted of a review of published articles using whole exome, whole genome, or targeted gene panel (>400 genes) sequencing of G1/G2 PNENs. Somatic variant data were collated to summarize abundant aberrant genes, cooccurring variants, and variant hotspots in PNENs divided into hereditary tumours with predisposing germline variants and sporadic tumours. Further, non-functioning and functioning PNENs were distinguished into two groups for pathway evaluation. In Paper II, MEN1 variants and potential driver genes were detected using exome and targeted sequencing in PNENs from patients with MEN1 syndrome from our own cohort. Menin expression was determined by immunohistochemistry (IHC). In paper III, sporadic insulinomas from our cohort were analysed using exome sequencing, gene expression microarray and IHC. Gene expression in insulinomas were compared to the human beta-cell line EndoC-βH1 and the 40 most differentially expressed genes by fold change (FC) were analysed for pathway enrichment.

**Results**- In Paper I, 14 datasets from published studies on 225 PNENs were included in the analysis, consisting of sporadic PNENs accounted 72.0% (162/225), hereditary PNENs 13.3% (30/225), and PNENs with unknown germline status 14.7% (33/225). The most frequent somatically altered genes in all PNENs were MEN1 (n=95; 42%), DAXX (n= 37; 16%) and ATRX (n=27; 12%), including mutations and CNVs. New mutational hotspots were identified in the histone-binding domain and ATPase domain of DAXX and ATRX, respectively. While functioning PNENs shared few variated genes, such as YY1, non-functioning PNENs had recurrent genetic alterations in genes associated with Phosphoinositide 3-kinase, Wnt, NOTCH, and Receptor Tyrosine Kinase-Ras signaling onco-pathways.

We collected 19 well-differentiated G1/G2 PNENs, where seven PNENs (37 %) were obtained from patients with MEN1 syndrome and 12 (63 %) were sporadic PNENs (median age 14 (8- 22) vs 27.5 (9-75), p-value=0.03). In Paper II, all MEN1-associated PNENs had absent nuclear menin expression, and consistently, somatic CNV loss of MEN1 was determined for 4/5 sequenced PNENs from MEN1 patients. Potential drivers in DNA repair, chromatin remodelling and mTOR pathways were identified.

Lastly, in Paper III, we identified 33 candidate genes in 12 sporadic insulinomas. Only ATRX (n=3) and CCND2 (n=2) were altered in more than one insulinoma. Through gene expression analysis of the 33 genes, we found two highly upregulated genes i.e. CCND2 (20.28 FC), and FGFR1 (10.17 FC), and three highly down regulated genes i.e. PAX6 (-261.35 FC), DPP4 (-25.36 FC), and ATP2B1 (-20.71 FC). Nine of the 40 most differentially expressed genes (22.5%) were associated with metabolism of cholesterol and lipids.

**Conclusion**- PNENs represent a genetically heterogeneous group of tumours with few recurrent DNA alterations. Somatic variations in the MEN1 gene occur frequently in PNENs from patients with and without MEN1 syndrome. Total MEN1 inactivation was detected in 4/5 PNENs from MEN1 patients, consistent with Knudson’s two hit hypothesis. Further molecular studies are required to better understand the impact of the candidate genes discovered in our molecular analyses. The candidate genes may be of interest in future drug discoveries.

1.   Education:

1980 High School, Odense Katadralskole, Mat. Biol. branch.

1981: Immatriculated at Odense University, natural sciences.

1990: Cand. Scient. degree, Experimental cell biology, molecular biology.

1999: Ph. D. from Aarhus University; “A preliminary genomic map of the American mink (Mustela vison)

2019: Clinical Laboratory Geneticist, European Board of Medical Genetics.

II Positions:

1990: Research assistant, Department of Pharmacology, IMB., Odense University.

1991: Military service.

1991: Research assistant, Department of Medical Microbiology, IMB, Odense University.

1992: Research scientist, Department of Animal Physiology and biochemistry, Danish Institute of Animal Science.

1996: Research scientist, Department of Breeding and Genetics, Danish Institute of Animal Science.

1997: Research scientist, Department of Biochemistry, Pharmacology and Genetics, OUH, Odense.

2006-: Founder of Amplexa Genetics A/S

2010-: Senior researcher, Department of Clinical Genetics, Odense University Hospital, Odense.

2011-: Associate professor, Institute of Health, University of Southern Denmark

2017-: Visiting Professor, Near East University, Faculty of Medicine, Department of Medical Genetics, Nicosia, Cyprus

**Supervision function**

Supervisor on 19 PhD projects, 40 science thesis projects, bachelor projects or other projects.

**Editor and Review positions**

Editor on PlosOne (more than 100 manuscripts) and Advances in Endocrinology, ContROL– Genetics

Review for PlosOne, Lipidology, European Journal of Endocrinology, SciTechnol, BioMed Central, Clinical Biochemistry, Frontiers in Genetics, Clinical Biochemistry, Frontiers in Genetics, SciTecTool.

Member of the National Genom Center Advisory board on Endocrinology, EndoGenNet.

Member of the National Genom Center Advisory board on interpretation.

CRN Genetics Workstream and CRN Council, the CHI Collaborative Research Network (CRN).

**Research councils**

The Norwegian Research Council

The French Research Council

**Membership of organisations**

Since 2019 member of Illumina sequencing expert panel.

Nordic Alliance for Clinical Genomics (NACG)

Danish Sociaty of Clinical Academics (DSKA)

Danish Sociaty of Clinical Genetecist (DSMG)

Odense Pancreas Center (OPAC)

content:
**Formal education training**.

I have participated in targeted courses, but most of my training as an educator has been on the ground. I have regularly lectured in pregraduate and postgraduate setting – medical students, medical doctors and nurses. I started teaching during my study to become a doctor, teaching nurses in biochemistry. In general, it is my impression that my teaching is considered to be of good quality and I have received very positive feed-back from students.

_Teaching related courses._ I have had formal training in the mediation of Evidence Based Medicine. In 2006, 4th to 9th June I participated in ”How to teach evidence-based clinical medicine” at the McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario (40 hours). 

Furthermore, I have participated in Evidence based medicine, 1st to 2nd and 13th to 14th June 2004 at the Nordic Cochrane Center, Copenhagen (32 hours). 

During my Ph.D. study I have had training in how to do “Oral presentations”, at The Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark (approximately 30 hours) – and have had further informal courses in oral presentations (approximately 20 hours) with feed-back from journalists.

**Administrative tasks in relation to education.**Since 2012 I have been co-programme director for the Graduate Programme for Clinical Research at the Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark. We have developed the leading element in this programme – “the communication of fundamental scientific expertise to researchers with clinically based projects” – and the graduate programme has become popular (with around 70 Ph.D. students signed up to the programme) and now offers a variety of Ph.D. courses. We introduced and completed the first pre-Ph.D. course, for doctors planning a Ph.D. study. This course had very positive feedback from the start and has continued in another Graduate Programme at the university. 

I have been a member of the Education Committee of Danish Society of Gastroenterology in the period 2003 to 2011 and as such have been planning and conducting annual post-graduate courses in gastroenterology and hepatology for physicians training in gastroenterology. Furthermore, I have been a member of the Endoscopy Committee for Danish Society of Gastroenterology from 2005 to 2014, planning and conducting annual/bi-annual courses in endoscopy for doctors training in gastroenterology and surgery. I am responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B

**Teaching experience**_Pregraduate students_ I have since 2003 been employed as clinical lecturer (associate professor) at Institute of Clinical Research, University of Southern Denmark. I have taught in the following modules in medicine: (1) K5 Diseases of the gastrointestinal tract, (2) K14 Clinical Courses (gastrointestinal diseases). The teaching lessons have been overview lectures, lectures for smaller groups of students in clinical problem solving, and patient demonstration (bed-side teaching). Moreover, I have participated in the training of medical students at the Department of Medical Gastroenterology. I am also responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B; where the lessons have been overview lectures, patient demonstration, and clinical problem solving.

_Supervisor for medical candidate research project_ I have since 2005 supervised eleven medical candidate’s research projects with subject reflecting gastrointestinal and hepatologic diseases and conditions (see curriculum vitae) and are currently, supervising a bachelor project in biomedicine

_Postgraduate teaching_ Since my graduation as a medical doctor I have taught regularly. 

• As a member of the Endoscopy Committee for Danish Society of Gastroenterology from 2005 to 2014 I have annually taught in endoscopy for smaller groups of doctors (around 20) with lectures and hands-on training in endoscopy. (Approximately 12 hours a year) 

• At lectures in Gastroenterology specialist training (approximately 10 hours yearly) 

• In the Rheumatologic specialist training 

• I regularly have post-graduate teaching session in training of gastroenterologists.

_Examination_ I have participated in OSCE examinations (20 hours per year) and have prepared multiple-choice questions for module K5 and free text questions and multiple-choice questions for Pharmacy students in module 3B.

**Teaching materials**I have written a chapter entitled Medicine in the treatment of gastrointestinal disorder in textbook of Basal and Clinical Pharmacology. Furthermore, I have written a section in textbook about Immunoinflammatory diseases – background and biological medicine, with focus on biological treatment of gastrointestinal diseases.

**Plans for teaching if appointed to the position**I plan to further develop my teaching skills and I feel comfortable with all forms of teaching methods, including overview lectures, problem based learning and bed-side teaching. I plan to continue with supervision of pre-graduate students doing medical candidate projects – projects where I find that my skills as a researcher with focus on evidence-based medicine are well-used. If possible I would appreciate to continue my teaching corresponding to the level of a B-lecturer at the university.

_Teaching related courses._ I have had formal training in the mediation of Evidence Based Medicine. In 2006, 4th to 9th June I participated in ”How to teach evidence-based clinical medicine” at the McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario (40 hours). 

Furthermore, I have participated in Evidence based medicine, 1st to 2nd and 13th to 14th June 2004 at the Nordic Cochrane Center, Copenhagen (32 hours). 

During my Ph.D. study I have had training in how to do “Oral presentations”, at The Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark (approximately 30 hours) – and have had further informal courses in oral presentations (approximately 20 hours) with feed-back from journalists.

**Administrative tasks in relation to education.**Since 2012 I have been co-programme director for the Graduate Programme for Clinical Research at the Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark. We have developed the leading element in this programme – “the communication of fundamental scientific expertise to researchers with clinically based projects” – and the graduate programme has become popular (with around 70 Ph.D. students signed up to the programme) and now offers a variety of Ph.D. courses. We introduced and completed the first pre-Ph.D. course, for doctors planning a Ph.D. study. This course had very positive feedback from the start and has continued in another Graduate Programme at the university. 

I have been a member of the Education Committee of Danish Society of Gastroenterology in the period 2003 to 2011 and as such have been planning and conducting annual post-graduate courses in gastroenterology and hepatology for physicians training in gastroenterology. Furthermore, I have been a member of the Endoscopy Committee for Danish Society of Gastroenterology from 2005 to 2014, planning and conducting annual/bi-annual courses in endoscopy for doctors training in gastroenterology and surgery. I am responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B

**Teaching experience**_Pregraduate students_ I have since 2003 been employed as clinical lecturer (associate professor) at Institute of Clinical Research, University of Southern Denmark. I have taught in the following modules in medicine: (1) K5 Diseases of the gastrointestinal tract, (2) K14 Clinical Courses (gastrointestinal diseases). The teaching lessons have been overview lectures, lectures for smaller groups of students in clinical problem solving, and patient demonstration (bed-side teaching). Moreover, I have participated in the training of medical students at the Department of Medical Gastroenterology. I am also responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B; where the lessons have been overview lectures, patient demonstration, and clinical problem solving.

• In the Rheumatologic specialist training

If possible I would appreciate to continue my teaching corresponding to the level of a B-lecturer at the university.

This work is released under a CC BY -ND license, which means that you are

anyone who creates software or other products or services implementing 

ISO 26324 to use the trademark DOI free of charge provided that: 

• the software, product or service is accurately described 

• DOI is identified as a trademark of the DOI ® Foundation 

• the superscript symbol ® is placed following the letters "DOI" at its first 

occurrence in any printed or electronic document describing or mar-

keting the software, product or service 

A re -sizable version of the DOI logo for Internet use under these conditions 

can be downloaded from the DOI ® web site as a convenience for compa-

nies, organizations and the press. Inclusion of this logo should not be used to 

imply DOI ® Foundation's endorsement of the company, product or services. 

For more information, see the Trademark Policy (https://www.doi.org/re-

sources/130718 -trademark -policy.pdf). 

Publication date: 2024 -11 -13D O I U R I s C H E M E 

3

CONTENTS 

PREFACE 4

CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION ................................ ................................ . 5

CHAPTER 2 SYNTAX ................................ ................................ ............ 6

CHAPTER 3 EQUIVALENCE ................................ ................................ .. 8

CHAPTER 4 DOI NAME RESOLUTION ................................ .................... 9

CHAPTER 5 RETRIEVING THE REFERENT IDENTIFIED BY A DOI NAME ..... 11 

CHAPTER 6 SECURITY CONSIDERATIONS ................................ ............ 12 

CHAPTER 7 IANA CONSIDERATIONS ................................ .................. 13 

CHAPTER 8 REFERENCES ................................ ................................ ... 14 

8.1 Normative References ................................ ................................ ................................ ..... 14 

8.2 Informative References ................................ ................................ ................................ .... 14 D O I U R I s C H E M E 

4

# PREFACE 

This document specifies the "doi" URI scheme. It has been prepared and 

published by the DOI Foundation ( https://www.doi.org/ ), and was subject to 

consensus review by DOI Foundation members, including its registration 

agencies. D O I U R I s C H E M E 

5

Chapter 1 

# INTRODUCTION 

A DOI name is a global unique identifier of a referent, which can be any 

digital, physical or abstract entity, including inventions, literary and artistic 

works, ideas, symbols, names, images, designs, etc. DOI names are, for ex-

ample, widely used to identi fy academic publications. The DOI system is 

specified in [iso26324] and [doi -handbook], with the former offering regular 

formal snapshot of the latter.    

> EXAMPLE 1: The DOI name " 10.5240/7481 -838B -59CA -63D0 -B9A8 -E”refers to My Neigh-
> bor Totoro , a 1988 film directed by Hayao Miyazaki .

A DOI name is persistent over time. This persistence is provided by the inde-

pendence of the DOI name from the referent itself and its descriptive ele-

ments. These descriptive elements of a referent, including location and own-

ership, can change over time, an d their current values are retrieved by re-

solving the DOI name. The set of elements retrieved by resolving a DOI 

name is called the DOI record. The DOI name resolution process uses the 

Handle System specified at [RFC3650], [RFC3651] and [RFC3652], as up-

dat ed by [DOI -RP]. 

This document specifies a URI scheme for DOI names. This scheme conforms 

to the syntax specified at [RFC3986] and formalizes the notation "doi:<DOI 

name>", which is in widespread use. When dereferenced as detailed in Sec-

tion 4, the URI corresponding to a DOI name yields the DOI record associ-

ated with the name. 

> EXAMPLE 2: "doi: 10.5240/7481 -838B -59CA -63D0 -B9A8 -E" is the URI corresponding to the
> DOI name above.

This document intended to satisfy the guidelines and registration procedures 

specified at [RFC7595]. D O I U R I s C H E M E 

6

Chapter 2 

# SYNTAX 

As specified at [doi -handbook ], a DOI name consists of an ordered se-

quence of Unicode code points of the Graphic type. The code points are 

arranged in a DOI prefix and a DOI suffix separated by U+002F SOLIDUS .

A DOI Name URI is a URI that corresponds to a given DOI name. As defined 

at [RFC7595 ], its scheme name SHALL be "doi" and its scheme -specific -

part SHALL conform to the following syntax (expressed using ABNF syntax as 

defined at [RFC5234]) :

scheme -specific -part = doi -encoded -prefix "/" doi -encoded -suffix 

doi -encoded -prefix and doi -encoded -suffix SHALL be the result of applying 

the following ordered sequence of steps to , respectively, the DOI prefix and 

DOI suffix :

1. express the ordered sequence of Unicode code points as a UTF -8

String, as defined at [Unicode ], without the byte order mark and with-

out any normalization; 

2. for every byte in the UTF -8 String: 

a. output the byte unmodified if the byte is either in the unreserved 

set, in the sub -delims set, equal to ":" or equal to "@";

b. otherwise, replace the byte with the US -ASCII byte triplet result-

ing from percent -encod ing the byte. 

The unreserved and sub -delims sets are specified at [RF C3986 ]. 

A DOI Name URI shall contain neither a query component nor a fragment 

component.  

> EXAMPLE 1: The DOI name "10.5594/SMPTE.ST2067 -21.2020" corresponds to the
> URI <doi:10.5594/SMPTE.ST2067 -21.2020>. D O I U R I s C H E M E

7

EXAMPLE 2: The DOI name " 10.6338/JDA.202212/SP_17(4).0000 " corresponds to the 

URI <doi:10.6338/JDA.202212%2FSP_17(4).0000 >. 

EXAMPLE 3: The DOI name "10.26321/Á.GUTIÉRREZ.ZARZA.02.2018.03" with the code 

point sequence <U+0031, U+0030, U+002E, U+0032, U+0036, U+0033, U+0032, U+0031, 

U+002F, U+00C1, U+002E, U+0047, U+0055, U+0054, U+0049, U+00C9, U+0052, U+0052, 

U+0045, U+005A, U+002E, U+0 05A, U+0041, U+0052, U+005A, U+0041, U+002E, U+0030, 

U+0032, U+002E, U+0032, U+0030, U+0031, U+0038, U+002E, U+0030, U+0033> corre-

sponds to the URI <doi:10.26321/%C3%81.GUTI%C3%89RREZ.ZARZA.02.2018.03>. 

NOTE 1: The sequence of code points comprising a DOI name is not normalized and 

equivalence between DOI names is based on code points. For example, two DOI 

names that differ only in the abstract character "Á" being encoded as <U+00C1> in the 

first and as < U+0041, U+0301> in the second are not identical. 

NOTE 2: Presenting a DOI name by rendering its sequence of code points to glyphs can 

be ambiguous since multiple code points or sequences of code points can result in the 

same glyphs. For example, U+002D HYPHEN -MINUS, U+2212 MINUS SIGN and U+2013 EN 

DASH a re rendered as similar glyphs. As another example, the abstract character "á" 

can be represented by either the code point U+00E1 or the sequence of code points 

<U+0061, U+0301>. Presenting a DOI name in its URI form resolves this ambiguity. 

NOTE 3: The algorithm for generating a DOI Name URI from a DOI Name is not generic, 

and care is needed when processing a DOI Name URI using a generic URI library. In the 

context of the generic URI syntax, a DOI Name URI is a URI where the hier -part compo-

nent is a path -rootless component. The path -rootless component itself consists of two 

segments, the corresponding to the doi -encoded -prefix and the second to the doi -en-

coded -suffix. 

NOTE 4: Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs ) are a kind of identifier specified in 

[RFC3987 ] and used in [RDF] . The IRI syntax is an extension of the URI syntax, and every 

URI is also an IRI. As such, a DOI Name URI can be used without modification whe rever 

an IRI is needed and the URI -to -IRI conversion algorithm specified at [RFC3987 ], 3.2 is 

not used .D O I U R I s C H E M E 

8

Chapter 3 

# EQUIVALENCE 

The following procedure SHALL be performed to determine whether two DOI 

Name URIs are equivalent: 

1. the scheme -specific -part of each of the two URIs is percent -decoded 

into a UTF -8 String; 

2. the two UTF -8 Strings are interpreted as two DOI names; 

3. the two DOI Name URIs are equivalent if the two DOI names are equiv-

alent, as defined at [doi -handbook]. 

NOTE: When testing for equivalence, DOI names are case -insensitive only with respect 

to the Basic Latin Unicode block. D O I U R I s C H E M E 

9

Chapter 4 

# DOI NAME RESOLUTION 

Resolving a DOI name means retrieving its DOI record, which contains the 

descriptive elements associated with the referent identified by the DOI 

name. 

A DOI name URI can be used to resolve its corresponding DOI name by per-

forming an HTTP GET request at the following URL (expressed using ABNF syn-

tax as defined at [RFC5234]): 

"https://doi.org/api/handles/" scheme -specific -part 

where scheme -specific -part is defined at Section 2, and the "https" scheme 

is specified at [RFC9110]. 

The body of the response is a JSON object, as defined at [RFC8259], that 

contains the following members: 

responseCode 

The property is a Number. The following values are defined: 

1 The resolution completed successfully. The HTTP response status 

code is 200. 

2 The resolution did not complete successfully because of a server 

error. The HTTP response status code is 500. 

100 The DOI name was not found. The HTTP response status code is 

404. 

200 No descriptive elements were found for the requested DOI 

name. The HTTP response status code is 200. 

handle 

The property is a String. It is equal to the DOI name for which resolution 

was requested. D O I U R I s C H E M E 

10 

values 

The property is an Object. It contains the descriptive elements for the 

referent identified by the DOI name. The contents of the property are 

specified at [RFC3651]. 

Figure 1 illustrates the DOI record, at the time of this writing, for the DOI 

name corresponding to the URI <doi:10.1000/182>. The DOI record was re-

trieved by performing an HTTP GET request to <https://doi.org/api/han-

dles/10.1000/182>.

"responseCode": 1, 

"handle": "10.1000/182", 

"values": [ 

{

"index": 1, 

"type": "URL", 

"data": { 

"format": "string",

},

"timestamp": "2004 -01 -21T14:14:17Z" 

}, 

{

"index": 100, 

"type": "HS_ADMIN", 

"data": { 

"format": "admin", 

"value": { 

"handle": "0.na/10.1000", 

"index": 200,

"legacyByteLength": true 

}

},

"timestamp": "2000 -06 -23T15:17:46Z" 

}

]

}    

> F i g u r e 1.D O I r e c o r d f o r t h e D O I n a m e " 1 0 . 1 0 0 0 / 1 8 2 " ( a t t h e t i m e o f t h i s w r i t i n g ) .D O I U R I s C H E M E

11 

Chapter 5 

# RETRIEVING THE REFERENT 

# IDENTIFIED BY A DOI NAME 

While Section 4 specifies the procedure for retrieving the DOI record 

associated with DOI name, the steps necessary to retrieve the actual 

referent described by the record depend on the nature of the refer-

ent, e.g., a referent can be a physical object. 

Some, but not all, referents can be retrieved by dereferencing an 

HTTP/HTTPS URI found in their respective DOI records, as illustrated in 

Figure 1 where the referent identified by the DOI name "10.1000/182" 

can be retrieved at "http://www.doi.org/hb.html". 

The single DOI resolution and multiple doi resolution functions at [doi -

handbook] specify the process of retrieving a referent that is available 

by dereferencing an HTTP/HTTPS URI. D O I U R I s C H E M E 

12 

Chapter 6 

# SECURITY CONSIDERATIONS 

A DOI name is an opaque string, which does not have a discernible mean-

ing on its own and is for use by humans and machines alike. It consists of a 

sequence of Unicode code points and the security considerations at 

[UNICODE -TR36] apply. In particular, and as noted at Section 2, presenting a 

DOI name by rendering its sequence of code points to glyphs can be am-

biguous. As a result, two DOI names rendering to the same sequence o f

glyphs can identify referents, including, for example, two software executa-

bles wi th wildly different side -effects. Presenting a DOI name in its URI form, 

which consists of a limited subset of characters, can lessen this risk. 

The DOI name resolution process is conducted using the Hypertext Transfer 

Protocol Secure, which ensures confidentiality and integrity of the transac-

tion, and the security considerations at [RFC9110] apply. 

The result of the DOI name resolution process is a JSON object and the secu-

rity considerations at [RFC8259] apply. D O I U R I s C H E M E 

13 

Chapter 7 

# IANA CONSIDERATIONS 

The following is the permanent URI Scheme Registration request, as defined 

in [RFC7595]:

quence of Unicode code points of the Graphic type. The code points are 

arranged in a DOI prefix and a DOI suffix separated by U+002F SOLIDUS .

at [RFC7595 ], its scheme name SHALL be "doi" and its scheme -specific -

part SHALL conform to the following syntax (expressed using ABNF syntax as 

defined at [RFC5234]) :

scheme -specific -part = doi -encoded -prefix "/" doi -encoded -suffix 

doi -encoded -prefix and doi -encoded -suffix SHALL be the result of applying 

the following ordered sequence of steps to , respectively, the DOI prefix and 

DOI suffix :

1. express the ordered sequence of Unicode code points as a UTF -8

String, as defined at [Unicode ], without the byte order mark and with-

out any normalization; 

2. for every byte in the UTF -8 String: 

a. output the byte unmodified if the byte is either in the unreserved 

set, in the sub -delims set, equal to ":" or equal to "@";

b. otherwise, replace the byte with the US -ASCII byte triplet result-

ing from percent -encod ing the byte. 

The unreserved and sub -delims sets are specified at [RF C3986 ]. 

A DOI Name URI shall contain neither a query component nor a fragment 

component.  

> EXAMPLE 1: The DOI name "10.5594/SMPTE.ST2067 -21.2020" corresponds to the
> URI <doi:10.5594/SMPTE.ST2067 -21.2020>. D O I U R I s C H E M E

7

URI <doi:10.6338/JDA.202212%2FSP_17(4).0000 >.

point sequence <U+0031, U+0030, U+002E, U+0032, U+0036, U+0033, U+0032, U+0031, 

U+002F, U+00C1, U+002E, U+0047, U+0055, U+0054, U+0049, U+00C9, U+0052, U+0052, 

U+0045, U+005A, U+002E, U+0 05A, U+0041, U+0052, U+005A, U+0041, U+002E, U+0030,

sponds to the URI <doi:10.26321/%C3%81.GUTI%C3%89RREZ.ZARZA.02.2018.03>.

be ambiguous since multiple code points or sequences of code points can result in the 

same glyphs. For example, U+002D HYPHEN -MINUS, U+2212 MINUS SIGN and U+2013 EN 

DASH a re rendered as similar glyphs. As another example, the abstract character "á" 

can be represented by either the code point U+00E1 or the sequence of code points 

<U+0061, U+0301>. Presenting a DOI name in its URI form resolves this ambiguity.

nent is a path -rootless component. The path -rootless component itself consists of two 

segments, the corresponding to the doi -encoded -prefix and the second to the doi -en-

coded -suffix.

tax as defined at [RFC5234]): 

"https://doi.org/api/handles/" scheme -specific -part

is specified at [RFC9110].

responseCode

404. 

200 No descriptive elements were found for the requested DOI 

name. The HTTP response status code is 200. 

handle

While Section 4 specifies the procedure for retrieving the DOI record 

associated with DOI name, the steps necessary to retrieve the actual 

referent described by the record depend on the nature of the refer-

can be retrieved at "http://www.doi.org/hb.html".

handbook] specify the process of retrieving a referent that is available

Chapter 6 

# SECURITY CONSIDERATIONS 

A DOI name is an opaque string, which does not have a discernible mean-

ing on its own and is for use by humans and machines alike. It consists of a 

sequence of Unicode code points and the security considerations at 

[UNICODE -TR36] apply. In particular, and as noted at Section 2, presenting a 

DOI name by rendering its sequence of code points to glyphs can be am-

biguous. As a result, two DOI names rendering to the same sequence o f

glyphs can identify referents, including, for example, two software executa-

bles wi th wildly different side -effects. Presenting a DOI name in its URI form, 

which consists of a limited subset of characters, can lessen this risk. 

The DOI name resolution process is conducted using the Hypertext Transfer 

Protocol Secure, which ensures confidentiality and integrity of the transac-

tion, and the security considerations at [RFC9110] apply. 

The result of the DOI name resolution process is a JSON object and the secu-

rity considerations at [RFC8259] apply. D O I U R I s C H E M E

Chapter 5 

# RETRIEVING THE REFERENT 

# IDENTIFIED BY A DOI NAME 

While Section 4 specifies the procedure for retrieving the DOI record 

associated with DOI name, the steps necessary to retrieve the actual 

referent described by the record depend on the nature of the refer-

ent, e.g., a referent can be a physical object. 

Some, but not all, referents can be retrieved by dereferencing an 

HTTP/HTTPS URI found in their respective DOI records, as illustrated in 

Figure 1 where the referent identified by the DOI name "10.1000/182" 

can be retrieved at "http://www.doi.org/hb.html". 

The single DOI resolution and multiple doi resolution functions at [doi -

handbook] specify the process of retrieving a referent that is available 

by dereferencing an HTTP/HTTPS URI. D O I U R I s C H E M E 

12 

Chapter 6 

# SECURITY CONSIDERATIONS 

A DOI name is an opaque string, which does not have a discernible mean-

ing on its own and is for use by humans and machines alike. It consists of a 

sequence of Unicode code points and the security considerations at 

[UNICODE -TR36] apply. In particular, and as noted at Section 2, presenting a 

DOI name by rendering its sequence of code points to glyphs can be am-

biguous. As a result, two DOI names rendering to the same sequence o f

glyphs can identify referents, including, for example, two software executa-

bles wi th wildly different side -effects. Presenting a DOI name in its URI form, 

which consists of a limited subset of characters, can lessen this risk. 

The DOI name resolution process is conducted using the Hypertext Transfer 

Protocol Secure, which ensures confidentiality and integrity of the transac-

tion, and the security considerations at [RFC9110] apply. 

The result of the DOI name resolution process is a JSON object and the secu-

rity considerations at [RFC8259] apply. D O I U R I s C H E M E

**Formal education training**.

I have participated in targeted courses, but most of my training as an educator has been on the ground. I have regularly lectured in pregraduate and postgraduate setting – medical students, medical doctors and nurses. I started teaching during my study to become a doctor, teaching nurses in biochemistry. In general, it is my impression that my teaching is considered to be of good quality and I have received very positive feed-back from students.

_Teaching related courses._ I have had formal training in the mediation of Evidence Based Medicine. In 2006, 4th to 9th June I participated in ”How to teach evidence-based clinical medicine” at the McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario (40 hours). 

Furthermore, I have participated in Evidence based medicine, 1st to 2nd and 13th to 14th June 2004 at the Nordic Cochrane Center, Copenhagen (32 hours). 

During my Ph.D. study I have had training in how to do “Oral presentations”, at The Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark (approximately 30 hours) – and have had further informal courses in oral presentations (approximately 20 hours) with feed-back from journalists.

**Administrative tasks in relation to education.**Since 2012 I have been co-programme director for the Graduate Programme for Clinical Research at the Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark. We have developed the leading element in this programme – “the communication of fundamental scientific expertise to researchers with clinically based projects” – and the graduate programme has become popular (with around 70 Ph.D. students signed up to the programme) and now offers a variety of Ph.D. courses. We introduced and completed the first pre-Ph.D. course, for doctors planning a Ph.D. study. This course had very positive feedback from the start and has continued in another Graduate Programme at the university. 

I have been a member of the Education Committee of Danish Society of Gastroenterology in the period 2003 to 2011 and as such have been planning and conducting annual post-graduate courses in gastroenterology and hepatology for physicians training in gastroenterology. Furthermore, I have been a member of the Endoscopy Committee for Danish Society of Gastroenterology from 2005 to 2014, planning and conducting annual/bi-annual courses in endoscopy for doctors training in gastroenterology and surgery. I am responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B

**Teaching experience**_Pregraduate students_ I have since 2003 been employed as clinical lecturer (associate professor) at Institute of Clinical Research, University of Southern Denmark. I have taught in the following modules in medicine: (1) K5 Diseases of the gastrointestinal tract, (2) K14 Clinical Courses (gastrointestinal diseases). The teaching lessons have been overview lectures, lectures for smaller groups of students in clinical problem solving, and patient demonstration (bed-side teaching). Moreover, I have participated in the training of medical students at the Department of Medical Gastroenterology. I am also responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B; where the lessons have been overview lectures, patient demonstration, and clinical problem solving.

_Supervisor for medical candidate research project_ I have since 2005 supervised eleven medical candidate’s research projects with subject reflecting gastrointestinal and hepatologic diseases and conditions (see curriculum vitae) and are currently, supervising a bachelor project in biomedicine

_Postgraduate teaching_ Since my graduation as a medical doctor I have taught regularly. 

• As a member of the Endoscopy Committee for Danish Society of Gastroenterology from 2005 to 2014 I have annually taught in endoscopy for smaller groups of doctors (around 20) with lectures and hands-on training in endoscopy. (Approximately 12 hours a year) 

• At lectures in Gastroenterology specialist training (approximately 10 hours yearly) 

• In the Rheumatologic specialist training 

• I regularly have post-graduate teaching session in training of gastroenterologists.

_Examination_ I have participated in OSCE examinations (20 hours per year) and have prepared multiple-choice questions for module K5 and free text questions and multiple-choice questions for Pharmacy students in module 3B.

**Teaching materials**I have written a chapter entitled Medicine in the treatment of gastrointestinal disorder in textbook of Basal and Clinical Pharmacology. Furthermore, I have written a section in textbook about Immunoinflammatory diseases – background and biological medicine, with focus on biological treatment of gastrointestinal diseases.

**Plans for teaching if appointed to the position**I plan to further develop my teaching skills and I feel comfortable with all forms of teaching methods, including overview lectures, problem based learning and bed-side teaching. I plan to continue with supervision of pre-graduate students doing medical candidate projects – projects where I find that my skills as a researcher with focus on evidence-based medicine are well-used. If possible I would appreciate to continue my teaching corresponding to the level of a B-lecturer at the university.

**Formal education training**.
I have participated in targeted courses, but most of my training as an educator has been on the ground. I have regularly lectured in pregraduate and postgraduate setting – medical students, medical doctors and nurses. I started teaching during my study to become a doctor, teaching nurses in biochemistry. In general, it is my impression that my teaching is considered to be of good quality and I have received very positive feed-back from students.
_Teaching related courses._ I have had formal training in the mediation of Evidence Based Medicine. In 2006, 4th to 9th June I participated in ”How to teach evidence-based clinical medicine” at the McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario (40 hours).
Furthermore, I have participated in Evidence based medicine, 1st to 2nd and 13th to 14th June 2004 at the Nordic Cochrane Center, Copenhagen (32 hours).
During my Ph.D. study I have had training in how to do “Oral presentations”, at The Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark (approximately 30 hours) – and have had further informal courses in oral presentations (approximately 20 hours) with feed-back from journalists.
**Administrative tasks in relation to education.**Since 2012 I have been co-programme director for the Graduate Programme for Clinical Research at the Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Southern Denmark. We have developed the leading element in this programme – “the communication of fundamental scientific expertise to researchers with clinically based projects” – and the graduate programme has become popular (with around 70 Ph.D. students signed up to the programme) and now offers a variety of Ph.D. courses. We introduced and completed the first pre-Ph.D. course, for doctors planning a Ph.D. study. This course had very positive feedback from the start and has continued in another Graduate Programme at the university.

I have been a member of the Education Committee of Danish Society of Gastroenterology in the period 2003 to 2011 and as such have been planning and conducting annual post-graduate courses in gastroenterology and hepatology for physicians training in gastroenterology. Furthermore, I have been a member of the Endoscopy Committee for Danish Society of Gastroenterology from 2005 to 2014, planning and conducting annual/bi-annual courses in endoscopy for doctors training in gastroenterology and surgery. I am responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B
**Teaching experience**_Pregraduate students_ I have since 2003 been employed as clinical lecturer (associate professor) at Institute of Clinical Research, University of Southern Denmark. I have taught in the following modules in medicine: (1) K5 Diseases of the gastrointestinal tract, (2) K14 Clinical Courses (gastrointestinal diseases). The teaching lessons have been overview lectures, lectures for smaller groups of students in clinical problem solving, and patient demonstration (bed-side teaching). Moreover, I have participated in the training of medical students at the Department of Medical Gastroenterology. I am also responsible for the annual teaching in gastrointestinal diseases in module 3B Clinical Pharmacology and Therapy B; where the lessons have been overview lectures, patient demonstration, and clinical problem solving.
_Supervisor for medical candidate research project_ I have since 2005 supervised eleven medical candidate’s research projects with subject reflecting gastrointestinal and hepatologic diseases and conditions (see curriculum vitae) and are currently, supervising a bachelor project in biomedicine
_Postgraduate teaching_ Since my graduation as a medical doctor I have taught regularly.
• As a member of the Endoscopy Committee for Danish Society of Gastroenterology from 2005 to 2014 I have annually taught in endoscopy for smaller groups of doctors (around 20) with lectures and hands-on training in endoscopy. (Approximately 12 hours a year)
• At lectures in Gastroenterology specialist training (approximately 10 hours yearly)
• In the Rheumatologic specialist training
• I regularly have post-graduate teaching session in training of gastroenterologists.

_Examination_ I have participated in OSCE examinations (20 hours per year) and have prepared multiple-choice questions for module K5 and free text questions and multiple-choice questions for Pharmacy students in module 3B.
**Teaching materials**I have written a chapter entitled Medicine in the treatment of gastrointestinal disorder in textbook of Basal and Clinical Pharmacology. Furthermore, I have written a section in textbook about Immunoinflammatory diseases – background and biological medicine, with focus on biological treatment of gastrointestinal diseases.
**Plans for teaching if appointed to the position**I plan to further develop my teaching skills and I feel comfortable with all forms of teaching methods, including overview lectures, problem based learning and bed-side teaching. I plan to continue with supervision of pre-graduate students doing medical candidate projects – projects where I find that my skills as a researcher with focus on evidence-based medicine are well-used. If possible I would appreciate to continue my teaching corresponding to the level of a B-lecturer at the university.

**Formal education training**.
I have participated in targeted courses, but most of my training as an educator has been on the ground. I have regularly lectured in pregraduate and postgraduate setting – medical students, medical doctors and nurses. I started teaching during my study to become a doctor, teaching nurses in biochemistry. In general, it is my impression that my teaching is considered to be of good quality and I have received very positive feed-back from students.
_Teaching related courses._ I have had formal training in the mediation of Evidence Based Medicine. In 2006, 4th to 9th June I participated in ”How to teach evidence-based clinical medicine” at the McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario (40 hours).
Furthermore, I have participated in Evidence based medicine, 1st to 2nd and 13th to 14th June 2004 at the Nordic Cochrane Center, Copenhagen (32 hours).
