# Discussion 

Hereditary v s. s poradic i nsulinoma subtypes have distinctive molecular landscape s. Our study of 

12 sporadic insulinomas revealed a marked genetic heterogeneity with few recurrent alterations 

among 33 candidate genes. The gene expression data revealed an accumulation of differentially 

expressed genes in pathways related to metabolism of cholesterol and fatty acids , compared to 

control beta cells .

Candidate genes 

We identified 3 3 candidate genes by exome sequencing of 1 2 insulinomas. Of these, three 

insulinomas did not harbor variants in genes associated with cancer or hyperinsulinism. The lack of 

variants may be due to a too thorough filtration pipeline , despite the additional ma nual analysis of 

six genes known to be associated with tumorigenesis in PNETs. Further, other factors may lead to 

tumorigenesis, such as epigenetics. A trend towards aberrant epigenetic regulation in PNETs with 

and without MEN1 predisposition has been prop osed before (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017, Wang, 

Bender et al. 2017, Iyer and Agarwal 2018, Pipinikas, Berner et al. 2019) . Variants in the genes 

associated with epigenetic regulation, including MEN1 , YY1 , ATRX and DAXX are well -documented 

and frequent in PNE Ts (Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Li, Huang et al. 2016, Chan, Laddha et al. 2018, 

Pipinikas, Berner et al. 2019, Hong, Qiao et al. 2020, Rindi, Mete et al. 2022) . As shown in Figure 3,

we only identified one somatic MEN1 variant with a low VAF and no DAXX alterations in our 

tumors . Th is low occurrence of MEN1 and DAXX alterations in sporadic insulinomas compared to 

other PNET subtypes is in accordance with other reports (Wang, Bender et al. 2017, Zheng, Liu et 

al. 2021) .Paper III 

> 24

In cohorts of sporadic insulinomas , the frequency of the recurrent p. (Thr372Arg ) mutation in YY1 

have been estimated to 0 -33 % (Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Lichtenauer, Di Dalmazi et al. 2015, Parekh, 

Modali et al. 2018) . In our study we only found th is variant in 1/1 2 sporadic insulinomas (8 %), 

which is similar to newer studies of cohorts of sporadic insulinomas , where only 8 % , and 13 % ,

harbo red the recurrent mutation, respectively (Wang, Bender et al. 2017, Parekh, Mod ali et al. 

2018) . Mutations in ATRX occurred in 3/1 2 (25 %) . In others reports, 0-17.6 % of PNETs ha d an 

acquired ATRX variant (Jiao, Shi et al. 2011, Wang, Bender et al. 2017) .

Likely germline variants 

We identified a likely germline variant in BRCA2 with a VAF of 0.61 in Insulinoma O, suggesting a 

germline origin . According to The Human Protein Atlas, BRCA2 is weakly expressed in normal 

pancreatic islets and o nly one other BRCA2 variant has been described before in a non -functioning 

PNET (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) . The likely germline variant in BRCA2 may represent a novel 

predisposin g factor for PNETs, if not a somatic event such as copy -neutral loss of heterozygosity .

Other likely germline variants with a VAF ≥40 was identified in NKX6.1 , ATP2B1 , GPR1 and 

SLC37A4 . Of special note, Insulinoma O harbored both the BRCA2, NKX6.1 and ATP2B1 variants 

with a high VAF. NKX6 -1 encodes the critical beta -cell programming factor in progenitor cells and 

induce proliferation of beta -cells through activation of Nr4a1, Nr4a3, and Aurora kinase 1 (gene: 

AURKA ) (Hobson, Draney et al. 2015) . The missense v ariant in NKX6.1 (p.( Tyr190Cys ), VAF 0.58) in 

Insulinoma O was associated with a decre ase of 2.25 -fold of NKX6.1 mRNA compared to the beta -

cell line EndoC -βH1. In PNETs and islets from mice with beta -cell specific Men1 -ablat ion, mRNA 

expression of pivotal transcription factors related to islet function including Nkx6.1 , NeuroD1 , Isl -1,Paper III 

> 25

and Maf A, was significantly decreased (Li, Su et al. 2015) . However, i n rat -derived insulinoma cell 

line INS 1E, ablation of NKX6.1 did not lead to a difference in glucose -stimulated insulin secretion 

(Pavluch, Engstová et al. 2023) . H eterozygous germline NKX6.1 -variants , p.(Ser317Leu) and 

p.(Pro329Leu) , have been identified in two patients with maturity -onset diabetes of the young 

(MODY) (Mohan, Radha et al. 2018) . Together, this indicates that loss -of -function in NKX6.1 may 

affect beta cell survival rather than decreased insulin secretion .

The last high allele frequency variant in Insulinoma O was found in ATP2B1 . ATP2B1 is weakly 

expressed in pancreatic islets according to The Human Protein Atlas, and little is known about this 

calcium transporter gene in beta -cells , called PMC A1. The missense variant in  ATP2B1 

p.(His1214Arg) is placed in the proximity of a phosphorylation site (Ser1216), and during GSIS the 

phosphorylation is upregulated  (26) . The positive charge of the His -residue remains after 

substitution to Arg, and ma y potentially facilitate the phosphorylation of the adjacent residue. 

However,  ATP2B1  silencing  results in higher intracellular Ca2+  concentration , which  trigger s insulin 

exocytosis. 

Taken together, the BRCA2 , Nkx6.1 and ATP2B1 variants found in the same insulinoma were likely 

of germline origin, although with little expression of BRCA2 and ATP2B1 in normal pancreatic 

tissue according to literature . A combin ation of these variants in germline may have had causative 

predisposing effects on the tumorigenesis. In the same insulinoma, three other somatic candidate 

genes were identified , suggesting a further complex causality in the combination of multi genetic 

germline and somatic genetic events. Paper III 

> 26

Down -regulated candidate genes 

Interestingly, PAX6 was both represented in the analyses of somatic variants (n=1) and in the 

analysis of the most DEGs (-261.35 FC) . The PAX6 missense variant (NP_000271.1:p. (Gly51Val) ) has 

previously been reported as pathogenic in association with a de novo germline va riant resulting in 

the development of irido -corneo -trabecular dysgenesis (accession ID: RCV000059340.4) (Prokudin, 

Simons et al . 2014) . In the pancreas, PAX6 codes for a key transcription factor regulating beta -cell 

development, integrity and maturity. Deficiency of PAX6 has been associated with a diabetes 

phenotype in mice, presenting with hyperglycemia and loss of beta -cell function (Swisa, Avrahami 

et al. 2017) . On the contrary, the significantly decreased gene expression of PAX6 in our study was 

associated with a phenotype of hyper insulin emic hypoglycemia. However, dedifferentiation of 

beta -cells may be the key event in insulinoma development, and our finding is consistent with the 

mouse study of Li et al . (Li, Su et al. 2015) , identifying that PNETs developed in Men 1 ablated mice 

have decreased Pax6 mRNA expression compared with control islets. Mutations in PAX6 have also 

previously been identified in one insulinoma  (Wang, Bender et al. 2017)  and non -functioning PNET 

(Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) .

Other highly down -regulated DEGs identified in our exome sequencing wa s ATP2B1 (-20.71 FC) 

described above , and DPP4 (-25.36 FC). DPP4 codes for Dipeptidyl peptidase -4 ( DPP4 ), which 

impairs insulin signaling by antagonizing GLP1 and catabolizing incretin hormones , and inhibitors 

of DPP4 ha ve been used as a mean against type 2 diabetes (Ca mpbell 2007) . Studies have found 

that DPP4 may exert negative effects on beta -cell survival and insulin secretion (Barchetta, Cimini 

et al. 2022) . The downregulation of DPP4 in insulinoma s may lead to increased in cretin response Paper III 

> 27

and hence hypersecretion of insulin. This further demonstrates the complexity of tumorigenesis 

and pathogenesis of the hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia in sporadic insulinoma .

Up -regulated candidate genes 

Two highly up -regulated genes were identified among our exome sequencing candidate genes, i.e. 

CCND2 (20.28 FC), and FGFR1 (10.17 FC) . CCND2 was one of the only two genes represented with 

mutations in more than one insulinoma in our multicenter cohort. The CCND2 mutatio ns were 

nonsense , and splice site , respectively. CCND2 codes for Cyclin D2 , which is partly responsible for 

the G1 -S transition dur ing cell cycle in complex with C yclin 4 and 6 (Fassl, Geng et al. 2022) .

Consistently with the high expression in insulinoma, Cyclin D2 has been shown to have a proto -

oncogenic potential (Rojas, Cadenas et al. 2007) , and additionally truncated C yclin D2 may have an 

oncogenic role in tumorigenesis in cytoplasm (Denicourt, Legault et al. 2008) .

FGFR1 encodes the fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) , responsible for e.g. survival and 

proliferation. Insulinoma M contained the variant p. (Glu692Lys ); with a VAF of 0.11 , in the tyrosine 

kinase domain . Identical variants have been detected earlier in analogous residues in the growth 

factor receptors FGFR4 (residue p. (Glu681Lys )) (Marks, McLellan et al. 2007) and ERBB2 (residue 

p. (Glu914Lys )) (Stephens, Hunter et al. 2004) in lung adenocarcinoma and glioblastoma, 

respectively. Furthermore, t he variant has been identified in a breast cancer biopsy (Grissom 

2021) . Point mutations in FGFR 1 leading to overexpression has been demonstrated before 

(Ellinghaus, Neureiter et al. 2022) , in line with the overall upregulation of FGFR1 in our microarray 

analysi s. A direct association between FGFR1 activity and the pancreatic transcription factor PDX1 

has been proposed, and the latter plays a crucial role in the establishment, fun ctionality and Paper III 

> 28

maturity of beta -cells. The activation of FGFR1 induces the gene expr ession of PDX1 , which plays a 

crucial role in the establishment, fun ctionality and maturity of beta -cells , including transcriptional 

activat ion of insulin and somatostatin (Yamashita -Sugahara, Matsumoto et al. 2016) . Consistently, 

the gene expression of SST , which encodes somatostatin, was highly increased in Insulinoma M ,

having the FGFR1 -variant .

Candidate genes not differentially expressed 

The f ive genes PWP1, YY1 , GPR1 , BAIAP3 , and SLC30A5 with variants detected by exome 

sequencing were not differentially expressed compared to control . Each of the se genes were 

altered in one insulinoma only and consisted of four missense mutations and one splice site 

mutation. The lack of differential expression may have three explanations: the combined analysis 

of all 12 insulinomas , missense varia nts often do not lead to change in gene expression , and 

variations in cellular subclones as suggested by the relatively low VAF of the variant s. 

Most differentially expressed genes 

We identified the 20 most up - and downregulated genes, when comparing mRNA expression 

between insulinomas and EndoC -βH1. The gene with the highest FC was SRGN (1 ,030 FC) , which 

encodes serglycin . Serglycin play s a role in inflammation and autocrine signaling and is highly 

expressed in various cancers (Korpetinou, Papachristou et al. 2015, Roy, Attarha et al. 2017, Wang, 

Xiong et al. 2020, Tanaka, Dayde et al. 2022) . Furthermore, serglycin is secreted by various cells, 

including tumor cells (Korpetinou, Papachristou et al. 2015, Chu, Huang et al. 2016) and the Paper III 

> 29

protein may be associated with the aggressiveness and survival rate for certain types of cancer 

(Wan g, Xiong et al. 2020) .

We clust ered the 40 most DEGs into two enriched clusters of annotation: Metabolism of 

cholesterol and metabolism of lipids. However, o nly 9 of the 40 genes (22.5%) were associated 

with the two clusters of annotation , and thereby no significant pathway association was achieved 

for 77.5 % of the DEGs . The two assigned clusters were containing overlapping genes, which may 

be related to the high similarity between the functional annotations. Cholesterol is a lipid which 

can be synthesi zed by all cells (Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) , and m etabolism of cholesterol may 

directly affect insulin secretion (Hao, Head et al. 2007, Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) . Hao et al . (Hao, 

Head et al. 2007) showed that depletion of cholesterol in islets increase s the insulin secretion 

independent on glucose and fatty acid concentratio ns . Further, dysregulation of the metabolism of 

cholesterol and fatty acids has been identified in patients with type 2 diabetes, resulting in loss of 

pancreatic islet cells (Cnop 2008, Oh, Bae et al. 2018, Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) . Especially 

chronic elevation of free fatty acids in the plasma may lead to lipotoxicity and negatively affect the 

beta -cell mass. Conversely, acute and transient elevation of free fatty acid metabolism in beta -

cells has the opposite effect and leads to inc reased insulin secretion and mass (Oh, Bae et al. 

2018) . These studies indicate that metabolism of cholesterol and other lipids may have impact on 

beta -cell function. Paper III 

> 30

Expression in islet tissues 

Using the Human Protein Atlas , we identified 15 of the DEGs in association with normal expression 

in pancreatic islet cells, further highlighting the importance of their gene -products in islets. Four of 

the islet -expressed genes ATG16L1 , MICAL1 , TTC39C , and ZNF5 12, were up -regulated .

ATG16L1 is part of a n E3 -like complex, responsible for autophagy and may also be interacting with 

C3 in regulation of cell death (King, Kulak et al. 2019) . In line with this, MICAL1 codes for a 

regulator of apoptosis, cancer cell growth and producer of reactive oxidative species (Deng, Wang 

et al. 2016) . A pathogenic variant in MICAL1 has previously been ident ified in insulinoma (Wang, 

Bender et al. 2017) . The third and fourth up -regulated gene s, TTC39C and ZNF512 , have unknown 

function s and may be a new candidate for additional functional investigation. 

Methodological considerations 

Formalin fixation of patient samples are suboptimal in molecular studies of variations in nucleic 

acids , particularly when using large -scale sequencing , such as whole -exome sequencing in the 

present study . FFPE samples are difficult to process due to the high degradation of nucleic acids. 

The rarity of insulinomas, however, limits or excludes the access to fr esh frozen insulinoma tissue 

in most centers. Further, our study has a methodological limitation in the compar ison of FFPE 

mRNA with the mRNA obtained from a cell line . Of note, a calculated high FC could not only be 

influenced by a high tumor expression, but also due to the use of mRNA -data from the control cell 

line, which lacks extracellular components, including different cell types and paracrine cell 

signaling. Paper III 

> 31

While germline variants were assessed using blood samples from five of the patients, likely 

germline variants were determined using a VAF score ≥0.40 from tumo r tissues. Guidelines and 

recommendations from The American Society of Clinical Oncology, American College of Medical 

Genetics and Genomics, and College of American Path ologists notes that VAF in tumo r tissue is 

expected to be present at approximately 0.5 and 1.0 , for heterozygous and homozygous germline 

alleles, respectively (Li, Datto et al. 2017, Montgomery, Selitsky et al. 2018) , and that the 

alt eration should be present in all of the sequenced cells. However, the interpretation of VAF 

depends on more factors including germline mosaicism, LOH, CNVs in tumor cells, 

insertions/deletions, structural rearrangements , and sequencing artifacts , such as shallow 

sequencing depths (Kraft and Godley 2020) . In a previous report , 96% of variants with a VAF 

between 0.40 and 0.60 could be confirmed as germline variants (Montgomery, Selitsky et al. 

2018) .

# Conclusion 

The sporadic insulinomas each had a distinct mutational profile, demonstrating a heterogeneity in 

the tumorigenesis of this subtype of PNETs. W e identified 33 candidate genes related to insulin 

hypersecretion and tumorigenesis with p athways of epigenetics, insulin biosynthesis an d

exocytosis, DNA repair, insulin signaling, beta -cell survival and metabolism . The candidate gene 

alteration occurred in only one tumor each , except for ATRX (n=3), and CCND2 (n=2). Three 

candidate genes were highly down regulated, PAX6, ATP2B 1, and DPP4 , and two were highly 

upregulated, CCND2 and FGFR1 , highlighting the importance of these genes. Clusters of 

metabolism of cholesterol and lipids were enriched , w hich may be implicated in the tumorigenesis Paper III 

32 

of insulinomas. Our findings may give novel insights in to beta -cell pathophysiology and insulin 

secretion, which may provide the framework for future studies on possible drug targets in 

diabetes and hyperinsulinism. Further experiments are esse ntial for the validation of the 

candidate genes.

# Abstract in English
Background - Pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) are rare , solitary tumours
which may occur in is olation or in association with here ditary syndromes, such as Multiple
Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1). MEN1 is caused by inactivation of the MEN1 gene,
encoding the tumo ur suppressor menin . A ccording to Knudson’s two hit hypothesis,
inactivation of MEN1 occurs in two steps; a first ‘hit’, often an inactivating germline mutation
in one allele, and a second somatic hit commonly achieved by loss of heterozygosity of the
second allele. In addition to MEN1 gene , the chromatin remodelling encoding genes DAXX and
ATRX are frequently altered in PN ENs . The maj ority of PNENs are non -functioning , however
PNENs may be functi oning , producing hormonal hypersecretion synd rome. The main type of
functioning PNENs are insulinoma s, which synthesize excessive amounts of insulin and may
cause events of hyperins ulinemic hypoglycemia. In sporadic insulinomas a recurrent variant
in the YY1 gene is often identified .
Aims - The aims of the thesis were to 1) review the previously reported exome and genome
data of G1 and G2 pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms to dete rmine the most frequently
altered genes, 2) explore the inactivation events of MEN1 gene in PNENs from patients with
MEN1 germline variants and 3) investigate the genetic and transcriptomic landscape of
collected PNENs.
Materials and methods - The first st udy (Paper I) consisted of a review of published articles
using whole exome, whole genome , or targeted gene panel (>400 genes) sequencing of G1/G2
PNENs . Somatic variant data were collated to summarize abundant aberrant genes, co -
occurring v ariants, and v ariant hotspots in PNEN s divided into  hereditary tumo urs with pre -
disposing germline variants and sporadic tumours.  Further, non -functioning and functioning
PNEN s were distinguished into two groups for pathway evaluation.  In  Paper II,  MEN1  variants

and pot ential driver genes  were detected using exome and targeted sequencing in PNENs
from patients with MEN1  syndrome  from our own cohort . Menin expression was determined
by immunohistochemistry (IHC). In paper III, sporadic insulinomas from our cohort  were
anal ysed using exome sequencing, gene expression microarray and IHC.  Gene expression in
insulinomas were compared to the human beta -cell line EndoC -βH1 and the 40 most
differentially expressed genes by fold change (FC) were analysed for pathway enrichment. Page 7 of 9 2
Results - In P aper I, 14 datasets from published studies on 225 P NEN s were included in the
analysis , consisting of s poradic PN EN s accounted  72.0% ( 162/225), hereditary PNEN s 13.3%
(30/225),  and PNE Ns with  unknown germline status 14.7% (33/225).  The most frequent
somat ically altered genes in all PNEN s were  MEN1  (n=95; 42%),  DAXX  (n= 37; 16%) and  ATRX
(n=27; 12%), including mutations and CNVs.  New muta tional hotspots  were identified in the
histone -binding domain and ATPase domain of DAXX and ATRX, respectively. Wh ile
functioning P NEN s shared few variated genes, such as  YY1 , non -functioning PNEN s had
recurrent  genetic alterations in  genes associated with  Phosphoinositide 3 -kinase, Wnt,
NOTCH, and Receptor Tyrosine Kinase -Ras signaling onco -pathways.
We collected 19 well -differentiated G1/G2 PNENs, where seven PNENs (37 %) were obtained
from patients with MEN1 syndrome and 12 (63 %) were sporadic PNENs ( median age 14 (8 -

# Abstract in English
22) vs 27.5 (9 -75) , p -value=0.03). In Paper II, all MEN1 -associated PNENs had absent nuclear
menin expression, and consistently, somatic CNV loss of MEN1 was determined for 4/5
sequenced PNENs from MEN1 patients. Potential drivers in DNA re pair, chromatin
remodelling and mTOR pathways were identified.
Lastly, in Paper III, we identified 33 candidate genes in 12 sporadic insulinomas. Only ATRX
(n=3) and CCND2 (n=2) were altered in more than one insulinoma. Through gene expression
analysis of the 33 genes , we found two highly upregulated genes  i.e.  CCND2  (20.28 FC), and
FGFR1  (10.17 FC),  and three  highly down regulated genes  i.e.  PAX6  (-261.35 FC),  DPP4  (-25.36
FC), and  ATP2B1  (-20.71 FC). Nine of the 40 most differentially expressed genes (22 .5%) were
associated with metabolism of cholesterol and lipids.
Conclusion - PNENs represent a genetically heterogeneous group of tumo urs with few
recurrent DNA alterations. Somatic variations in the MEN1 gene occur frequently in PNENs
from patients with and without MEN1 syndrome. Total MEN1 inactivation was detected in 4/5
PNENs from MEN1 patients, consistent with Knudson’s two hit hypothesis. Further molecular
studies are required to better understand the impact of the candidate genes discovered in our
molecular analyses. The candidate genes may be of interest in future drug discoveries. Page 8 of 9 2

# 1. Introduction
## 1.1. Tumours of the neuro endocrine pancreas
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (PNETs) are among the most comm on neuroendocrine
tumours (NETs) with an incidence rate of 0.48 per 100,000 individuals (1, 2) . PNETs account
for less than 3 % of all pancreatic malignancies  (3) , and are  de fined as a hyperplastic enti ties  of
more than  5 mm in diameter . For comparison,  islets of Langerhans range in size from  50 -400
μm in diameter  (4) .
1.1.1. Development and differentiation of pancreatic neuroendocrine cells
NETs derive from neuro endocrine cells , which are functionally and morphologic ally defined
by the production of hormones and neuropeptides (5) . T he neuroendocrine cells contain
secretary granules for hormone releasing , and play an important role in orchestrating the
regulation of hormone -dependent physiological processes, such as metabolism and
cardiovascular functions (5) .
During embryonic development, the pancreas is formed through the differentiation of
multipotent endodermal cells. T he neur oendocrine cells of the pancreas are believed to arise
from a common progenitor cell, which subsequently at E18.5 form the islets of Langerhans
(6) , comprising more than a million islets distributed throughout the pancreas . The distinct
cell -type composition of islets varies among individuals (7) , and include s cells producing
glucagon ( alpha ), insulin ( beta ), somatostatin ( delta ), pancreatic polypeptide (gamma), and
ghrelin (e psilon) (7, 8) .
1.1.2. Dedifferentiation to pancreatic neuroendocrine ne oplasms
Uncontrollable proliferation of pancreatic neuroendocrine cells may result in hyperplasia, and
additional factors, such as genetics and micro -environmental changes may facilitate the
dedifferentiation of the cells (9) . Dedifferentiation refers to the loss of characteristics that
identifies a differentiated cell at the terminal, mature stage (10) . As an example, insulinomas

to intermediate -grade, and G3 to high -grade categories. Neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC) of
the gastrointestinal and pancreatobiliary tract refe rs to uniformly, poorl y d ifferentiated high -

Poorly differentiated NECs are in co mparison to well -differentiated NETs more aggressive in

mutations in RB1 , TP53 , KRAS , CDKN2A , CCNE1 , and MYC (20) . Further, compared to

distinction of endocrine and exocrine tumours is fairly important (21) . In terms of
classification, the functionality of the PNET is irrelevant (22) .
1.1.4. Non -functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
PNETs can be stratified into functioning or non -functioning, depending on a clinical ly
measurable disorder before tumour resection. N on -functioning PNETs are the most common,
accounting for 85% (3) , and do not cause syndromes of hormone excess. However, they may
metastasize causing morbidity and mortality. The lack of hormo nal syndrome makes non -
functioning PNETs difficult to detect, and such PNETs may be found unintentionally during
examinations of unrelated diagnoses (22, 23) . Otherwise, non -functioning PNETs often are
identified in advanced stages with symptoms related to tumour size or liver metastases,

PNETs are worse compared to functioning PNETs (8, 25) . Clinically, non -functioning PNE Ts
may change over time and cause a hormone hypersecretion syndrome (1) . Different types of
non -functioning PNETs occur a nd may be stratified into alpha -cell like and beta -cell like
depending on the gene expression of the transcription factors ARX and PDX1 , respectively
(26) . The collation has been beneficial in terms of clinical outcomes.
1.1.5. Functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
Functioning PNETs include insulinoma, glu cagonoma, gastrinoma, vasoactive intestinal
peptide tumour (VIPoma), and others that may produce hormonal hypersecretion syndrome.
Interestingly, the type of hormone is not limited to normal islet -cell hormones, and may
include hormones from the parathyroi d (parathyroid hormone and parathyroid hormone
related peptide), pituitary (adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and growth hormone),
hypothalamus (corticotropin -releasing hormone and growth hormone -releasing hormone)
and the gastrointestinal tract (gastrin and VIP) (1) .Page 19 of 9 2
1.1.5.1. Insulinoma
Although rare, the most common type of functioning PNET is insulinoma (27, 28) , occurring in
1-4 per million individuals every year (29) . Insulinom as are NET s of pancreatic origin, which
synthesize excessive amounts of insulin due to monoclonal proliferation of insulin -positive
beta cells. Often, insulinomas affect s the glucose homeostasis resulting in hyperinsulinaemic
hypo glycaemia (HH) (30, 31) . Normally, p lasma glucose concentrations are maintained within
a narrow physiological range to maintain glucose homeostasis. The tight regulation is
mediated by the intricate interplay of neu ral, hormonal and cellular factors (32) . One of the

maintain plasma glucose levels between 70 and 110 mg/dL (3.9 –6.1 mmol/L). The GSIS
pathway is described in details in the Appendix , section 10.2 .
1.1.5.1. Diagnosis of insulino ma
The definition of an insulinoma includes a clinical ly measurable disorder, i.e. overproduction
of insulin that leads to hypoglycaemia. HH refers to a condition and effect of low blood glucose
levels caused by elevated insulin action s (33) . Many studies have tried to identify a threshold
for the plasma glu cose concentration for diagnostic purposes  (32, 34) , however a single
threshold may  be challenging to identify as symptoms may appear at different concentrations
(35) . The hypogly cemic symptoms are typically divided into two classes: Neurogenic and
neuroglycopenic, depending on the physiological mechanisms  (32) .
PNE Ts that produce insulin but are not associated with a clinical syndrome (such as
hypoglycaemia) do not fulfil the criteria for insulinoma s and are designated as insulin -
producing NENs. Insulinomas occur very rarely in children and only very few paediatric cases
of malignant insulinomas are known (36) , correspondingly insulinomas have a low rate of
malignancy and 90 % of insulinomas have been reported to be benign (37) , meaning that the
risk of metastatic spread is low. Page 20 of 9 2

## neuroendocrine tumo urs
PNETs with no association to tumour syndromes may be called sporadic . Studies have already
found genes that are frequently altered in sporadic PNETs, including MEN1 , DAXX , ATRX , YY1
and genes related to the mTOR pathway (38, 39) . Changes in MEN1 , DAXX and /or ATRX has
been associated with an alpha -cell like signature (8) . Death domain -associated protein
(DAXX ), the protein encoded by DAXX -gene is a histone H3.3 chaperone (38, 40) , and the
incorporation of H3.3 at the telomeres is facilitated by an interaction between DAXX and
alpha -thalassemia/mental retardation, X -linked ( ATRX ) protein . Consequently, the act leads
to alternative lengths of telomeres, providing a prolonged cell survival, which has been
rep orted in different cancer types (41, 42) . Loss of DAXX and ATRX has been associated with
increased metastasis -occurrence and reduced survival (41 -43) .
Specifically in spo radic insulinomas, a recurrent variant (p.Thr372Arg) in YY1 has been
identified (39, 44 -47) . The m issense m utation has been identified in 0-30 % of insulinomas
(39, 45, 48) , and is mostly apparent in females in the Asian population (48) . In functional
assays, the variant was considered to cause gain of function of YY1 in one study (39) , however
the upregulation of YY1 and its target genes could not be det ermined in other studies using
insulinoma cell lines (45) . The oncogenic potential has also been discussed, as two studies
could not confirm a proliferativ e effect of the YY1 -missense substitution (45, 49) . The somatic
variation has been associated with increased insulin secretion in absence of mitogenic
stimulation in beta cells (50) . The genes CACNA2D2 and ADCY1 were upregulated in

insulinomas with YY1 -mutant. On protein level, o verexpression of the pore -forming Ca 2+ -
channel subunit CACNA2D2 results in constitutive Ca 2+ channel activity. A dditionally ,
increased levels of intra cellular Ca 2+ are expected to activate the adeny lyl cyclase ADCY1,
catalysing the reaction of ATP to cyclic AMP (50) (Figure 1 ). Of note, ADCY1 is normally not
expressed in the endocrine pancreas, but in central ner vous system , among other (51) .
Additional functions of YY1 in transcription ha ve been propo sed, and the recurrent mutation
is located in the DNA -binding domain, potentially altering the transcription factor activity
(45) .Page 21 of 9 2

Further, sporadic PNETs harbour alterations in genes associated with the  mammalian target
of rapamycin (mTOR)  pathway.  mTOR is a serine/threonine protein kinase, whi ch belongs to
the phosphatidylinositol 3 -kinase (PI3K) -related kinase family  (52) , and  interacts with
different proteins  to create  two comple xes called mTORC1 and mTORC2 , respectively ( Figure
2). PI3K, Akt and mTOR have been shown to be frequently hyperactivated in the majority of
cancers  (52) . The pathway is a critical mediator of the survival and proliferative effects of
many oncogenes, including the EGF receptor and PI3K it -self  (53) . Likewise, variants in the
inhibitor of Akt -activation, phosphatase and tensin homolog ( PTEN ) is frequently  reported  in

## 1.3. Syndrom es associated with PNET develo pment
Most PNE Ts occur as a sporadic disease, however five to ten percent occur in association with
hereditary syndromes, such as Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1) , and more rarely
von Hippel -Lindau disease (VHL), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), a nd tuberous sclerosis
(TSC) (1) .
Other p redisposing germline variations has also been suggested regarding development of
PNET s, and includes variants in the genes BRCA2 , MUTYH , CHEK2 (43) , PTEN (60) and
CDKN1B (61) .Page 23 of 9 2
1.3.1. MEN1 tumourigenesis
The MEN1 syndrome is inherited through an autosomal dominant trait, characterised by the
occurrence of neoplasms in several endocrine organs, including the pituitary, parathyroid
glands, and the pancreatic neuro endocrine islets. Other non -endocrine organs may also be
implicated (62) . Animal studies have demonstrated that mutations in Men1 can be related to
non -neuroendocrine proliferation, such as lung cancer (63, 64) , melanomas (65) and liver
cancer (66, 67) .
MEN1 syndrome is caused by alterations in the tumour suppressor gene MEN1. While 90 % of
MEN1 patients have a familial, inherited form of the disease, approximately 10 % of patients
have a de novo MEN1 variant (68) . In addition, a mosaic form of the disease has also been
described (69) . The diagnosis of MEN1 is established if the patien t has a MEN1 germline
variant, a fa mily history of MEN1 or simultaneous presence of tumo urs from at least two of
the three most common MEN1 affiliated organs, i.e . the pituitary, parathyroid and endocrine
pancreas. Nowadays, the confirmation of the diagnos is most often includes a genetic test for
MEN1 alterations. In up to 25 % of patients with MEN1 manifestations, no MEN1 variants can

develops due to variants in the cyclin -dependent kinase inhibitor ( CDKN1B ) gene (61, 71 -73) .
Patients with MEN4, however, do very rarely develop pancreatic neuroendocrine tumo urs
(70) .
1.3.1.1. Patient group description
The penetrance of MEN1 is high, exceeding 90 % in affected families carrying a MEN1 variant
(74) . The syndrome affects all age groups, and patients from five to 81 years have been
repor ted (75) . However, patients with the same germline mutation may present with variable
clinical manifestations (76) .
Thorough follow -up tumo ur screenings of confirmed MEN1 syndrome patients improve the
overall survival. Convers ely, the delay of a diagnosis of index patients in MEN1 families tend
to increase the cases of metastatic neuroendocrine tumo ur manifestations in the family (70) .Page 24 of 9 2
1.3.1.2. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumo urs in MEN1
PNETs arise in 30 -80 % of patients with MEN1 (3) , and they generally develop at an earlier
age in patients with MEN1 (10 -50 years) compared to sporadic forms (50 -80 years) (3, 28) .
Compared to the sporadic counterparts, MEN1 -associated PNETs tend to be more aggressive
with reported metastases in up to 33 % of cases (3) .
1.3.1.3. MEN1 gene
The 10 exon -long MEN1 gene was first mapped in 198 8 (77) and cloned in 19 97 (78) . It is
located on chromosome 11q13 and the gene product menin consists of 610 amino acid
residues . The gene encodes the putative tumo ur suppres sor menin , and through the “ two -hit

MEN1 gene is achieved (79, 80) .
1.3.1.4. Knudson’s two -hit hypothesis
The t wo -hit hypothes is states that an accumulation of two inactivated alleles are required for
the full inactivation of tumour suppressor genes. While the first ‘hit’ is often an inherited
germline heterozygous deleterious variant, the second ‘hit ’ is a somatic variation, suc h as a
mutation or loss of heterozygosity (LOH). Potential mechanisms resulting in a soma tic second
hit are listed below and summed up in Figure 3 .
1) Loss of heterozygosity
Inactivation of the healthy second allele can be achieved by several mechanisms ,
inc luding LOH , which accounts for 90% of MEN1 second hits (76, 81) . The mechanisms
of LOH may be somatic deletion of the healthy allele, duplication of the first germline
hit (copy -neutral LOH (cnLOH) ).
In one patient, a de novo germline inactivation of MEN1 was caused by Alu/Alu -
mediated rearrangements, which are associated with Alu repetitive elements and
resulted in MEN1 deletion on one allele (82) . The possibility that such rearrangements
could occur somatically does exist, even though it has not been described yet.
It is expected that LOH cause a loss or decrease of MEN1 transcription and translation,
however in one study of sporadic parathyroid tumours with LOH of 11q13 , a loss of Page 25 of 9 2
MEN1 mRNA could not be detected (83) , perhaps due to strong compensatory activity
upon menin deficiency (84) .
2) Soma tic mutations in MEN1 locus
More than 1300 variants in the MEN1 gene locus have been reported both from
patients with and without MEN1 syndrome (76) . Both germline and somatic variants
are distributed throughout the entire coding region of the MEN1 gene with no

partic ular mutational hotspots (85) . Few variants wi thin the untranslated regions have
also been found in addition to MEN1 fusions due to larger deletions (82) . Loss of
function mutations, including nonsense, framesh ift and splice site mutations are
predicted to lead to a truncation of menin or complete loss due to nonsense mediated
decay (NMD) (86, 87) . Several studies have tried to find genotype/ phenotype
correlations (76, 85, 87 -90) , with only a few connections between genotype and
tumour type or aggressiveness.
3) Epigenetic regulation , including DNA methylation and microRNA inactivation
More directly, the definition of epigenetics is the study of heritable alterations in gene
expression that do not involve changes to the underlying DNA sequence (91) .
At the time of the development of the two -hit hypothesis, Knudson did not describe the
epigenetic inactivation of MEN1 , however research in the field has later redefined the
concept of inactiva tion (92 -94) . For instance, DNA methylation of CpG islands may
result in lack of transcription (95) of MEN1 .
Another possibility is epigenetic silencing by microRNAs and studies have suggested
that miR -24 -1 can bind to the conserved 3 ’ UTR region of MEN1 mRNA and negatively
regulate the po st -transcriptional expression . This mechanism mimics the second hit of
the two -hit hypothesis and could be a mechanism of controlling the haploin sufficiency
that occurs when a single allele is insuffi cient to fulfil the complete functionality
produced from two wild -type alleles (96 -98) . This model based on hapl oinsufficiency Page 26 of 9 2
is supported by mous e studies (97, 99) . Further , the microRNA miR -17, which is
induced by glucose and hyperglycemia, also can bind to the 3’UTR of MEN1 mRNA,
thereby promoting Min 6 beta -cell proliferation (100) . Histone modifications may also

Studies h ave shown that the expression of the MEN1 gene is regulated by menin in a
feedback loop (84) . In line with this , it has been suggested that menin directly
regulates the gene expression of the before mentioned m iR -24 -1 (98) .

1.3.1.5. The function of menin
Menin is ubiquitously expressed and appears to have several biological functions in the cell.
The expression vari es betwe en tissues and may depend on different factors, including
metabolism (101) . In the majority of PNETs, menin is expressed in the nucleus (102) . The
protein is a regulator of histone modifications (8, 67, 103 -105) , transc ription (106) ,
proliferation (107, 108) , DNA repair (65, 109, 110) , and apoptosis (111) among others. Menin
is highly conserved among species (63) , but has no similarity among other proteins. Several
MEN1 and MEN1 -li ke animal models have been described, including in Drosophila

(MENX), causing a multitumour syndrome sharing features of the human MEN1 and MEN2

Complete ablation of Men1 in a mouse model is lethal at the embryonic state (E11.5 -E13.5)
and leads to deficiencies in multiple organs, including lack of closure of the neural tube and
heart hypotrophy (112) . However, heterozygous MEN1 (+/ -) mice had a normal de velopment
until the age of 8 months, where mice developed hyperplastic lesions in the pancreas (112) .
1.3.1.5.2. Menin as an epigenetic regulator of histone modifications
Menin interacts with the identical N -terminal portion of mixed lineage leukemia ( MLL )
proteins via a deep central pocket in a h ighly specific manner (113) . The C -terminal region of
MLL1 and MLL2 harbo urs a SET -domain possessing histone 3 lysine 4 (H3K4)
methyltransferase activity (113) . The menin -his tone methyl transferase -complex (menin -
HMT -complex) is comprised of the p roteins menin, MLL1/MLL2, RBBP5 and the cofactors
WDR5 and ASH2L (67) . Methylation of H3K4 has emerged as a key epigenetic marker for
activati on of gene transcription. Mono - and tri -methylation of H3K4 triggers the chromatin to
become more lightly packed achieving an open structure, which results in a higher
accessibility of transcription -regulating proteins, including RNA polymerase -complexes,
transcription factors and co -factors (114) . The tri methylation of H3K4 (H3K4me3) by the
menin -HMT -complex is targeted to specific gene promoter regions (115) and gene loci, e.g.

their transcription. When menin is over -expressed, H3K4me3 modification is enhanced, and
vice versa when menin is knocked down (106) .
An inhibitor of the MLL/menin interaction is called MI -2 and specifically targets the
H3K4me3 . The disruption of the complex retracts H3K4me3 enrichment (116) . In leukemia,
MLL -fusion proteins are well -known drivers , leading to proliferation and blockage of myeloid
differentiation. The MLL -fusion is not dependent on menin, but the methyltransferase SETD2
to ensure genome stability during MLL -leukemogenesis (117) . Accordingly, the histone
modifications catalysed by menin -HMT -complex appears to be different between cell types.
In lung cancer induced in mice , menin and Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2 ) bind to
the PTN promotor and the presence of menin affect the occurrence of the repressive
chromatin mark H3K27m e3, thus suppressing the transcription of the proliferation -inducing
PTN -gene (64, 118) . The binding of menin confirms the tumour suppressing function of the
protein, although a direct interaction between the H 3K27me3 catalysing PRC2 -complex, EZH2
and menin has not been demonstrated (118) .
1.3.1.5.3. Cytoplasmic interaction partners
In endocrine and non -endocrine tissues, menin directly interacts with 1) Akt in the PI3K
pathway (119) and 2) beta -catenin in the W nt pathway (120) as a negative regulator . Th e
binding of menin interferes with the cell ul ar location of each of the proteins. Akt is an
essential player in the PI3K /mTOR pathway , and acts as a regulator of vital cellular functions,

such as proliferation and apoptosis (52) . However, menin can bind directly to Akt and inhibit
the transfer and activation and thereby prevent the downstream cascade of the pathway
(119) . Of note, the PI3K pathway may not be implicated in insulinoma tumorigenesis (121) ,
even though insulin can stimulate the pathway in a n autocrine manner (122) .
In addition to Akt, menin can bind to beta -catenin and repress the translocation of the protein
into the nucleus , and activate degradation of beta -catenin (123) . These functions further
indicate that menin works as a tumour suppressor. Page 29 of 9 2
1.3.1.5.1. Interaction with transcription factor
One of menin ’s many interaction partners is the transcription factor JunD. When menin binds
to JunD, the ability of transcript ional activation declines, opposite of the H3K4me3 mark. This
results in a repression of transcription, which normally is catalysed by JunD (124) .
1.3.1.5.2. Aberrant menin function
Missense mutations in regions of MEN1 that disrupt the interaction between menin and its
interaction partners, such as MLL1/MLL2 or JunD, have been reported in MEN1 patients. The
lack of interaction correlates with loss of menin’s tumour suppressor function (124) ,
highlighting the importance of m enin as an epigenetic regulator. Page 30 of 9 2

# 2. Aim s of the thesis
The aims of the thesis were to
1) review the previously reported exome and genome data of G1 and G2 PNENs to
determine the most frequently altere d genes,
2) explore the inactivation events of MEN1 gene in PNENs from patients with MEN1
germline variants and
3) investigate the genetic and transcriptomic landscape of collected PNENs .Page 31 of 9 2

# 3. Experimental setup
The following section is provide d to clarify the chosen methods used in Paper I -III. The
section contains text elements that have been published as part of my master ’s thesis (125) .
Figure 4 depicts the methods in the three papers. In Paper I, we reviewed somatic variants
and copy number variations (CNVs) in G1/G2 PNETs from published papers. I n Paper II, we
aimed to identify the MEN1 second hit in MEN1 patients, and further genetic mechanisms to
understand the MEN1 tumorigenesis. Lastly , in Paper III we wanted to identify somatic
variant in sporadic insulinoma samples, which could be causative for the hyperinsulineamic
hypoglycaemia and tumour development.
Figure 4. Overview of the methods and experimental setup conducted for each of the three
papers. PNETs: pancreatic neuroendocrine tumo urs. CNV: copy number variation. G:
histological grade Page 32 of 9 2

# 3. Experimental setup
## 3.1. Somatic variations in h uman pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
In all three papers, the somatic alterations in PNETs were the main focus. Somatic variants
refers to the Greek word ‘ soma ’, which means parts of an organism other than the
reproductive cells (126) . Due to a tissue -specific variation in the accumulation of mutations ,
we assume that variants occurring in PNET cells, but not in the patient’s plasma cells, are
somatic. In all three papers, somatic variants in PNETs are analys ed using public next
generation sequencing (NGS) data (Paper I) or data from exome sequencing of our own cohort
(Paper II and III) .

# 3. Experimental setup
## 3.2. Paper I
In Paper I we aimed to make a review and a meta -analysis of somatic variants identified in
PNETs. We wanted to compare genetically predisposed PNETs with sporadic PNETs , and
further functioning and non -function ing PNETs. A pathway analysis of functioning and non -
functioning PNETs was performed.
3.2.1. Search string
We used the different types of functioning PNETs obtained from WHO 2017 (127) in our
search string, including Insulinoma , Glucagonoma, Somatostatinoma, Gastrinoma, VIPoma,
Serotonin -producing tumo urs, and ACTH -producing tumo urs. Further , synonymous words for
PNETs were used, including Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumo ur, Pancreatic neuroendocrine
neoplasm, Gastroenteropancreat ic, GEP -NET, GEPNET, PNET, P -NET, PanNET, Pan -NET, and
PNEN. Additionally , we searched for “sequencing” or “NGS” to narrow the search, thereby
excluding datasets lacking the words “sequencing” or “NGS” in the abstracts.
3.2.2. Inclusion criteria
Studies identify ing somatic variants in human PNETs using whole exome sequencing ( WES ),
whole genome sequencing ( WGS ) and/or sequencing of more than 400 genes were included
in the review. We selected a cut -off of 400 genes based on a Japanese study (128) using data
from The Cancer Genome Atlas, indicating that cancer -panel sizes at or above 400 genes were
comparable to WES in identifying somatic mutations. Studies without a CNV -analysis was not
excluded. We chose not to include well -differentiated G3 PNETs, as G3 NETs and NEC not Page 33 of 9 2
were separated in the WHO guidelines until 2017 (43) . Thus, we only included well -
differentiated G1 and G2 PNETs in the analyses.
3.2.3. Meta -analysis
A Mutation Annotation Format (MAF) -like file was cr eated and consisted of genetic data and

# 3. Experimental setup
## 3.3. Paper II and III
Experimental approaches to detect somatic varia tions in PNETs using exome sequencing,
gene expression microarray and immunohistochemistry. Figure 5 depicts the central dogma
and the methods of choice uncovers the variations on DNA, RNA and protein levels. In Paper
II, MEN1 gene is in focus and the iden tifica tion of a second hit. In Paper III we aimed to
identify candidate genes in relation to tumorigenesis and hormonal secretion.
Figure 5. The central dogma. DNA is transcribed to RNA, and RNA is translated to protein.
Regulation of the process may o ccur from epigenetics, such as histone or DNA methylation or
non -coding RNAs.
3.3.1. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumo ur samples
All samples used in Paper II and Paper III were formalin -fixed and paraffin -embedded (FFPE)
archival samples. Page 34 of 9 2
3.3.2. Somatic gene variations in cohort
NGS -studies have revealed a genetic inter - and intratumoral diversity (129) . We performed
exome sequencing to detect somatic mutations in our c ohort of PNETs . By the use of enrichment
approaches (Exome 2.0 from Twist) , only the exome and clinically relevant non -coding regions
were targeted for sequencing. The Exome 2.0 probes are designed to provide deep coverage of
genes associated with clinical phenotypes to increase the confidence level of detection of true
variants (130) . The libraries were sequenced on a Novas eq 6000 (Illumina ) platform.
Genomic Analysis ToolKit (GATK) and Dragen (Illumina) were used to filter the raw sequencing
data . The data processing is achieved using bioinformatical tools, which effectively resolves the
DNA reads and align them against a reference genome (GRCh38 from National Center for
Biotechnology Information (NCBI)). Du plicated reads ar e excluded and variations in tumo ur
DNA can be determined when compared to the reference genome and a germline sample (131)
(when present) . Point mutations and indels are uncovered from each sample and CNVs may

## 3.3. Paper II and III
also be identified . Potential pathogenic variations can be detected by filtration of synonymous,
benign or abundant variants in the population.
3.3.3. Gene expression
RNA was isol ated and libraries were prepared using Clariom S Pico Assay, human, which is
suitable for FFPE samples (recommended 2 -50 ng purified RNA template following the
GeneChip™ 3’ IVT Pico Kit Manual Workflow User Guide , (132) ). RNA is reverse transcribed to
single stranded complementary DNA (ss cDNA), and adapters containing a T7 -promoter
sequence is added to the 5’ end of the DNA. The reverse transcription is initiated at different
loci of the RNA molecules to capture degraded RNA and as well as coding and non -coding
RNA. The template RNA is degraded using RNase H. The ss cDNA is converted to double
stranded cDNA (ds cDNA) using a Taq DNA polymerase. The enzyme T7 RNA polymerase was
used for the generation of amplified complementary RNA (cRNA) in an in vitro transcription
as described by van Gelder et al. (133) . The cRNA amplification was performed using 12 PCR
cycles as an increase in number of PCR cycles was recommended for poor quality RNA
samples to improve cRNA yield (132) . After cRNA purification, the generation of first s s cDNA
and ds cDNA is catalys ed by reverse transcription and DNA polymerization, respectively. Page 35 of 9 2
Purified newly synthesized ds cDNA wa s fragmented and biotin -label led prior to array
hybridization (132) . The gene expression was analys ed using the gene expression microarray
Clariom S. The array contains probes (>211,300) for binding of 20, 000 well -annotated genes
as well as spike -in controls from B. subtilis (134) . The arrays are washed, stained and scanned
resulting in the creation of a CEL file for further analyses.

In search of control samples, we ordered age -matched donor islets from four individu als from

until use. To resemble the tumo ur samples, we formalin -fixed and paraffin embedded the
islets, using the following protocol (135) , without addition of agarose blue bead. We used 20
sections for RNA extraction from each FFPE block , pooled the RNA , and used the same
microarray kits as for the tumo ur samples. The control will be used in Paper II, however, the
statistical tests has not been performed yet.
To find a beta -cell control for the insulinoma samples, we searched the gene expression
omnibus (GEO ) Datasets from National Library of Medicine , NCBI . Search details: "Clariom
S"[All Fields] AND "Homo sapiens"[porgn] AND "beta cells"[All Fields]. A single dataset met
the search criteria: “Stear oyl CoA desaturase is a gatekeeper that protects human ß cells
against lipotoxicity and maintains their identity,” with the accession ID: GSE130208. The
dataset contains Clariom S gene expression data from six samples using the human beta -cell
line EndoC -βH1. Three of the samples were treated with siRNA mediated knockdown of
Stear oyl CoA desaturase (called siSCD) and the three other samples were negative controls
using ONTARGETplus non -targeting control pool siRNA (Dharmacon, GE Healthcare Life
Sciences, Velizy -Villacoublay, France) (136) . We chose to use the three negative control
sample s as control, even though the sample is a non -FFPE beta -cell line. The use of beta -cells
in comparison to insulinoma mRNA expression has been conducted before (49) .
3.3.4. Protein expression
PNETs constitute a heterogeneous group of neoplasms with distinct biological behavio ur
depending of the site of origin and the degree of diff erentiation and proliferation (137) .
Immunohistochemical analyses of the tumour tissue allows for the characterization and Page 36 of 9 2

# 3. Experimental setup
## 3.3. Paper II and III
classification of the tumour to determine 1) the neuroendocrine origin of the tumour, 2) the
functionality, 3) the histological grade, and 4) the status of menin -expression.
3.3. 4.1. Neuroendocrine markers
Specific molecul ar markers are characteristic for cellular events, including dif ferentiation and
proliferation. Typical markers used to identify neuroen docrine differentiation are
chro mogranin A and synaptophysin. The latter is an integral m embrane glycoprotein, widely
ex pressed in normal neuroendocrine cells of the gastrointestinal tract as well as PNENs (138) .
While synaptophysin is the most sensitive marker with high intensity, chromogranin A is the
most specific marker in the diagnos is of well -differentiated NETs (137) . Chromogranin A is
present in the secretory granule s of islet cells and the expres sion pattern can be scant ly
presented at the rim of positive stains or as dots at the Golgi cell site (139) . Thus, to confirm
neuroendocrine di fferentiation, both markers can be use d concurrently. An unconventional
neuroendocrine marker is the transcription factor insulin gene enhancer protein 1 (i slet -1).
Numerous studies have demonstrated that this marker has an increased sensitivity and
specificity compared to other neuroendocri ne markers (140, 141) . Islet -1 is widely
distributed in normal islet cells and have been detected in various types of PNETs (139, 141) .
Hence, to determine the (pancreatic) neu roendocrine origin of the PNETs , the FFPE sections
were immunohistochemically stained with chromogranin A, and/or synaptophysin , and i slet -
1.
3.3. 4.2 . Hormone expression
PNETs may potentially express distinct hormones. The expression of is let hormones was
examined by immunohistochemistry , including insulin and glucagon, and for patients with
MEN1, somatostatin, VIP and gastrin were also included.

## 3.3. Paper II and III
3.3.4 .3 . Proliferative marker
Ki67 proliferation index was estimated and used to assess the histological grad e of each
tumour. Compared to mitotic count the latter works as a better measurement of tumo ur
behaviour (138) . The determination of the proliferation index es and resultant tumo ur grade
were performed by Sönke Detlefsen .Page 37 of 9 2
3.3.4 .4 . Menin staining
Staining of menin was performed to determine the expression of menin in patients with and
without MEN1 syndrome. The immunohistochemical procedure was optimized during the
study, as menin staining was un tested in the lab.

The following sectio n describes the methods used in the three papers and contains text from

# 4. Material s and m ethods
## 4.1. Review
4.1.1. Search string criteria
Genetic datasets of PNETs using WES , WGS , and targeted gene -panels of more than 400 genes
were searched for in Pubmed on 25 th of September 2023 using the following search criteria:
”Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”), “Pancreatic
neuroendocrine neoplasm” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”),“Insulinoma” AND (”sequencing”
OR ”NGS”), “Glucagonoma” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”),”S omatostatinoma” AND
(”sequencing” OR ”NGS”),”Gastrinoma” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”),“VIPoma” AND
(”sequencing” OR ”NGS”),, “Serotonin -producing tumors” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”),,
“ACTH -producing tumors” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”), “Gastroenteropancrea tic” AND
(”sequencing” OR ”NGS”), “GEP -NET” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”), “GEPNET” AND
(”sequencing” OR ”NGS”), “PNET” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”), “P -NET” AND (”sequencing”
OR ”NGS”), “PanNET” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”), “Pan -NET” AND (”sequencing” OR
”NG S”), “PNEN” AND (”sequencing” OR ”NGS”).
All pancreatic functional tumo ur types in the search were retrieved from Guilmette et al. 2019
(142) and WHO 2017 Classification of Tumors of Endocrine Organs (127) . The search
included words appearing in the title and/or abstract of each article.
4.1.2. Exclusion criteria
Exclusion criteria included studies on cell -lines and human studies on extra -pancreatic

## 4.1. Review

and NECs; Studies with data without proper sample characteristics were excluded. Studies
without obtainable full text or main dataset were also excluded. Replicated data were only
presented once from the ori ginal study.
4.1.3. Meta -analysis pipeline
The meta -analysis of included data involved the following steps: 1) Select all datasets in each
published database comprising samples belonging to the chosen conditions. 2) For each Page 39 of 9 2
separate dataset, find and select PN ETs with a tumo ur grade of G1 or G2. 3) Categorize the
samples based on tumo ur type (functional vs non -functional) and sporadic vs hereditary
when specified, retrieve DNA variations, including mutations, and CNVs ; including
amplifications (Amp), deletions (Del), and cnLOH of gene region or whole chromosome),
where applicable, 5) exclude synonymous variants, 6) exclude intronic variants, 7) exclude
common variants identified in the general population (the Genome Aggregation Database
(GnomAD ), frequency < 1%) , 8) list the mutations and CNVs in genes somatically altered in
PNETs, 9) compose data to a single mutation annotation format MAF -like file for analysis as
described below.
4.1.4. Correction of data
One dataset was aligned to the reference genome GRCh38 and wa s converted to GRCh37 using
LiftOver ( https://genome.ucsc.edu/cgi -bin/hgLiftOver ). Twelve intronic variants in CUX could
not be converted. Alterations on nucleotide level were predicted using the s oftware Transvar
(143) using the amino acid alteration and coding sequence (CDS) as input. The generated
nucleotide alteration (reference and alternative allele) was compared to four of the included
datasets (20, 25, 39, 49 ), n=78/225. By using the software, both strands could be considered
altered, thus we accepted the generated nucleotide if it followed the base pairing rule in

## 4.1. Review

(20, 144) , and these were generated using the genomic coordinates of the CDS and the
represented amino acids (reference and alternative amino acid) or nucleotide change,
respectively. The study of Scarpa et al. (43) used a different annotation when describing
indels, and the HGVS annotation was achieved using Transvar based on the genomic
coordinates of the CDS and the chromosome number. A few splice -variants were excluded due
to m issing data.
4.1.5. Mutation annotation format -file generation
Data were collected from each included article and the data were listed in a MAF -like
structure. The collection of data was achieved in excel and the data -frame was compiled to a
CSV -file bef ore the generation of the MAF -file in R. The resultant MAF -like file was generated
for all samples and consisted of the following information: Genetic data, including Human
Genome Organization gene nomenclature symbol, variant classification, variant type, Page 40 of 9 2
reference allele, tumo ur seq allele1, tumo ur seq allele2, and amino acid change along with the
tumo ur sample barcode and the respective article. Clinical data about metastasis, tumo ur
type, and tumo ur syndrome was also added to the MAF file for each tumo ur sample barcode.
When applicable, CNV data were collected and added to an additional customized table in a
second file. The file could be merged to the MAF -like file during the meta -analysis.
4.1.6. Analysis of sequencing data
The generated MAF -like file inclu ding all retrieved sample information was used for further
analysis. We categorized each PNET of a patient into sporadic vs. hereditary, including
germline variations in MEN1 , VHL , NF1 , CDKN1B , BRCA2 , MUTYH , CHEK2 , PTEN , by use of the
descriptions from the articles and corresponding datasets. Further, each PNET was
categorized into non -functional (e.g. PPomas, and other PNETs without hypersecreting

according to the retrieved p ublished data. Further, the presence of distant metastases was
registered, if published.
The R -package Maftools (145) was used to produce a summary of the file, oncopl ots and a plot
of implicated oncogenic pathways, along with analyses of gene -specific mutations, co -
occurrence of mutations, and variant enrichment.
The pathogenicity of missense mutations in DAXX and ATRX was assessed using Polyphen -2
(146) . Protein domains in DAXX and ATRX were retrieved from Wang et al. (147) .

antigens in tissue samples to further char acterize the specimen . The stain ings were
performed at the D epartment of Clinical Pathology at Odense University Hospital and includes

Chromogranin A, Islet -1, Insulin, Gluc agon, Somatostatin, VIP , Gastrin, Ki67 and menin. In
Paper III antibodies against Synaptophysin, Islet -1, Insulin, Glucagon and Ki67 were used for
the immunostaining. Page 41 of 9 2

4.2.1. Tumour classification
Tumours were classified based on WHOs classification system from 2017 (127) . PNETs were
classified by proliferation rate of neoplastic cells , which was det ermined using Ki67 index .
Based on the proliferation rate, PNETs we re divided into low grade (G1), intermediate grade
(G2), and high grade (G3). The Ki67 index was determined by Professor, consulting
pathologist Sönke Detlefsen , who assessed all tumours. Page 42 of 9 2

# 4. Material s and m ethods
## 4.3. Tumour enrichment and tissue preparation
Tumour tissue s were enriched using micro - and macrodissection and healthy surrounding
pancreatic tissues were discarded . By doing this, t he possibility of false negative results
decreases and the real tumo ur informa tion on DNA and mRNA level could be accessed. This is
especially important during the identification of MEN1 mutations in tumo ur tissues and the
discovery of other tumour specific feature .
4.3.1. Laser microdissection
Tumour FFPE blocks were cut into sections of 8 μm using a microtome and placed on a
polyethylene terephthalate ( PET) membrane slide from Molecular machines and industries
GmbH (MMI) . Each section was deparaffinised using xylene for 2.5 -3 min depending on the
visual appearance of the paraffin presenc e. The rehydration was performed using etha nol in
decreasing concentration, i.e. t wo min incubation in 99 % ethanol, 96 % ethanol and 70 %
ethanol , respectively. The tissue -containing PET membrane was paired with a Superfrost
gla ss and the tumo ur tissue wa s isolated using a MMI cellcut laser instrument. This method
was only used for subsequent RNA isolation.
4.3.2. Macrodissection
Tissue sections were cut from FFPE tumour blocks and placed onto a Superfrost glass.
Macrodissection was performed in accordance with  instructions provided by Prosigna Breast
Cancer Prognostic Gene Signature Assay (NanoString, #2019 -9 LBL -C0191 -10). T issues were
heated to 60 degrees and tissues were deparaffinised using xylene and rehydrated using a
decreasing concentration of ethanol. Af ter rehydration in 3% glycerol, each tissue was
delicately cut using a razor blade to isolate the tumour material.  After dissection , the tissues
were placed into  Eppendorf tube s ready for DNA and mRNA isolation , respectively .

# 4. Material s and m ethods
## 4.4. Exome sequencing
4.4.1. DNA purific ation
Slides from FFPE samples were collected in a microtube and DNA was extracted using
Maxwell® RSC DNA FFPE Kit, ( cat# AS1450, Promega Corporation) on a Maxwell RSC
Instrument. DNA concentrations were measured on a Qubit fluorometer, using the DNA High Page 43 of 9 2
Sensitivity A ssay and subsequently, DNA was diluted to 200 ng (FFPE) or 50 ng (blood
sample) , respectively. Extracted DNA was transferred to Microtubes -50 AFA Fiber H slit V2
(cat# 520240, Covaris) and fragmented using a Covaris Ultrasonicator, ME220 wi th standard
settings for 16 or 18 iterations for FFPE and blood, respectively. Samples were concentrated
using a vacuum concentrator (Scanvac Scanspeed 40 (Labogene)).
4.4.2. Library Preparation and exome sequencing
Library preparation was conducted using the Twist library preparation kit for mechanical
fragmentation (cat# 104176). Indexing was performed using xGen Dual Index UMI Adapters
(IDT). Multiple libraries were poo led together and s equenced on a Novaseq 6 000 Illumina
sequencing platform.
4.4.3. Bioinformatic analys is
We used two pipelines to identify DNA variations from the exome sequencing, i.e. GATK and
Dragen (Illumina) . Using GATK, r aw reads were put th rough a quality control pipeline
(FastQC). Reads were aligned to the reference genome G RCh38 (NCBI) using Burro ws –
Wheeler aligner -maximum exact matches (148) . Ma rkDuplicates from Picard (website:
http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard), was used to identify duplicate reads , and Qualimap
(149) was executed as a quality control of aligned sequencing data. Raw variant calling of
germline variants were filtered using Haplotype caller. Mutect2 was used for calling somatic

## 4.4. Exome sequencing
variants (SNV and indels). Insulinomas without a normal sample for control was processed
using the ‘tumor -only’ mode.
4.4.4. Gene variant filtering
The software VarSeq v. 2.5.0 (Golden Helix, Inc., Bozeman, MT) was used for the downstream
fil tering of gene variants and CNV/LOH analysis . All variants were named in accordance with
the Human Genome Variation Society ( http://varnomen.hgvs.org ). Page 44 of 9 2
4.4.4.1. Filtration of somatic varian ts in pancreatic neuroendocrine t umours
Somatic v ariant filtering of da ta from exome sequencing of insulinoma samples (Paper III)
was performed as shown in Figure 6. The filtering chain was identical for all insulinomas . The
selected pipeline is described in details below:
Quality filteri ng
Read depth in variant locus > 20 reads , a variant allele frequency (VAF) ≥ 0.1 (i.e.
10% of reads) , and alternative allele depth ≥ 2 reads were in cluded. The read
depth indicate s the number of DNA molecules aligned to the specific locus.
Filtering based on sequence ontology
The following sequence ontologies were included: frameshift, (disruptive)
inframe indels, missense, splice -region and stop codon, gained/lost variants.
Thereby synonymous variants and variants in introns were excluded.
Inclusion of s omatic , uncommon variants
VAF in healthy tissues < 0.01 (i.e. 1% of reads) was included. This step was
avoided for those PNEN samples without a normal sample . Subsequently ,
common variants in the human healthy population were excluded using GnomAD
(150) , where VAF of ≤ 0.001 was accepted . Genes in top 100 of FrequentLy
mutAted GeneS (FLAGs) (151) were also excluded in the variant filtering.
Filtering using functional prediction tools
Nonsynonymous variants and splice -site variants were filtered based on dbNSFP

tools  (including SIFT, PolyPhen -2, MutationTaster, MutationAssessor, and
FATHMM) . Variants were excluded when four or five prediction tools predicted
the variant as tolerated, or zero of the prediction tools predicted the variant as
damaging. Furthermore, Rare Exome Variant Ensemble Learner ( REVEL ) (2016 -
06 -03)  (153)  was used to identify damaging non -synonymous and splice site
variants (score ≥  0.5  was  accepted  (range 0 to 1 )). Indels and  varia nts in  splice
site regions  were filtered using Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion
(CADD)  v. 1.6  (154) , where a  PHRE D score ≥ 10  was  accepted , corresponding to Page 45 of 9 2
top 10% of scores observed from G nomAD structural variants (PHRED score
ranging from 0 (potentially benign) to 48 (potentially pathogenic )).
Literature search
Lastly, a literature search was conducted to determine , which genes were
functionally associated with e.g. HH and tumorigenesis. All gene s included after
the filtration and their encoded proteins were thoroughly investigated.

4.4.4.2. Somatic variants in frequently altered genes
An e xclusive search for variants was performed in frequently altered genes in PNETs, namely
MEN1 , DAXX , ATRX , YY1 , VHL  and  CDKN1B  in Paper III, meani ng that raw data was assessed

variants in  MEN1  was conducted in  Paper  II in P NET s from patients with MEN1 syndrome .
4.4.4.3. Copy number variation analysis of the MEN1 locus
In Paper II, t he CNV and LOH analyse s in MEN1 were performed using Golden Helix Varseq v
2.2.5. The software calls CNV events based on Z -score, ratio -plot, and VAF metrics, and LOH
events based on VAF and genotype quality. CNVs were computed using Coverage Statistics
using the coding regions of hg38 (plus/minus 20 nucleotides in the non -coding regions), and
more than 10 samples with less than 20 % difference from each individual tumo ur sample
were used as reference. CNVs were predicted with very high sensit ivity.
Ratios in the MEN1 locus were computed using the equation: (normalized target depth /
normalized mean depth across controls), and gives the ability to differentiate between
homozygous and heterozygous deletion events. While no CNV event is present at ratio values
of ~1, ratio values of approximately 0, 0.5 and 1.5 indicates homozygous deletions,
heterozygous deletions, and duplications, respectively.
Z-scores were computed as ((normalized target depth – normalized mean depth across
controls) / stan dard deviation of control). While ratio and Z -score provide the primary
evidence of CNV, VAFs may be used in the CNV analysis. VAFs close to 1 and 0 could represent
deletion events, and thereby also LOH. Note that regions with abnormal VAFs were excluded
from the normalization process to prevent skewing of the normalized read depth in case of
larger CNV events. LOH was considered when a combination of the following cut -off values
were exceeded: Ratio (cut -off: <0.75 or >1.25) (155, 156) , Z -score (cut -off: < -2.0 or >2.0)

4.4.4.4. Targeted sequencing panel
In Paper II, Oncomine Comprehensive Plus Panel w.2.5 (Thermo Fi sher Scientific) was used to
identify CNVs, SNVs, and indels in 517 cancer -related genes. DNA was isolated using
Maxwell® 16 FFPE Plus LEV DNA Purification Kit (Cat. # AS1134) and RNA was isolated using
RNeasy FFPE (Qiagen, cat. #73504). The concentration was measured using a Qubit
Fluorometer (Invitrogen). Library preparation was performed as described by the
manufacturer (Oncomine Comprehensive Assay Plus User Guide, June 2022). Sequencing was
conducted on an Ion Torrent S5 instrument (Thermo Fisher Scien tific).
Bioinformatics
Data were accessible using the Ion Reporter (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and BAM files were
manually assessed using Genome Browser (Golden Helix). Filtering of SNV was performed as
described (section 2.4.3. in (158) ), and further, variants with SIFT score < 0.05 and PolyPhen -
2 score >0.453 were included, intron variants and benign variants (Clinvar) were excluded
and variants with a Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) global variant allele frequencies
(GAF) > 0.01 were excluded. Indels were filtered and excluded based on UCSC common SNPs,
Clinva r (benign), overall coverage < 100x, Phred score < 200, Ion Reporter p -value > 0.01,
allele frequency < 10% or equal to 100%. For all samples, potential germline variants
including SNPs and indels, were excluded based on the germline variant calls obtained using
the normal sample from the exome sequencing. Included variants from the Oncomine panel
were collated with the exome sequencing -data of the PNENs.

# 4. Material s and m ethods
## 4.4. Exome sequencing
CNV calls generated by Oncomine Comprehensive Assay Plus were filtered based on CNV p -
value < 0.05, an d only calls determined as “loss”, “g ain” or “LOH” were considered.

# 4. Material s and m ethods
## 4.5. Gene expression microarray
4.5.1. RNA p urification
For insulinomas in Paper III, RNA was purified using the RNeasy FFPE kit (Qiagen) . Proteinase
K digestion time was increased from 15 min to 3 hours, otherwise the isolation was
performed following the manufacturers instructions. RNA was eluted in 20 μl nuclease free
water. Subsequently, c oncentration s were measured using a Qubit RNA HS Assay kit or Qubit
RNA BR Assay kit on a Qubit fluoro meter (Invitrogen) .Page 48 of 9 2
4.5.2. Gene expression profiling preparation
Purified total RNA was prepared for the reverse transcription procedure. Total RNA (40 ng)
was used in addition to a HeLa control RNA sample (500 pg ). The latter was used to verify
that the reagents work as expected. A Poly -A RNA control solution was used as spike -in
control to monitor the labelling and hybridization process. The Poly -A RNA control stock was
appropriately diluted to arrive at the same proportionate final concentration as each sample.
The subsequent procedure was done according to the GeneChip 3’ IVT Pico Kit Manual
Workflow U ser Guide (Applied Biosystems, C at# 902790) (132) . A total of 12 cycles were
added to the Pre -IVT Amplification PCR protocol to improve cRNA yield of the poor quality
RNA. Purified cRNA was stored at -80 °C before yield assessment and pu rified ds -cDNA was
stored at -20 °C before fragmentation, labelling and subsequent hybridization. All RNA
samples were processed in triplicates.
4.5.3. Analysis of gene expression
The microarray data were analys ed using the Transcriptome Analysis Console Sof tware
(Version 4.0.2 Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA). For each microarray experiment, the
Signal Space Transformation Robust Mult iclip Analysis ( SST -RMA) method on gene level was
applied on a per -chip basis for background correction . Afterwards, th e relative log expression
signals were compared between controls and samples. All samples carried Poly A labelling

## 4.5. Gene expression microarray
and hybridization controls ( B. Subtilis genes) , and samples with aberrant control signal
intensities were excluded from the further analysis. After quality control, the included
insulinoma samples from Paper III were compared with the three beta -cell control samples
(GSE130208) (136) using the ebayes ANOVA method. A probeset wa s considered to be
expresse d if 50% of samples in each group (insulinoma vs. control) have values detected
above background (threshold p -value < 0.05). The following filter criteria were applied to
identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs): Fold Change: > 2 or < -2, p-val ue : < 0.05, and
FDR p-val ue : < 0.05 .
Single cell RNA -sequencing data from healthy pancreas cells from Segerstolpe et al . (Suppl.
Table 2, sheet 8, (7) ) were used to filter genes associated with ductal (408 cell type spec ific
genes) and acinar cells (332 cell type specific genes) . Ductal and acinar cell type specific gene Page 49 of 9 2
enrichment were collated with genes enriched (>2 fold) in insulinoma samples compared to
control (Paper III) and discarded from the further analysis .
Th e 20 most upregulated and downregulated genes were identified based on fold change (FC) .
Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) (159) was used for
functional enrichment analysis.  Pathway enrichment analysis was exerted using Kyoto
Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathw ay enrichment analysis, Biocarta, and
wikiPathways. Further functional categories were identified using UP KEYWORDS (molecular
function). Lastly, Gene Ontology (GO) terms for molecular function were exerted for the
variants through the DAVID online tool. T he Human Protein Atlas was accessed to identify
proteins normally expressed in pancreatic islets. An analysis was performed using  Search
Tool  for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins (STRING) for protein network
association.

# 4. Material s and m ethods
## 4.6. Statistical analyses
P-values were determined using two -tailed Fishers -exact test, a Freeman -Halton extended
Fishers exact test, or Mann -Whitney U test where appropriate. P -values less than 0.05 were
considered significant. Data were analyzed using R (v. 4.2.3.). Gene expression data from
Paper II were analyzed using ANOVA (ebayes) including false discovery rate (FDR>0.05) in
the Transcriptome Analysis Console Software (Version 4.0.2 Thermo Fisher Scientific,

## 5.1. Paper I - Review of somatic variants in well -differentiated PNETs
Fourteen articles were successfully chosen after thorough assessment. Data were comprised

predisposing variants, hence CHEK2 /MUTYH and MEN1 /MUTYH , respectively. Thirty -three of
the 225 PNETs (14.7%) were not specified as having a germline predisposition or not.
Patients with a germline predisposition were significantly younger than sporadic patients at
the time of resection. There was not significant difference b etween the predisposed and
sporadic patients regarding the occurrence of distant metastases. The majority of PNETs were
non -functioning ( 156/225, 69.3%) , and among the functioning PNETs (45/225, 20% ), most
PNETs were diagnosed as insulinoma (37/45, 82.2%) .
