# 6. Discussion
## 6.1. Main findings
MEN1 gene w as the most frequently altered gene in our review (Paper I) across tumo ur types
and functionality. Variants in MEN1 were scattered throughout the gene with no evident
hotspots, as described i n other studies (76) .
6.1.1. MEN1 second hit
In Paper I, we identified 14 MEN1 patients and 12 of these presented with germline variants
resulting in predicted l oss of function in MEN1 , including frameshifts, nonsense mutations , a
splice site mutation and one MEN1 locus del etion . The second hit in MEN1 was reported in
13/14 MEN1 patients, and included LOH in 12/13 PNETs ( 92.3% ) and a missense mutation
was identified in one PNET with CNV and one without (2/13, 15.4 %) , respectively . These
results are in line with the literatur e, where 90% of MEN1 patients exhibit somatic LOH of
MEN1 (76, 81) .
In our small cohort of seven PNEN s from patients with a MEN1 diagnosis in Paper II, we had
issues when attempting to uncover the mechanisms behin d the second hit in one PNEN . The
detected somatic variants in the coding region of MEN1 were all benign, thereby MEN1
mutations were excluded as a cause. However, in one PNET (PNET K) we did detect a novel 5’
UTR missense mutation in the MEN1 locus (c. -7C >A). An adjacent varia nt has earlier been
found (c. -6G>A), although this variant was reported as benign/likely benign (160, 161) . The
identification of CNV s using exome sequencing can be challenging (162) , however, we
identified  CNV of chromosome 11 in two tumors,  and exonic  CNV  in  MEN1  gene locus  in two
of the  examined  PNENs .
6.1.2. Lack of a second hit
We found a nuclear loss of menin in all PNENs from MEN1 patients, suggesting t hat a second

# 6. Discussion
## 6.1. Main findings
hit may be present in all seven PNENs. However, w e could not identify a second hit in one
PNEN from a patient with MEN1 (PNEN L), using exome sequencing and targeted sequencing.
Interesting ly for PNEN L, CNV loss or LOH on gene level was ident ified in chromosome 1, 2, 6,
8, 11, 12, 16 and 22 using Oncomine Comprehensive Assay Plus (Table 4 ), but the Z -score of
these chromosome in Figure 11 were mostly within the normal range ( -2 to 2). These findings Page 68 of 9 2
could indicate that the CNV analysis using e xome sequencing may be misleading , even though
the number of gene -specific CNVs are low (cf. Table 4 ). Other studies have also found it
challenging to identify a second hit in neuroendocrine neoplasms from patients with MEN1
syndrome (163, 164) . An eventual compensatory mechanism involving miRNAs may also be a
potential explanation for the loss of menin in this PNEN (96, 165) .
6.1.3. Driver genes in PNET development
In Paper I, we identified frequently altered genes in 225 PNETs from 14 datasets, with
differentiation between heredity and functionality. Further, e xome sequencing of pancreatic
tumour samples from MEN1 patients (Paper II) and insulinomas (Paper III) was conducted to
identify genes associated with the tumorigene sis of the tissues. The analysis in Paper I

# 6. Discussion
## 6.2. Methodological considerations
6.2.1. Exo me sequencing
6.2.1.1. True positives and false positive variants
False positive results in somatic variant identification may appear due to artefacts,
contamination, or germline variants . Despite biological differences, technical and
methodological errors may cont ribute to inaccurate data. Artefacts comprise nucleotides that
are misread during sequencing, sequencing artefacts and misaligned reads. One of the main
players is the polymerase in the PCR reaction. The risk of errors exists and errors may appear
as an ar tefact in the final sequencing data. It may be hard to distinguish between artefacts and
true variants, however the depth of the read (> 2) may help to identify true variants even in a
subclonal tissue with diverse tumour and stromal cells.
PCR duplicates stick out and is an indicator of multiple chain reactions of the same DNA
sequences . Th rough GATK/Varseq filtering and manual filtering, variants found in duplicates
due to PCR amplification, were filtered and read as one. Thus, filtering of read depth of PCR
duplicates decrease the depth of the alternative variant and only variants detected in more
than two reads were included in the final literature search and candidate gene discovery in
Paper III .
6.2.1.2. Variant filtering
We did not identify the common vari ant in YY1 (T hr372Arg ) in our output after filtering, even
though one of the PNENs (from patient N) harboured the variant. The variant did not pass the
filter step using the REVEL prediction tool due to a score of 0.439. Our threshold was ≥0.5,
hence the v ariant was filtered out. The strict pipeline could potentially exclude interesting
variants, which is a limitation. Likewise, too weak filtering could result in an output of benign
variants.
We did, however, visually attend and inspect each of the commonl y mutated genes ( MEN1 ,
YY1 , ATRX , DAXX , and CDKN1B ) in Paper III (and MEN1 in Paper II) to identify variants,
independent of the variant filtering pipeline. Page 73 of 9 2

# 6. Discussion
## 6.2. Methodological considerations
A blood sample for germline detection was not provided for seven of the insulinoma patients.
In th ose cases, the somatic gene variants were identified using the ‘tumour only’ mode during
Mutect2 filtering of raw variants. Here, the tools compares the variants with a set of reference
samples to detect potential common germline variants. However, variant calling using
“tumour -only” may not discriminate rare germline variants from somatic variants. In Paper III
we could not determine if five (somatically called) variants in BRCA2, NKX6.1 , ATP2B1 , GPR1
and SLC37A4 with VAF ≥40 were germline or somatic.
6.2.2. Gene expression microarray
We assume that the level of a given mRNA positively correlates with the expression of the
associated protein. However, it might give a simplified picture of the real events. A list of
factors, which may influence the correlation between mRNA and protein expre ssion includes
mRNA degradation and decay rate, polyadenylation, protein degradation , translation rates,
alternative splicing, translation lag among others (Figure 17 ).
Figure 17 . Factors affe cting the mRNA and protein levels. During transcription, RNA
polymerase transcribes DNA to pre -mRNA. Transcription is error -prone and the event of
polymerase slipping may occur . After DNA is transcribed to pre -mRNA , the pre -mRNA enters
the spliceosome whic h contributes to the correct production of intron -less mRNA. Altered
splicing due to splice -site mutations, spliceosome errors often leads to downstream
degradation via nonsense mediated decay (NMD) . Epigenetic regulation, such as miRNA
binding may also re sult in degradation prior to translation. The image was generated in

It has been suggested that RNA -molecules from FFPE sample are more subjected to chemical
degrading (5’ -3’) compared to fresh frozen samples (184) . This occurrence of degradation
may impair the binding to microarray probes design ed to bind at the 5’ end of mRNA from

## 6.2. Methodological considerations

probe -bound mRNA in between samples.
6.2.3. Disconcordance between exome sequencing and microarray data
Filtered probably dam aging variants discovered in exome sequencing does not always result
in change of gene expression. The low level of concordance may result from variants with low
alternative VAF , possibly from tumour subclones, which may represent a fraction of analysed
tu mour cells. The microarray data is obtained from sections of a whole tumour sample, where
the alternative allele may only account for a minimal change in the overall global gene
expression. Additionally, missense variants rarely have an impact on the gene expression, but
may cause an alt eration during protein folding, or during binding to other molecules,
including miRNAs or interacting proteins.
On the other hand, the gene expression data may point towards DEGs that are not contained
in the exome sequenc ing data. It could be assigned to 1) epigenetic alterations, including
histone modifications and DNA methylation , 2) or the chosen c ontrol sample , namely on DNA
level the patient -matched DNA contro l versus a beta -cell line (Paper III) on RNA level . Hence,
germline variants that are excluded in the filtering of exome sequencing -data , may represent
DEGs at mRNA level.

# 6. Discussion
## 6.3. Strengths
6.3.1. Paper I
Our study included the systematic search for eligible articles and large sample size from 14
datasets in comparison to in dividual datasets. Moreover, we only included datasets obtained
from sequencing of more than 400 genes, to ensure a high number of sequenced genes in the
analyses to accommodate the bias of small, selected gene panels. Another strength of Paper I
is the in clusion criteria of reported G1/G2 PNETs to ensure the exclusion of G3 PNETs, as the
grading system of G3 changed in the WHO 2017 guideline (127) .Page 75 of 9 2
6.3.2. Paper II
PNENs from patients with MEN1 syndrome are rare (1) , and the inclusion of seven PNE Ns is a
strength of th is paper, compared to other similar papers (162, 163, 185) . All germline variants
could be identified in the MEN1 SNV analysis, even the intronic variant c.784 -9G>A. The
specific CNV -callers used in our study has pr eviously been used in other studies (157) ,
confirming the validity of the method. The use of two DNA sequencing techniques verified the
CNV of PNEN K.
6.3.3. Paper III
The number of insulinomas were compatible to other ins ulinoma -studies (39, 48) . In somatic
gene variant filtering we used a strict pipeline with use of several prediction tools, to ensure
the inclusion of variants predicted as damaging.
The human beta cell line EndoC -βH1 was used as control in the gene expression analyses in
Paper III. The cell line resembles healthy beta -cells in terms of glucose and incretin induced
insulin secretion (186) . The use of beta -cells in comparison t o insulinoma mRNA expression
has been conducted before (49) .

# 6. Discussion
## 6.4. Limitations
6.4.1. Paper I
First, t he search string was narrowed down to contain ‘sequencing’ or ‘NGS’, meaning that
abstracts without these words were excluded from the article search. Along with this, only
articles from Pubmed was considered, and thereby articles from other databases were not
considered. Secondly, each of the included 14 articles used distinct methods for the DNA
isolation, library preparation , and sequencing, which may have implications on the results. Six
of the articles did not report the average read depth and some of the articles only identified a
few variants (162, 185, 187) compared to others (20, 144, 188) . Of note, after retrieving the
variants, we excluded synonymous and intronic variants, even thoug h such variants can alter
the splicing of genes (189) .
Thirdly, CNV information could only be gathered from 33% of the PNETs, of which we only
included structural variations, i.e. amp, del, and cnL OH as structural variations. C linically
imp ortant CNVs could, therefore, be present in the remaining 66% of PNETs .Page 76 of 9 2
Lastly, we chose to term patients without germ line predisposition as ‘sporadic’, even though
most articles only used the term ‘sporadic’ when patients were germline MEN1 negative.
Thu s, the ‘sporadic’ PNETs could potentially harbor germline variants in germline
predisposing genes, including VHL , PTEN , CDKN1B , BRCA2 , CHEK2 , and MUTYH .
6.4.2. Paper II
The formalin fixation may especially affect the DNA and RNA quality. As presented in Figure
10 , and further in the Suppl . Table in Paper II , many variants in MEN1 gene was present in 3
to 7 reads, indicating an artefact, potentially from the formalin fixation. Further, unreliable
LOH data may occur due to frequent reaction failures during DNA amp lification from FFPE
tissue (190) .

# 6. Discussion
## 6.4. Limitations
It is estimated that 11.1 % of MEN1 germline mutations are associated with splice site defects
(191) , however exome sequencing and targeted sequencing may not detect intronic variants.
Further, CNV calls are mor e reliable when using other techniques than exome sequencing,
such as WES, multiplex ligation -dependent probe amplification or array comparative genomic
hybridization (192) . Our cut -off thresholds for ratio and Z -sc ores in the MEN1 CNV analysis
may be too strict , as PNETs with chromosome 11 loss presented with ratio and Z -scores above
0.75 and -2, respectively. Moreover, regions with low coverage may be hard to distinguish
from heterozygous regions in the CNV analysi s (192, 193) .
6.4.3. Paper III
The insulinoma gene expression signals were compared to a control (GSE130208) (136) from
another study. First , the gene expression microarray was no t performed in our lab, and
differences between the laboratory setup, including the array -scanning may be a limitation.
Accordingly, t he study did not describe the assay to prepare RNA for microarray
hybridisation. Secondly, the use of a beta -cell line in comparison to FFPE tumo ur tissues may
have some limitations regarding the different handlings of the specimen, and the presence of
surrounding tissue in the FFPE block. The contamination of non -endocrine cells were
reflected by the high signal intensities of acinar/ductal cell -specific genes in the insulinomas.
Thirdly, the presence of non -endocrine cells in the FFPE blocks may lead to a degradation of Page 77 of 9 2
RNAs, as RNase activity is increased in the exocrine pancreas (194) . The presence of non -
endocrine pancreatic gene expression may arise from contamination during macrodissection
or stromal cells.
Another control sample from our lab, such as beta -cells from donor islets (49) or normal
pancreas ti ssue (29) , may be used in our analysis of DEGs in insulinomas before submission of
the paper.

# 7. Summarizing c onclusion s
We examined the genetic lands cape of well -differentiated G1/G2 PNETs, to identify the most
frequent somatically altered genes and potential drivers of PNET tumorigenesis. In Paper I,
MEN1 was the most frequently altered gene across all types of PNETs. Consistent with
Knudson’s two hit hypothesis, 13/14 PNETs in Paper I and 4/5 PNETs in Paper II harboured
an identified second hit in MEN1 .
DAXX and ATRX variants were also abundant in Paper I, and mutational hotspots were
identified in both genes. DAXX variants were not detected in our o wn cohort of 19 PNETs.
ATRX variants were identified in 3/12 sporadic insulinomas (Paper III) and one MEN1 -
associated PNEN (Paper II). Additional potential drivers in PNENs from patients with MEN1
syndrome were associated with DNA repair and mTOR pathways.
Thirty three candidate genes were identified in sporadic insulinomas (Paper III), and only two
genes were identified in more than one insulinoma, indicating a heterogeneity of somatic
variants in these PNETs, consistent with findings in Paper I. Candidat e genes with differential
gene expression in insulinomas compared to EndoC -βH1, i.e . PAX6, ATP2B1, DPP4, CCND2 , and
FGFR1 were identified. Clusters of enriched pathways were identified in Paper III, i.e.
metabolism of cholesterol and lipids. To sum up,  som atic gene  alterations in  well -
differentiated  G1/G2 PNETs are diverse, but with distinct differences between sporadic vs.
hereditary, and functional vs. non -functional PNETs. Page 78 of 9 2

# 8. Perspectives
PNENs have malignant potential, why they are resected regardless of t heir hormonal function.
The identification of mutatio ns in novel candidate genes in PNENs could be an important
discovery and may lead to future studies in therapeutic drug targets. For insulinomas, t he
characterization of hypersecreting beta -cells could further elucidate the molecular regulation
of insulin secretion, which may help to decrease the knowledge gap of beta -cell dysfunction in
HH and diabetes. However, further experiments are pivotal for the validation of candidate
genes.

# 8. Perspectives
## 8.1. Functional studies
To investigate the actual consequence of the candidate gene variations found in our study, the
performance of gene -depletion studies in vitro and in vivo could be conducted . Several
pancreas -specific neuroendocrine cell lines alr eady exists, such as BON1, MIN6, INS -1E and
EndoC -βH1. Downregulation of candidate genes could be conducted using for instance small
interfering RNA ( si RNA) mediated knock down, or c lustered regularly interspaced short
palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 knock out.
After successful d epletion of a candidate gene, the changes in proliferation could be assessed
using BrdU assay, which stains newly synthesized DNA. Hormone secretion could be assessed
using immunoassays, such as enzyme -linked immunosorbent assay or a fluorescent marker.
We did attempt multiple times to perform a heterozygous Men1 knock out in zebrafish using
the gene editing tool CRISPR /Cas9. It would be a novel animal model of MEN1 (63) . The
efficacy of the knockout was low a nd after several attempts, we decided to wait.

# 8. Perspectives
## 8.2. Epigenetic analyses
The three genes, which are most frequently altered in PNETs, e.i. MEN1 , DAXX , and ATRX, are
all epigenetic regulators (38) . We wanted to examine the abundancy of H3K4me3 and
H3K27me3 in PNETs with and without MEN1. With the issue of the collected tumour samples
being formalin fixed, paraffin embedded, we could not use the conventional chromatin
immunoprecipitation (ChIP) protocol. However, in our sear ch, we found other alternatives,
including fixed -tissue ChIP sequencing (FiT -seq) (195) and the fixed -tissue ChIP -seq for
H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac) profiling (FiTAc -seq) (196) . We did follow the protocol for the Page 79 of 9 2
histone methylation profiling using the guideli nes presented in reference (196) , and include d
serial dilutions of antibodies using five different FFPE PNET samples. Unfortunately, the
quality of the tissues and the data output made us believe that more optimization is needed.
Hence, we would like explore the epigenetic regulation of PNETs with va riants in epigenetic
modulators, such as MEN1 , DAXX , ATRX , and YY1 .
Additional DNA methylation analyses could be conducted to determine the second hit. We
want to use the Infinium MethylationEPIC array on the PNETs from MEN1 patients. The array
identifies methylation of selected CpG islands and may also be used for a CNV analysis, to
determine the second hit in the remaining PNET. Further, a successful gene expression
analysis will be conducted as soon as possible for the MEN1 -associated PNENs.

10 .1. Glucose -stimulated insulin secretion
During high glucose concentrations in the plasma, the gluco se transporter GLUT2 facilitates
the influx of glucose into the beta -cell. The initiating and rate -limiting enzyme of the glycolysis
is the glucokinase (hexokinase IV) in beta -cells. The enzyme has a lower affinity to the glucose
compared to other hexokina ses (197) . After conversion of glucose to glucose -6-phostate, the
glycolytic pathway continues and generates pyruvate molecules. The metabolism of pyruvate
occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, where pyruvate drives t he production of ATP through the
citric acid cycle (198) . The ATP generation increase s the ratio of ATP/ADP, which leads to a
closure of ATP sensitive K +-channels and th ereby hinders the influx of K + cations into the beta -
cell. Instead, the closure induce a plasma membrane depolarization, which activates the
cellular influx of Ca ++ through a voltage -gated Ca ++ channel. Intracellular Ca ++ stimulates the
release of insulin granules (11) . Transcription factors PDX1, NEUROD1 and MAFA are critical
for the insulin synthesis and the elevation of glucose stimu lates their activity. Preproinsulin is
transcribed in the nucleus, folded in the endoplasmic reticulum, and cleaved to create insulin
molecules for secretion (199) .

Abstract
Well -differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) can be non -functional or functional ,
e.g. insulinoma and gluc agonoma. The majority of PNETs are sporadic, but PNETs also occur in
hereditary syndromes, primarily multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) . The Knud son
hypothesis stated a second, somatic hit in MEN1 as the cause of PNETs of MEN1 syndrome . In the
rece nt years, reports on genetic somatic events in both sporadic and hereditary PNETs have
emerged, providing a basis for a more detailed molecular understanding of the pathophysiology . In
this systematic meta -analysis review, w e made a collation and statisti cal analysis of aggregated
frequent genetic alterations and potential driver events in G1/ G2 PNETs. Published studies using
whole exome, whole genome, or targeted gene panel (+400 genes) sequencing of G1/G2 PNETs
were identified. Fourteen datasets from published stud ies were included with data on 221 patients
and 225 G1/G2 PNETs, which were divided into sporadic tumors, and hereditary tumors with pre -
disposing germline variants , and tumors with unknown germline status . Further, non -functioning
and functioning PNETs we re distinguished into two groups for pathway evaluation. Paper I

Sporadic PNETs accounted 72.0% (162/225), hereditary PNETs 13.3% (30/225), unknown
germline status 14.7% (33/225). The most frequently altered gene was MEN1 , with somatic variants
and copy number va riations in overall 42 % (95/225) ; hereditary PNETs ( germline variations in
MEN1 , VHL , CHEK2 , BRCA2 , PTEN , CDKN1B , and/or MUTYH ) 57 % (16/3 0); sporadic PNETs
36% (58/162 ); unknown germline status 64% (21/33) . The MEN1 point mutations/indels were
distributed throughout MEN1 .
Overall, DAXX (16 %, 37/ 225) and ATRX -varia nts (12 %, 2 7/225) were also abundant with missense
mutations clustered in mutational hotspots associated with histone binding , and translocase activity,
respectively. DAXX mutations occurred more frequently in PNETs with MEN1 mutations , p<0.05 .
While functioning PNETs shared few variated genes, non -functioning PNETs had more recurrent
variations in genes associated with the Phosphoinositide 3 -kinase, Wnt, NOTCH, and Receptor
Tyrosine Kinase -Ras si gnaling onco -pathways.
In conclusion, the somatic genetic alterations in G1/G2 PNETs are diverse, but with distinct
differences between sporadic vs. hereditary, and functional vs. non -functional PNETs. Increased
understanding of the genetic alterations ma y lead to identification of more drivers and driver
hotspots in the tumorigenesis in well -differentiated PNETs , potentially giving a basis for new drug

Introduction
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) represent a rare tumor type acc ounting for less than 3 %

# Paper I-III Paper I
of all pancreatic malignancies (1) . Most PNETs develop sporadicall y. Here as only five to ten
percent of PNETs occur due to hereditary syndromes including multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
(MEN1), and more rarely von Hippel -Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous
sclerosis (2) .
According to the Knudson’s two -hit hypothesis from 1993, PNETs occurring in patients with
MEN1 syndrome are likely caused by a somatic second hit in MEN1 in the PNET in individuals
carrying a germline MEN1 mutation (3, 4) . The MEN1 gene encodes the putative tumor suppressor
menin, which plays a role in biological processes such as histone and transcription regulation (5 -9) ,
DNA repair (10) , and apoptosis (8) .
Somatic variants in MEN1 gene are reported in 25 -44 % of all PNETs (11 -14) . Additionally, DAXX
and ATRX , both encoding chromatin -remodelers , are f requently altered somatically in PNETs, as
well as other genes in the mTOR and DNA repair pathways (11, 12) . PNETs may be non -
functioning, or functioning leading to a clinically measurable hormonal hypersecretion s yndrome
such as insulinoma and glucagonoma. A mutational hotspot in YY1, (p.Thr372Arg), has been
identified in 8 -30 % of sporadic insulinomas (15 -17) . Along with YY1 , other genes have been
proposed to be drivers in insulinomas (18, 19) , although the ir relative frequenc ies are rather low .
In the last decades, investigations with expanded genetic analyses have provided an explosion of
our knowledge on somatic gene changes in tumors in general , which may contribute to clinical
diagnosis, prognosis, treatment and categorization of patients. Little is known, however, about
tumor genetics by expanded genetic analyse s in well differentiated (wd) -PNETs .Paper I
> 4
Understanding the tumor gene tics of PNETs may provide a basis for improved diagnosis and

# Paper I-III Paper I
management for PNET patients and may contribute to the discovery of new drug targets as the
mTOR -inhibitor everolimus and the kinase inhibitor sunitinib malate (20 -22) . Given these
perspectives, we aimed to review published DNA sequencing data gained by expanded genetic
analyses of wd -PNETs to shed light on the frequently altered genes in association to genetically
predisposed patients and distinct functio nality of PNETs.

We included studies using WES, WGS and/or a gene panel of more than 400 genes to determine
the somatic vari ants in PNETs. The cut -off of 400 genes was chosen based on a Japanese study with
use of da ta from The Cancer Genome Atlas (25) , showing that cancer -panel sizes at or above 400

functioning and non -functioning PNETs were included. Both studies using formalin -fixed paraffin -
embedded (FFPE) and fresh frozen samples were included.
Exclusion criteria included studies on cell -lines and human studies on extra -pancreatic tissues ,
carc inoma s, non -islet PNETs , metastatic tissues, PNETs with tumor grade G3 only and NECs;
Studies with d ata without proper sample characteristics were excluded. Studies without obtainable
full text or main data set were also excluded. Replicated data were only presented once from the
original study. The literature search flow chart is presented in Figure 1 . The full list of excluded and
included papers is listed in Suppl. Table 1 -2 and Table 1 , respectively .
Meta -analysis pipeline
The meta -analysis of included data involved the following steps: 1) Select all datasets in each

published database comprising samples belonging to the chosen conditions. 2) For each separate
dataset, find and select PNETs with a tumor grade of G1 or G2. 3) Categorize the samples based on
tumor type (functional vs non -functional) and sporadic vs hereditary when specified , retrieve DNA Paper I

Data correction
One dataset was aligned to the reference genome GRCh38 and was converted to GRCh37 using
LiftOver ( https://genome.ucsc.edu/cgi -bin/hgLiftOver ). Twelve intronic variants in CUX could not
be converted. Alterations on nucleotide level were predicted using the software Transvar (26) using
the amino acid alteration and coding sequence (CDS) as input. The generated nucleotide alteration
(reference and alternative allele) was compared to four of the included datasets (13, 15, 19, 27) ,
n=78/22 5. By using the software , both stra nds could be considered altered, thus we accepted the
generated nucleotide if it followed the base pairing rule in comparison to the datasets. Two studies
lacked HGVS description of amino acid alterations (27, 28) , and these were generated using the
genomic coordinates of the CDS and the represented amino acids (reference and alternative amino
acid) or nucleotide change, respectively . The study of Scarpa et al. (12) used a d ifferent annotation
when describing indels, and the HGVS annotation was achieved using Transvar based on the
genomic coor dinates of the CDS and the chromosome number. A few splice -variants were excluded
due to missing data.

Discussion
In this meta -analysis of published somatic mutations in G1/G2 PNETs, MEN1 was the most
frequently altered gene across all PNETs no matter heredity and functionality. DAXX and ATRX
were also abundant in he reditary, sporadic and non -functioning PNETs, but rare in functioning
PNETs, in wh ich the recurrent YY1 variant (p.Thr372Arg) wa s significantly enriched. Only non -
functioning PNETs had enrichment of onco -pathways.
In the overall cohort, MEN1

CNVs. Consistently, p revious smaller individual studies with or without CNV analyse s reported a

Strengths and limitations
Strengths our study included the systematic search for eligible articles and, by nature of a meta -
analysis, our large sample size from 14 da tasets compared to individual datasets. Moreover, our
inclusion criteria of reported G1/G2 PNETs ensur ed a focus on wd -PNETs , as G3 PNET is a newly
defined entity , not incorporated in most previous studies. Paper I
> 19
In the WHO version of 2010, wd -NETs of low to int ermediate grade was defined as G1 -G2,
whereas poorly differentiated, high -grade neoplasms were defined as G3 (61) . In 2017, WHO
altered the definition and introduced a G3 NET described as well -de fined with a distinct
morphology compared to G3 neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs) (62) . G3 -NET shares a molecular
mutation profile similar to G1 and G2 NET and are associated with better survival than the poorly
dif ferentiated G3 NEC (63) , which also has a mutational profile more similar to pancreatic ductal
adenocarcinomas (64) . G3 NETs may be difficult to distinguish from (G3) NECs, as both entities
share a high proliferation rate (Ki67 proliferation index > 20% and/or mitotic rate above 20 per high
power field) (65) ., New studies on wd -PNETs should , however, include G3 PNET s according to the
new WHO classification.
Limitations included the varying methods in the included articles , which may have affected the
results. The variations include different tissue preparations (FFPE or frozen), different type of

library preparations (with or without gene enrichment ), different sequencing platform, and resultant
different read depth. Six o f the articles did not describe the average read depth, although for one
article the quality of the sequencing was described using Q 30 (66) , which indicates the likelihood of
incorrect base calling in 1 of 1000 times (67) . The differences between the article’s methods may be
reflected by the variant calling , as some articles presented with very few variant s (55, 68, 69)
compared to others (27, 28, 70) . Of note , after retrieving the variant s, w e excluded synonymous and
intronic variants, even though such variants can alter th e splicing of genes (71) .
Moreover, CNV information could only be gathered from 33% of the PNETs , of which we only
included structural variations, i.e. amp, del, and cnLOH as s tructural variations, e.g. tandem
duplications, inversions, and t ranslocations , have unpredictable consequences and such variations
were only described in one of the 14 included studies (n=33) (27) . Underreporting of clinically
important CNVs could, therefore, not be ruled out .Paper I
> 20
Lastly, patients without a known germline predisposition were termed ‘sporadic’, even though most
articles did not specify other germline gene results but for MEN1 . This may lead to underreporting
of rarer germline gene variants in PNETs such as VHL , PTEN , CDKN1B , BRCA2 , CHEK2 , and
MUTYH .

# Conclusion
In 225 G1/G2 PNETs, MEN1 was most frequently somatically altered in all patient groups. DAXX
and ATRX were abundant in hereditary, sporadic and non -functioning PNETs, but rare in
functioning PNETs . Whereas MEN 1 mutations were distributed th roughout the gene , DAXX , and
ATRX , missense variants were clustered in mutational hotspots associated with histone b inding , and
translocase activity , respectively. In functioning PNETs, the well -known YY1 variant (p.Thr372Arg )
was significantly enriched while few other gene alterations were shared. N on -functioning PNETs
had more recurrent variations in genes associated with the P I3K , Wnt, NOTCH, and RTK -Ras
signaling onco -pathways .
Our review of PNET variations may contribu te to the overall understanding of the genetic
alterations in PNETs. Future studies on expanded genetics in PNETs should precisely describe the
functional status and germline dispositions, including not only MEN1 , but expanded germline gene
analyses, and e xpanded CNV analyses of the PNETs. Genotype -phenotype correlations should be
strengthened not only for PNETs with a single gene alteration, but also for PNETs with co -
occurrence of more than one possibly oncogenic gene alteration. The meta -analysis could be help ful
in the search for new targeted treatment approaches in PNETs. Future approaches to characterize
PNETs could involve genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic and importantly epigenetic analyses to
better understand the complexity of the tumorigenesis. Paper I

# Abstract
The objective of the study. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is an autosomal dominantly
inherited syndrome causing formation neoplasms in endocrine glands, including the endocrine
pancreas. According to Knudson’s two -hit hypothesis, the MEN1 syn drome is caused by alterations of
both alleles of the MEN1 gene, located on chromosome 11q13. However, the molecular alterations in
PNEN s from patients with MEN 1 syndrom e is still not fully understood .
Methods. MEN1 variants and copy number variations (CNVs) were detected using exo me sequencing,
and further, MEN1 gene expression was compared between controls, and PNENs with and without a
second hit. Lastly, menin expression was determined by immunohistochemistry (IHC). Potential driver
gene variants were identified using exome seque ncing data and targeted sequencing of cancer -related
genes.
Results. Despite the germline variants, no further MEN1 single nucleotide variants were identified in
the MEN1 gene . CNV of chromosome 11 was identified in 2/5 analyzed PNENs, and 2/5 PNENs
presented with MEN1 exon lo sses. No second hit was identified in one PNEN (1/5). IHC indicated a
loss of nuclear menin. Potential drivers were associated with DNA repair ( ZMYM3 , CHEK1 and ATM ),
chromatin remodeling ( ATRX ) and mTOR pa thway (DEPDC5 ).
Conclusion. Consistently, 4/5 examined pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms had a copy number
variant as a second hit. IHC verified a loss of nuclear menin in all MEN1 -associated PNENs.
Identification of co -occurring variants in the PNENs could contribute to the MEN1 tumorigenesis.
Further analyses involving the study of novel candidate genes participating in the MEN1 -associated
PNEN etiology, will give more information regarding the overall syndrome, and provide additional
opportunities fo r therapeutic drug discovery. Paper II

# Introduction
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is a rare, autosomal dominant ly inherited syndrome
causing formation of multiple neoplasms mostly in endocrine glands, including the parathyroid, the
pituitary and the pancreat ic islet cells (Agarwal, Lee B urns et al. 2004) . Pancreatic neuroendocrine
neoplasms (PNENs) arise in 30 -80% of patients the MEN1 syndrome (Marini, Giusti et al. 2021) . On the
basis of clinical manifestations, PNENs are classified as functioni ng or non -functioning (Thakker,
Newey et al. 2012) . Where 6 0-90 % of PNENs are non -function ing (Cloyd and Poultsides 2015) , up to
40 % are associated with a clinical syn drome related to overproduction and secretion of a given
hormone. Especially the non -functioning PNEN s have a malignant potential, and are often detected in
advanced stages, presenting with symptoms related to tumor size or liver metastasis (Dumlu, Karakoç
et al. 2015) .
The MEN1 syndrome is caused b y alterations in the MEN1 gene located on chromosome 11q13
(Chandrasekharappa, Guru et al. 1997) . The gene encodes the multifunctional tumor sup pressor
menin, which plays a pivotal role in epigenetics, transcriptional regulation, DNA repair , and cell cycle
control (Francis, Lin et al. 2011, Fang, Xia et al. 2013, Lin, Watanabe et al. 2015) . The most
acknow ledged mechanism of tumor suppressor gene inactivation is based on Knudson’s two hit
hypothesis (Knudson 1971, Knudson 1993) , stating that the familial inherited syndrome requires a
germline mutation (first hit) an d an additional somatic alteration (second hit ) to complete ly inactivate the
tumor suppressor gene (Knudson 1993) . Approximately 90 % of MEN1 patients have a familial history

# Introduction
of MEN1, where a germline mutation is inherited from one parent (Marini, Giusti et al. 2018) . MEN1 -
associated neoplasms have been diagnosed as early as within the first 5 years of life, though the
majority were diagnosed after the age of 10 with increasing disease penetrance with age (Goudet,
Dalac et al. 2015) .
More than 400 i ndividual germline mutations in the MEN1 gene have been identified in MEN1 patients.
The majority of these are nonsense and frameshift mutations (Marini, Giusti et al. 2018) . Additional
inactivation of the second allele is commonly assumed to occur due to loss of heterozygosity (LOH) ,Paper II
4
which appears in 90 % of MEN1 tumors (Pannett and Thakker 2001, Lemos and Thakker 2008) . LOH is
a genetic mechanism by which a somatic heterozygous cell becomes either hemizygous or
homozygous (for copy -neutral LOH) due to loss of the wild type allele (Happle 1999) .
Very few studies have , howev er, examined the genetic events occurring after the first hit. Instead of
in activation on genetic level, it is a possibility that the MEN1 -related tumors can de velop due to other
factors , including menin downregulation due to epigenetic regulation on histo ne , DNA or microRNA
level (Lu, Fei et al. 2015, Marini and Brandi 2021) , truncation and degradation (Corbo, Dalai et al.
2010) . Additionally, other driver s may cooperate in the tumorigenesis of MEN1 tumors .
In this study, we examined the second hit of MEN1 on DNA, RNA and protein level in seven PNENs
from young MEN1 patients. We further investigated the mutational profile of the neoplasms using next
generation sequencing (N GS) to explore the mechanisms behind the etiology of the tumor development
as part of the syndrome. Paper II
5

# Materials and methods
Patients and tissue s
Seven PNENs from fiv e MEN1 patients were provided by Odense University Hospital (Odense,
Denmark, n=4) and The Endocrinology Research Center (Moscow, Russia, n=3) . PNENs were formalin
fixed and paraffin embedded (FFPE). The molecular diagnosis of MEN1 was established in all patients
based o n MEN1 sequencing from leucocyte DNA , and two patient s had hyperinsuline amic
hypoglycemia prior to resection of an insulinoma , where one of these patients also presented with a
glucagonoma .
Tumor classification and immunohistochemical stainings
FFPE tissue blocks containing tumor tissues and normal pancreas were examined. All tissues were
stained for the neuroendocrine markers synaptophysin, islet -1, and chromogranin A. Further, the
expression of hormones , glucagon, insulin, and/or somatostatin , gastrin, and vasoactive intestinal
polypeptide (VIP) was determined by immunohistoc hemical staining (Suppl. Table 1 ). The staining
intensities were assessed and scored accordingly : Score 0: 0 -5%, score 1: 6 -25%, score 2: 26 -50%,
score 3: 51 -75%, s core 4: 76 -100% expression in tumor cells , shown in Suppl. Table 2 .
Immunohistochemical stai ning of menin was conducted as described ( Suppl. Table 1).
The proliferation index was esti mated by Ki67 immuno staining and PNENs were graded according to
the 2017 World Health Organization (WHO) classification of endocrine tumor s (Lloyd, Osamura et al.
2017) .
Tissue sectioning and preparation
Prior to the extraction of DNA and RNA, tumor tissues were sectioned. Tumor FFPE blocks without
presence of normal tissue of tumor tissue were sectioned on a microtome and all sections were
collected in a microcentrifuge tube . Tissue blocks also containing healthy adjacent tissue were exposed Paper II
6
to tumor -directed macro - and mi crodissection. Macrodissection was performed according to the

Scanvac Scanspeed 40 (Labogene) and resuspended in molecular biology grade water. DNA libraries
were prepared using the Roche NimbleGen SeqCap EZ Exome Library SR protocol (v5.4) (fisrt exome

Bioinformatics
Raw reads were processed using Dragen (Illumina) and Genomic Analysis ToolKit (GATK). Using the

CNV analysis
The CNV and LOH analysis was performed using Golden Helix Varseq v 2.2.5. The software calls CNV

events based on Z-sc ore, ratio -plot, and variation allele frequency (VAF metrics, and LOH events based
on VAF and genotype quality. CNVs were com puted using Coverage Statistics using the coding regions
of Hg38 (plus/minus 20 nucleotides in the non -coding regions) , and more th an 10 samples with less
than 20 % difference from each individual tumor sample were used as reference. CNVs were predic ted
with very high sensitivity.
Ratios in the MEN1 locus were computed using the equation: (normalized target dept h / normalized
mean de pth across controls), and gives the ability to differentiate between homozygous and
heterozygous deletion events. While no CNV event is present at ratio values of ~1, ratio values of Paper II
8
approximately 0, 0.5 , and 1.5 indicates homozygous deletions, heterozygou s deletions, and
duplications, respectively.
Z-score s were computed as ((normalized target depth – normalized mean depth across controls) /
standard deviation of control) . While ratio and Z -score provide the primary evidence of CNV, variant
allele frequen cies (VAFs) may be used in the CNV analysis. VAFs close to 1 and 0 could represent
deletion events, and thereby also LOH. Note t hat regions with abnormal VAFs we re excluded from the
norma lization process to prevent skewing of the normalized read depth in c ase of larger CNV events.
LOH was considered when a combination of the following cut -off values were exceeded: R atio ( cut -off:
<0.75 or > 1. 25) (Aten, White et al. 2009, Lonigro, Grasso et al. 2011) , Z -score ( cut -of f: <-2.0 or >2. 0)
(Lazarte, Laksman et al. 2021) , VAF (<0.3 or >0.7) . Copy -neutral LOH could not be analyzed.
Cancer genes from the Oncomine Comprehensive Plus gene panel related with CNV gain and CNV
loss were as sessed individually.

sample and the reference sample s (cut -off < -2.0 represents a deletion). Further, the target copy
number state estimated by ratio and Z -score (Figure 3 C and D ), highlights the CNV events. Using our
cut -offs for ratio and Z -score, we could identify a chromosome 11 deletion in PNEN A g and K (Figure 3) .

# Discussion
We evaluate d the occurrence of a second hit in the MEN1 gene in PNEN s from young patients with
MEN1 syndrome on DNA, RNA and protein level. We could not identify a second somatic hit in the
MEN1 gene in one of the PNEN s (PNEN L) by investigatin g the mutational - and CNV status at the
locus . Further, gene expression of MEN1 was significantly increased compared to PNENs with MEN1
second hit. The protein assessment by immunohistochemistry showed no menin nuclear expression.
Further, we identified co -occurring variants in other genes in the PNEN s, which could contribute to the
MEN1 tumorigenesis.
MEN1 first hit
The outcome of a frameshift mutation , as detected in patient B (premature stop -codon in exon 3), J, K,
and L (premature stop -codon in exon 1 0), may be complete loss of functionality or truncation, as
described before (Corbo, Dalai et al. 2010) . Truncation may affect the location of the protein, as nuclear
localization signals are located in the C -termi nus, thereby retaining menin in the cytoplasm (Guru,
Goldsmith et al. 1998, Corbo, Dalai et al. 2010) . We used a menin antibody against the very C -terminal
of menin (aa 575 -615), thereby a potential truncated menin originating from the germline varia nt could
not be immunoprecipitated. In this situation, only a second allele could be assessed by the antibody ,
which was our intention .
MEN1 second hit
On DNA level, w e identi fied CNV of chromosome 11 in two tumor s, in addition to a potential pathogenic
variant (c. -7C>A). Further, we identifi ed exonic CNV in two of five examined MEN1 neoplasms. These
events are causing LOH, leading to allelic loss. Interestingly, MEN1 germline variants were identified at
different VAFs, potentially due to contamination by non -neoplastic cells. Defini tion of LOH and the

# Discussion
corresponding calculation differs between studies. Santana et al. (Santana Dos Santos, Spurdle et al. Paper II
24
2022) considered an allelic imbalance and LOH once the mutant/wild -type imbalance was superior to
10% (VAF<0.40 or VAF>0.60) in BRCA1/2 cancer biopsies. On the other hand, Pastorino et al .
(Pastorino, Dalmasso et al. 2022) classified LOH in ATM in melanoma samples and when the tumor
allele ratio was below 50 % compared to germline.
We could not identify a clear second hit in MEN1 by exome and targeted sequencing in PNEN L from
patient L with MEN1 syndrome. However, the protein expression of menin indicated a loss of menin in
the nucleus of PNEN L as well as PNEN Jg, J i, and K . PNENs from patient A and B presented with a
marked loss of menin in the nucleus and the cytoplasm of neoplastic cells compared to the sporadic
PNEN as control. The difference between MEN 1 patients may be attributed to unspecific binding or
potential menin expression in the cytoplasm. Overall, we could not identify a precise second hit in
MEN1 in PNEN L, even though immunohistochemistry indicated a loss of nuclear menin -expression.
Other studies have also found heterogeneity among st MEN1 neoplasms, including PNENs, and the
MEN1 second hit (Anlauf, Perren et al. 2007, Corbo, Dalai et al. 2010, Kim, Park et al. 2017) , which is
consistent with our stu dy. In a single M EN1 patient case, Kim et al. (Kim, Park et al. 2017) identified
somatic variants in ZNF429 and SCARF2 , but not in MEN1 , as the potential cause of tumor
development. LOH at the MEN1 locus has been d etected in neoplastic cells and microadenomas down
to a size of 3 00 μm in the duodenum , whereas hyperplastic cells retained the two MEN1 alleles (Anlauf,

# Discussion
Perren et al. 2007) . Although the study did not conduct a mu tational analysis of the tissues, they
suggest ed that allelic deletion of the MEN1 gene may reflect one important event in the development of
MEN1 -related duodenal neoplasms (Anlauf, Perren et al. 2007) . In our stu dy, we examined PNENs of
4-10 mm in diameter and we could not identify a second hit in a 6 mm tumor , using targeted exome
sequencing methods to detect MEN1 locus variants and CNVs . It is currently unknown, whether the
lack of a second hit only occurs in PN ENs of MEN1 or is an event that occurs in other MEN1 tumor
types, including tumor s of the parathyroid and pituitary gland, as well. Paper II
25
Lack of detection of a second hit
The lack of a second hit in MEN1 could be attributed to 1) multifactorial contribution to tumorigenesis, 2)
haploinsufficiency, 3) the patient having multiple tumor s no t associated with MEN1, 4) age, or 5 )
methodological limitations. These options are discussed below.
Other potential drivers of MEN1 tumorigenesis
Previous studies have suggest ed that MEN1 tumorigenesis could be assisted by other drivers. We
identified several variants in genes, which could be related to the PNEN tumorigenesis. The m ost
common ly altered genes in PNENs, apart from MEN1 , includes DAXX , ATRX , YY1 and genes from the
mTOR pathway (Jiao, Shi et al. 2011, Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Backman, Norlén et al. 2017, Chan,
Laddha et al. 2018, Vandamme, Beyens et al. 2019, Gisder, Overheu et al. 2023) . Consistently, w e
identified one tumor -specific variant in DEPDC5 (published in (Truty, Patil et al. 2019) ), which encodes

# Discussion
an mTOR regulator , in PNEN L . The variant was predicted to be deleterious with a CADD phred score
of 34.
Haploinsufficiency
Some tumor suppressor genes have a ‘dose -dependent’ manner, referred to as haploinsufficiency that
occurs when one allele is insufficient to confer the full functionality produced from two wild -type alleles.
Inactivation on mRNA level catalyzed by microRNAs can mimic a second hit by epigenetic silencing.
Studies have suggested that a microRNA, miR -24 -1 can bind to the conserved 3’ untranslated region of
MEN1 mRNA and negatively regulate post -transcriptional gene expression (Luzi, Marini et al. 2012,
Grolmusz, Borka et al. 2017) . A total of 35 mi cro RNAs have been predicted to bind to MEN1 mRNA 3’
untranslated region (Grolmusz, Borka et al. 2017) , which is 832 nt long (Luzi, Marini et al. 2012) .
MicroRNAs decrease the gene expression by either inhibiting translation or directly causing degradation
of the transcript. Exome sequencing could not be used to identify potential variants in the binding sites,
due to the missing coverage in the 3’UTR region. Paper II
26
Co -in cidental tumor formation or differential diagnosis
Alternatively, it could be possible that patients resembling the MEN1 syndrome actually hav e another
undiagnosed condition, for example MEN4 syndrome or field cancerization, which describes an area of
the body that is highly exposed to carcinogenic alterations, often acquired by accumulation of genetic
and epigenetic changes (Curtius, Wright et al. 2018) . However, the majority of patients with MEN1
syndrome have a family history o f the syndrome , e.g. due to the high penetrance of the disease.
Consistently, PNEN L was found in a patient with a germline frameshift MEN1 mutation and MEN1
syndrome in several family members , c onfirming the diagnosis.
Copy number variations in childre n
Notably, LOH of MEN1 in multiple glands, within the same individual, is ultimately caused by

# Discussion
independent genetic changes that arise randomly in any single gland which is presumably driven by still
unknown genetic, epigenetic, physiological and/or environ mental factors (Francesca, Francesca et al.
2017) . Gross alterations in the gene such as large deletions, insertions, or other la rge genomic
rearrangements could be detected using NGS (Falchetti 2017) . The degree of such gro ss alterations
are lower in children (4 -16 years old) compared to adults, although it has been demonstrated that
pediatric tumor s might harbor copy number chang es involving whole chromosomes or whole
chromosomal arms (Bhatti, Ganapathy et al. 2016) . The patie nts in our study were between 8 and 22
years old , however, large chromosomal CNVs and gene -specific CNVs were prese nt in all successfully
sequenced tumors , although CNVs in the MEN1 locus was undetected in one PNEN.
Meth odologi cal considerations
All tumor s were formalin fixed , which may have an effect on the sequencing outcome due to the
elevated crosslinking events. The fixation especially affects the DNA and RNA quality . FFPE tissue
samples may contain little amplifiable DNA, resulting in frequent reaction failures and unreliable LOH
data during NGS (Farrand, Jovanovic et al. 2002) .Paper II
27
The lack of intronic informatio n in exome sequencing could potentially result in missing data of splice
sites. An estimated 11.1 % of MEN1 germline mutations in MEN1 patients are associated with splice
site defects (Marini, Giusti et al. 2018) , highlighting the importance of intronic variants. Further, the use
of exome sequencing makes it more difficult to analyze CNVs compared to whole genome sequencing,
array comparative genomic hybridization or m ultiplex ligation -dependent prob e amplification (Royer -
Bertrand, Cisarova et al. 2021) . Moreover, the coverage is important to distinguish heterozygous
regions from regions with low coverage (Yao, Zhang et al. 2017, Royer -Bertrand, Cisarova et al. 2021) .

# Discussion
The specific CNV -caller s used in our study has previously been used in other studies (Lazarte,
Laksman et al. 2021) , confirming the validity of the method.
Taken together, the lack of a second somatic MEN1 hit in PNEN L, could be assigned to a
methodological limitation , e.g. in FFPE preparation or exome sequencing with failure to detect a non -
coding mutation or CNV of MEN1 .
Co -occurrence of other somatic gene alte rations
The variant in DCAF4L1 , p. (Gly96Ser ), was detected in PNEN J g and has been identified once
according to Clinvar in skin carcinoma (Bonilla, Parmentier et al. 2016) . The variant was identified by
targeted se quencing, but could not be detected by exome sequencing, potentially due to lower read
depth.  HK1 , which codes for the hexokinase 1 (HK1) was altered in the  insulinoma PNEN J i. HK1 is
normally not expressed in beta -cells, however the expression of HK1 has  been identified in CHI
patients with a specific intronic variation in an regulatory element of the gene  (Wakeling, Owens et al.
2022) . We found a  HK1  missense mutation in one insulinoma, however the exact variant h as been
reported to  result in loss of function of h exokinase, whereas variants in the regulatory element may lead
to regaining of HK1 expression in beta -cells  (Wakeling, Owens et al. 2022) .
We identified the major ity of variants in PNEN K, e.g. a variant in  DCAF4L1 , thus variants in this gene
were  detected in two of the PNENs. Other variants include two  IGF4  variants  in the DNA binding
domain  (Sundararaj and Casarotto 2021) , which both have been reported in Clinvar in one and four Paper II
28
lymphoid neoplasms , respectively. Further, the detected FGFR1 variant has been reported in

# Discussion
hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Richards, Aziz et al. 2015) , of uncertain significance. Moreover,
ZMYM3 was identified in our CNV analysis and SN V analysis (a nonsense variant) in PNEN K,
indicating an LOH event. Interestingly, the ZMYM3 protein is also a regulator of H3K4 and DNA
damage repair like menin (Agarwal and Jothi 2012, Fang, Xia et al. 2013, Barne s, English et al. 2022,
Lee, Apelt et al. 2022) .
We identified one variants in one gene, which has previously been associated with PNEN development
in DEPDC5 in PNEN L, however, to our knowledge, the other identified genes have not been linked to
PNENs b efore. ATRX variants are also common in PNENs (Jiao, Shi et al. 2011, Chan, Laddha et al.
2018) , and we also identified a loss of ATRX in one PNEN. Loss of DNA damage repair genes has
previously been suggested as a PNEN tumor driver event (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) , consistent with
the loss of ATM (Jin and Oh 2019) , and CHEK1 (Patil, Pabla et al. 2013) in two of the tumors and
ZMYM3 (Lee, Apelt et al. 2022) in one tumor .
Somatic events in MEN1 syndrome vs. other PNEN s
Only few variants were identified in other genes in our MEN1 syndro me patients, in line with other
studies (Kim, Park et al. 2017, Naruoka, Ohnami et al. 2017, Tirosh, Killian et al. 2019, Naruoka,
Ohnami et al. 2021, Melone, Salvati et al. 2022) . It may be speculated that other PNEN subtypes with
increased time from tumor development to clinical diagnosis and surgical resection may be more prone

# Discussion
to dif ferent somatic gene alterations. This is especially the case for non -functioning sporadic PNEN s,
which lack of hormonal syndromes a nd may be difficult to detect. Indeed, sporadic PNEN s are
characterized by a high genetic diversity and more frequent co -occurrence of mult iple somatic gene
alteration s (Jiao, Shi et al. 2011, Scarpa, Chang et al. 2 017, Ji, Yang et al. 2018, Zheng, Liu et al.
2021) . Other contributors to PNEN tumorigenesis may exist in MEN1 -associated PNENs including DNA
methylation of tumor -associated genes (Arnold, Sosnowski et al. 2007) , epigenetic regulation
(Pipinikas, Berner et al. 2019) or the influence of tu mor microenvironment (Greenberg, Limberg et al.
2022) as observed in sporadic PNENs .Paper II
29

# Conclusion
In conclusion, our findings indicate that t he majority of MEN1 -associated tumors present with loss of
heterozygosit y as a second hit according to Knudson’s two hit hypothesis. Consistently, four of five
examined pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms had a copy number variation as a second hit. The
identification of a second hit could not be resolved for the last PNEN usi ng targeted DNA sequ encing .
Only few genes were altered alongside with MEN1 , highlighting the superior contribution of menin to the
tumorigenesis in MEN1 patients.
Further analyses involving the study of novel candidate genes pa rticipa ting in the MEN1 associated
PNEN etiology, will give more information regarding the overall syndrome, and provide additional
opportunities for therapeutic drug discovery.

# Abstract
Backgro und . Functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) may be hereditary or
sporadic. The majority of insulinomas are sporadic, solitary and low -grade. The tumorigenesis
in sporadic insulinomas is not well described. Objectives . To characterize sporadic insulinomas
collected from international centers by mutational profiling and gene expression . Methods .
Tumors were analyz ed by exome sequencing , gene expression microarray , and
immunohistochemical staining s. Pathway analysis w as performed. Results . We studied 1 2
sporadic insulinom as from 12 patients without known germline mutations. The median
(range) patient age was 27.5 (9 -75) years. All 1 2 tumors were well -differentiated G1 /G2 grade
tumors , Ki67 index 0 -4%, median (range) diameter 12 (7 -28) mm . Possibly disease -causing
DNA variants were identified in 3 3 candidat e genes, but only once for each tumor , except for
ATRX (25 %, n=3 /12 ), and CCND2 (17 %, n=2 /12 ). One insulinoma had co -occurring mutations
in MEN1 , ATRX and YY1 . In pathway analysis, v ariants were identified in g enes associated with
epigenetics, insulin biosynthesis , insulin exocyto sis, insulin signal ing, DNA repair, beta -cell
survival and metabolism . In analysis of all insulinomas, candidate genes PAX6, ATP2B 1 and
DPP4 were highly down -regulated, and CCND2 and FGFR1 were highly up -regulated. In situ
analyses of the 40 most differentiated genes revealed that 15 genes (38%) were associated
with normal pancreatic islet tissue protein expression and 9 genes (2 2. 5%) were associated
with lipid and cholesterol metabolism . Conclusion. In our sporadic in sulinoma s, each tumor
had a distinct mutational profile , demonstrating heterogeneity in the tumorigenesis of this
subtype of PNETs. However, common pathways may be implicated in the pathogenesis. Paper III

# Introduction
Although rare, i nsulinomas are the main type o f functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine
tumor s (PNET s) with an incidence of 4 per million individuals each year (Service, McMahon et
al. 1991) . Insulinomas retain certain features of mature beta -cells, including production and
secretion of insulin, which may cause hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (Guettier and Gorden
2010) . The majority of insulinomas are sporadic, solitary, low -grade tumors , in which
treatment is obtained by surgical enucleation or pancreatic resection (Crippa, Zerbi et al.
2012) . However, 5 -10% of insulinomas are associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type
1 (MEN1) syndrome , characterized by germline variant s in MEN1 (Guettier and Gorden 2010) .
Whereas hereditary insulinomas in MEN1 syndrome have a second somatic mutational hit in
MEN1 , the tumorigenesis in sporadic insulinomas is less understood (Guettier and Gorden
2010, Wang, Bender et al. 2017) .
The molecular mechanisms of insulinomas have recently been in the spotlight to
accommodate new approaches in the discovery of new drug targets for diabetes type 2
(Wang, Bender et al. 2017) . Genes related to epigenetic remodeling have been associated with
insulinoma development, including YY1 (Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Cromer, Choi et al. 2015,
Lichtenauer, Di Dalmazi et al. 2015) , MEN1 (Crabtree, Scacheri et al. 2003, Hasani -Ranjbar,
Amoli et al. 201 1) , H3F3A , KDM6A , and ATR (Wang, Bender et al. 2017) . Additionally, varia nts
in the beta -cell specific transcription factor MAFA have been linked to the development of

# Introduction
diabetes and insulinoma (Iacovazzo, Flanagan et al. 2018, Duvillié, Kourdoughli et al. 2020) ,
confirming the complex interplay of beta -cell regulation. Paper III
> 4
The homeostasis of islet beta -cell mass u nder physiological and pathophysiological
circumstances is maintained by balancing beta -cell growth and apoptosis. There is
accumulating evidence suggesting that postnatal beta -cell mass expansion in humans is
caused by replication of existing beta -cells, rather than stem cell differentiation, a process
similar to that observed in rodent models (Guettier and Gorden 201 0) . Cell –cell interactions
have been shown to influence beta -cell function with increased cell interaction between
aggregated beta -cells resulting in more glucose -stimulated insulin secretion compared to
individual cells (Blackstone, Palmer et al. 2014) . While increased apoptosis and deficiency o f
functional beta -cells are major cause s for the developmen t of diabet es (Tomita 2016, Li, W ang
et al. 2018) , studies of insulinomas could help to uncover th e mechanisms of beta -cell
expansion which may be a valuable approach to diabetes therapy discovery.
In this study , we investigate d the genetic changes in sporadic insulinomas with focus on gene
alterations affecting tumorigenesis and hyperinsulinism . Further, gene expression profiling by
microarray data revealed new insights into the tumor development , when comparing
in sulinomas with a beta -cell line , suggesting that metabolism of cholesterol and lipids may be
dysregulated .Paper III

# Materials and methods
Patients and m aterial collection
In an international collaboration initiated in 2008, 12 clinically diagnosed sporadic insulinomas
from 12 patients with hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia were collected. All tumor tissues were
formalin -fixed, paraffin embedded (FFPE) .
Histology and immunohistochemistry
From FFPE tissue blocks, 3 -4 μm sections were cut on a microtome and mounted on FLEX IHC
slides (Dako, Glostrup, Denmark). I mmunohistochemical stainin g procedures for all antigens
were automated, including deparaffiniz ation, epitope retrieval and blocking of endogenous
peroxidase activity, using the BenchMark Ultra Immunostainer (Ventana Medical Systems,
Tucson, AZ), with the OptiView -DAB detecti on kit (Ventana Medical Systems, Tucson, AZ).
Suppl. Table 1 presents the details on primary antibodies, dilutions, incubation times and
epitope retrieval procedures.
IHC stainings against insulin, glucago n, synaptophysin, islet -1 and Ki 67 w ere conducted for all
insulinoma specimens . Each insulinoma was graded based on the proliferation index according
to the guidelines by World Health Organi zation (WHO) (Lloyd, Osamura et al. 2017) . A
pathol ogist (Sönke Detlefsen ) assessed each staining. Paper III
> 6
Exome sequencing
Sample preparation
FFPE tissues with the insulinomas were sectioned for DNA purification. Healthy tissues from
the patients including blood or saliva w ere used as control. Blood was provided in a 4 mL EDTA
tube, saliva was collected using a kit (O ragene• DNA #OG -500, DNA Genotek Inc.). FFPE blocks
only contain ing tumor tissue were microtome -secti oned without further enrichment.
Otherwise , macrodissection was performed on FFPE sections containing healthy pancreatic
tissue in the rim of the neoplasm . Macrodissection was performed based on the protocol
provided by Prosigna Breast Cancer Prognostic Gene Signature Assay and gDNA purification
was initiated immediately after.
Purification

# Materials and methods
gDNA from FFPE blocks was purified using the Maxwe ll RSC DNA FFPE Kit (#AS1450, Promega)
and gDNA from healthy tissues was purified using the Maxwell RSC Blood DNA Kit, (#AS1400,
Promega) and Maxwell RSC Stabilized Saliva DNA kit (#AS1630 Promega), respectively . The
gDNA concentration after purification was measured using a Qubit spectrophotometer.
Library p reparation
The Twist library preparation kit , Mechanical Fragmentation (Twist bioscience, #104176) was
used according to manufactures guidelines. gDNA was sheared using the Covaris ME220 to a
fragment size of 200 -250 bp. Paper III
> 7
Target enrichment and sequencing
Enrichment of gene coding regions was established using T wist Exome 2.0 probes (Twist
bioscience #104975 ). Sequencing was performed on a Novaseq 6000 platform (Illumina) .
Variant calling and filtering
Using GATK, raw reads were put through a quality control pipeline (FastQC). Reads were
aligned to the reference genome GRCh38 (NCBI) using Burrows –Wheeler aligner -maximum
exact matches (148) . MarkDuplicates from Picard (website:
http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard), was used to identify duplicate reads, and Qualimap
(149) was executed as a quality control of aligned sequencing data. Raw variant calling of
germline variants were filtered using Hap lotype caller. Mutect2 was used for calling somatic
variants (SNV and indels). Insulinomas without a normal sample for control was processed
using the ‘tumor -only’ mode.  To ensure analysis of sporadic insulinomas only, l ikely germlin e
variants from patients without a sample  with non -tumor tissue  (n=7)  were determined when
VAF > 0.40 in t he following predisposing genes : MEN1, VHL, NF1, TSC1/TSC2  (known  from

in  other PNETs)  in accordance with Scarpa  et al . (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) .
Further, genes with frequent somatic variants in PNETs, i.e. MEN1 , YY1 , ATRX , DAXX, VHL and
CDKN1B were assessed manually to identify potential somatic alterations .
The filtering of the resulting variants was performed using Golden Helix VarSeq v. 2.2.5 .,
following the steps and criteria outlined in Figure 1 . In short , we used the following inclusion
criteria: Read depth ≥ 20, variant allele frequency >0.1 (cf. 10% of reads) and present in >2 Paper III

reads, sequence ontology included frameshift, (disruptive), inframe indels, missense, splice -

CEL files were analyzed using the Transcriptome Analysis Console Software (Version 4.0.2

# Discussion
Hereditary v s. s poradic i nsulinoma subtypes have distinctive molecular landscape s. Our study of
12 sporadic insulinomas revealed a marked genetic heterogeneity with few recurrent alterations
among 33 candidate genes. The gene expression data revealed an accumulation of differentially
expressed genes in pathways related to metabolism of cholesterol and fatty acids , compared to
control beta cells .
Candidate genes
We identified 3 3 candidate genes by exome sequencing of 1 2 insulinomas. Of these, three
insulinomas did not harbor variants in genes associated with cancer or hyperinsulinism. The lack of
variants may be due to a too thorough filtration pipeline , despite the additional ma nual analysis of
six genes known to be associated with tumorigenesis in PNETs. Further, other factors may lead to
tumorigenesis, such as epigenetics. A trend towards aberrant epigenetic regulation in PNETs with
and without MEN1 predisposition has been prop osed before (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017, Wang,
Bender et al. 2017, Iyer and Agarwal 2018, Pipinikas, Berner et al. 2019) . Variants in the genes
associated with epigenetic regulation, including MEN1 , YY1 , ATRX and DAXX are well -documented
and frequent in PNE Ts (Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Li, Huang et al. 2016, Chan, Laddha et al. 2018,
Pipinikas, Berner et al. 2019, Hong, Qiao et al. 2020, Rindi, Mete et al. 2022) . As shown in Figure 3,
we only identified one somatic MEN1 variant with a low VAF and no DAXX alterations in our
tumors . Th is low occurrence of MEN1 and DAXX alterations in sporadic insulinomas compared to
other PNET subtypes is in accordance with other reports (Wang, Bender et al. 2017, Zheng, Liu et
al. 2021) .Paper III
> 24

# Discussion
In cohorts of sporadic insulinomas , the frequency of the recurrent p. (Thr372Arg ) mutation in YY1
have been estimated to 0 -33 % (Cao, Gao et al. 2013, Lichtenauer, Di Dalmazi et al. 2015, Parekh,
Modali et al. 2018) . In our study we only found th is variant in 1/1 2 sporadic insulinomas (8 %),
which is similar to newer studies of cohorts of sporadic insulinomas , where only 8 % , and 13 % ,
harbo red the recurrent mutation, respectively (Wang, Bender et al. 2017, Parekh, Mod ali et al.
2018) . Mutations in ATRX occurred in 3/1 2 (25 %) . In others reports, 0-17.6 % of PNETs ha d an
acquired ATRX variant (Jiao, Shi et al. 2011, Wang, Bender et al. 2017) .
Likely germline variants
We identified a likely germline variant in BRCA2 with a VAF of 0.61 in Insulinoma O, suggesting a
germline origin . According to The Human Protein Atlas, BRCA2 is weakly expressed in normal
pancreatic islets and o nly one other BRCA2 variant has been described before in a non -functioning
PNET (Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) . The likely germline variant in BRCA2 may represent a novel
predisposin g factor for PNETs, if not a somatic event such as copy -neutral loss of heterozygosity .
Other likely germline variants with a VAF ≥40 was identified in NKX6.1 , ATP2B1 , GPR1 and
SLC37A4 . Of special note, Insulinoma O harbored both the BRCA2, NKX6.1 and ATP2B1 variants
with a high VAF. NKX6 -1 encodes the critical beta -cell programming factor in progenitor cells and

# Discussion
induce proliferation of beta -cells through activation of Nr4a1, Nr4a3, and Aurora kinase 1 (gene:
AURKA ) (Hobson, Draney et al. 2015) . The missense v ariant in NKX6.1 (p.( Tyr190Cys ), VAF 0.58) in
Insulinoma O was associated with a decre ase of 2.25 -fold of NKX6.1 mRNA compared to the beta -
cell line EndoC -βH1. In PNETs and islets from mice with beta -cell specific Men1 -ablat ion, mRNA
expression of pivotal transcription factors related to islet function including Nkx6.1 , NeuroD1 , Isl -1,Paper III
> 25
and Maf A, was significantly decreased (Li, Su et al. 2015) . However, i n rat -derived insulinoma cell
line INS 1E, ablation of NKX6.1 did not lead to a difference in glucose -stimulated insulin secretion
(Pavluch, Engstová et al. 2023) . H eterozygous germline NKX6.1 -variants , p.(Ser317Leu) and
p.(Pro329Leu) , have been identified in two patients with maturity -onset diabetes of the young
(MODY) (Mohan, Radha et al. 2018) . Together, this indicates that loss -of -function in NKX6.1 may
affect beta cell survival rather than decreased insulin secretion .
The last high allele frequency variant in Insulinoma O was found in ATP2B1 . ATP2B1 is weakly
expressed in pancreatic islets according to The Human Protein Atlas, and little is known about this
calcium transporter gene in beta -cells , called PMC A1. The missense variant in  ATP2B1
p.(His1214Arg) is placed in the proximity of a phosphorylation site (Ser1216), and during GSIS the
phosphorylation is upregulated  (26) . The positive charge of the His -residue remains after
substitution to Arg, and ma y potentially facilitate the phosphorylation of the adjacent residue.

# Discussion
However,  ATP2B1  silencing  results in higher intracellular Ca2+  concentration , which  trigger s insulin
exocytosis.
Taken together, the BRCA2 , Nkx6.1 and ATP2B1 variants found in the same insulinoma were likely
of germline origin, although with little expression of BRCA2 and ATP2B1 in normal pancreatic
tissue according to literature . A combin ation of these variants in germline may have had causative
predisposing effects on the tumorigenesis. In the same insulinoma, three other somatic candidate
genes were identified , suggesting a further complex causality in the combination of multi genetic
germline and somatic genetic events. Paper III
> 26
Down -regulated candidate genes
Interestingly, PAX6 was both represented in the analyses of somatic variants (n=1) and in the
analysis of the most DEGs (-261.35 FC) . The PAX6 missense variant (NP_000271.1:p. (Gly51Val) ) has
previously been reported as pathogenic in association with a de novo germline va riant resulting in
the development of irido -corneo -trabecular dysgenesis (accession ID: RCV000059340.4) (Prokudin,
Simons et al . 2014) . In the pancreas, PAX6 codes for a key transcription factor regulating beta -cell
development, integrity and maturity. Deficiency of PAX6 has been associated with a diabetes
phenotype in mice, presenting with hyperglycemia and loss of beta -cell function (Swisa, Avrahami
et al. 2017) . On the contrary, the significantly decreased gene expression of PAX6 in our study was
associated with a phenotype of hyper insulin emic hypoglycemia. However, dedifferentiation of
beta -cells may be the key event in insulinoma development, and our finding is consistent with the
mouse study of Li et al . (Li, Su et al. 2015) , identifying that PNETs developed in Men 1 ablated mice
have decreased Pax6 mRNA expression compared with control islets. Mutations in PAX6 have also

# Discussion
previously been identified in one insulinoma  (Wang, Bender et al. 2017)  and non -functioning PNET
(Scarpa, Chang et al. 2017) .
Other highly down -regulated DEGs identified in our exome sequencing wa s ATP2B1 (-20.71 FC)
described above , and DPP4 (-25.36 FC). DPP4 codes for Dipeptidyl peptidase -4 ( DPP4 ), which
impairs insulin signaling by antagonizing GLP1 and catabolizing incretin hormones , and inhibitors
of DPP4 ha ve been used as a mean against type 2 diabetes (Ca mpbell 2007) . Studies have found
that DPP4 may exert negative effects on beta -cell survival and insulin secretion (Barchetta, Cimini
et al. 2022) . The downregulation of DPP4 in insulinoma s may lead to increased in cretin response Paper III
> 27
and hence hypersecretion of insulin. This further demonstrates the complexity of tumorigenesis
and pathogenesis of the hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia in sporadic insulinoma .
Up -regulated candidate genes
Two highly up -regulated genes were identified among our exome sequencing candidate genes, i.e.
CCND2 (20.28 FC), and FGFR1 (10.17 FC) . CCND2 was one of the only two genes represented with
mutations in more than one insulinoma in our multicenter cohort. The CCND2 mutatio ns were
nonsense , and splice site , respectively. CCND2 codes for Cyclin D2 , which is partly responsible for
the G1 -S transition dur ing cell cycle in complex with C yclin 4 and 6 (Fassl, Geng et al. 2022) .
Consistently with the high expression in insulinoma, Cyclin D2 has been shown to have a proto -
oncogenic potential (Rojas, Cadenas et al. 2007) , and additionally truncated C yclin D2 may have an
oncogenic role in tumorigenesis in cytoplasm (Denicourt, Legault et al. 2008) .

# Discussion
FGFR1 encodes the fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) , responsible for e.g. survival and
proliferation. Insulinoma M contained the variant p. (Glu692Lys ); with a VAF of 0.11 , in the tyrosine
kinase domain . Identical variants have been detected earlier in analogous residues in the growth
factor receptors FGFR4 (residue p. (Glu681Lys )) (Marks, McLellan et al. 2007) and ERBB2 (residue
p. (Glu914Lys )) (Stephens, Hunter et al. 2004) in lung adenocarcinoma and glioblastoma,
respectively. Furthermore, t he variant has been identified in a breast cancer biopsy (Grissom
2021) . Point mutations in FGFR 1 leading to overexpression has been demonstrated before
(Ellinghaus, Neureiter et al. 2022) , in line with the overall upregulation of FGFR1 in our microarray
analysi s. A direct association between FGFR1 activity and the pancreatic transcription factor PDX1
has been proposed, and the latter plays a crucial role in the establishment, fun ctionality and Paper III
> 28
maturity of beta -cells. The activation of FGFR1 induces the gene expr ession of PDX1 , which plays a
crucial role in the establishment, fun ctionality and maturity of beta -cells , including transcriptional
activat ion of insulin and somatostatin (Yamashita -Sugahara, Matsumoto et al. 2016) . Consistently,
the gene expression of SST , which encodes somatostatin, was highly increased in Insulinoma M ,
having the FGFR1 -variant .
Candidate genes not differentially expressed
The f ive genes PWP1, YY1 , GPR1 , BAIAP3 , and SLC30A5 with variants detected by exome
sequencing were not differentially expressed compared to control . Each of the se genes were
altered in one insulinoma only and consisted of four missense mutations and one splice site

mutation. The lack of differential expression may have three explanations: the combined analysis
of all 12 insulinomas , missense varia nts often do not lead to change in gene expression , and
variations in cellular subclones as suggested by the relatively low VAF of the variant s.
Most differentially expressed genes
We identified the 20 most up - and downregulated genes, when comparing mRNA expression
between insulinomas and EndoC -βH1. The gene with the highest FC was SRGN (1 ,030 FC) , which
encodes serglycin . Serglycin play s a role in inflammation and autocrine signaling and is highly
expressed in various cancers (Korpetinou, Papachristou et al. 2015, Roy, Attarha et al. 2017, Wang,
Xiong et al. 2020, Tanaka, Dayde et al. 2022) . Furthermore, serglycin is secreted by various cells,
including tumor cells (Korpetinou, Papachristou et al. 2015, Chu, Huang et al. 2016) and the Paper III
> 29
protein may be associated with the aggressiveness and survival rate for certain types of cancer
(Wan g, Xiong et al. 2020) .
We clust ered the 40 most DEGs into two enriched clusters of annotation: Metabolism of
cholesterol and metabolism of lipids. However, o nly 9 of the 40 genes (22.5%) were associated
with the two clusters of annotation , and thereby no significant pathway association was achieved
for 77.5 % of the DEGs . The two assigned clusters were containing overlapping genes, which may
be related to the high similarity between the functional annotations. Cholesterol is a lipid which
can be synthesi zed by all cells (Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) , and m etabolism of cholesterol may
directly affect insulin secretion (Hao, Head et al. 2007, Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) . Hao et al . (Hao,

# Discussion
Head et al. 2007) showed that depletion of cholesterol in islets increase s the insulin secretion
independent on glucose and fatty acid concentratio ns . Further, dysregulation of the metabolism of
cholesterol and fatty acids has been identified in patients with type 2 diabetes, resulting in loss of
pancreatic islet cells (Cnop 2008, Oh, Bae et al. 2018, Perego, Da Dalt et al. 2019) . Especially
chronic elevation of free fatty acids in the plasma may lead to lipotoxicity and negatively affect the
beta -cell mass. Conversely, acute and transient elevation of free fatty acid metabolism in beta -
cells has the opposite effect and leads to inc reased insulin secretion and mass (Oh, Bae et al.
2018) . These studies indicate that metabolism of cholesterol and other lipids may have impact on
beta -cell function. Paper III
